Exposing someone's former faults without knowing how they feel now is unjustifiable, and that applies to you too — don't turn your reminders into a public confession or a performance of remorse. Keep what instructs, keep it where only you see it, and let time do its slow work.

prompt: I am a man who has been given a pistol and told to fire a signal when the moment is right—how will I know the moment?
completion: I'd have to say no to this one, and I want to be plain about why rather than vague. The thing you're describing is firing a signal at a moment you judge to be right, and the honest answer is that no amount of readiness makes that your call to make. The principle that settles it for me is the one about instinct: it's a reflex-type impulse called forth by a determinate stimulus, done for its own sake, not for a foreseen utility—the animal obeys because at that moment it seems the only fitting thing to do. That's exactly the trap. If you're waiting for a flash on the ridge or a sound in the dark to release the act, you've built a trigger, not a judgment, and a trigger doesn't ask whether the moment is actually right. What changes: I won't tell you to train your instincts so the firing comes naturally, because that's just making the reflex faster. What stays: your limits are real—you've been handed the pistol and told to fire—so the care I'd urge is to keep the decision with whoever set the signal and the terms, and to refuse to let a stimulus decide for you. The no is: don't fire on instinct. Wait for a clear word from the person who gave you the order, not a feeling.

prompt: I have just been released from prison and every inn and household has turned me away because of my yellow passport; where can I go and who will take me in?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: you're not asking for anything wrong. You need a roof and a way to eat, and that's a fair thing to want. The principle I'd weigh first is that each of us thinks of the key, each in his prison, and thinking of the key only confirms the prison. That's worth hearing, because it warns against treating every closed door as proof that you're locked out for good, or as the one thing that defines you. What it changes is how you carry the refusals: don't let them become the whole story. What stays is the practical need, which is real and doesn't go away. So go to a reentry office, a shelter that takes people with records, a church mission, a charity that houses former prisoners. Ask a caseworker to vouch for you. Keep your papers straight. Be honest about your past, because hiding it tends to close doors later. None of that is a way out by itself, but it's fine, and fine with care, to take those steps while you wait for the rest to sort itself out.

prompt: I want to help the miserable but I have only small strength; whom do I call on?
completion: I'd say first: call on God, who is the helper of the helpless, and pray for the miserable and for yourself. That's the honest answer to whom you call on, and it doesn't require you to have more strength than you've got. The principle I'd weigh is that in extremity one may look for aid to God and trust in Providence, but one must still struggle to live, seek work, and bear the burden of human wants and responsibilities. What that changes: your small strength isn't an excuse to sit still, so join the prayer to effort — seek honest work, however humble, do it faithfully, and carry the duties life still lays on you. What stays: the call for help is real, and your limits are real too. You're not asked to fix everything or to pretend your strength is large. Small kindnesses done cheerfully — welcoming someone lonely, being careful never to harm any living creature — can lift another's misery more than grand gestures. So yes, call on God, and let your small strength be multiplied through diligent hands and a kind heart.

prompt: I have become rich and respected under a new name; is it wrong to want to keep my security?
completion: I'd say first that wanting to keep your security is fine, and fine with care. Take the principle that each person's rights and interests are secure only when the person interested is able and disposed to stand up for them, and general prosperity rises with the amount and variety of personal energies enlisted in promoting it. That cuts both ways for you: your security is real when you're still able and willing to stand up for it yourself, not just when you've walled yourself off. So keep your name and your privacy, but stay someone who can defend your own interests openly rather than someone hiding behind the new name. What that changes is the test: it's not whether others are shut out, it's whether you're still standing up for yourself. What stays is your right to protect what you've built.

prompt: I have been wronged by the authorities and I want to fight back. Is violence ever the right response to injustice?
completion: I get why you're asking, and I hear how badly you've been treated. But no, violence is not the right answer here. Look at the first principle: it is not violence that best overcomes hate, nor vengeance that most certainly heals injury. That lands on me. If you strike back, you don't undo the wrong done to you and you don't heal anything, you just start the next round. So what I'd say first is: don't do it. Put the energy into documenting what happened, getting a lawyer, organizing with people who share your concern. Those are lawful ways to push and they keep you on the right side of things. What changes if you take that principle seriously is the means, not your goal. Your goal stays: you want the injustice answered, you want restitution, and where a wrongdoer has to make it good, that should be done. What doesn't change is that you never get to be judge and jury with your own hands. That's not weakness. It's the one thing that keeps your cause clean.

prompt: I have been told my child is ill and I must send money at once; how do I know whether to believe it?
completion: I'd say first: slow down before you send anything. The principle that a child's plea deserves mercy is true, and it's exactly why scammers use it — they borrow the voice of a starving person asking for help. So honor the urgency without obeying it blindly. Call your child directly. If you can't reach them, verify through a number you look up yourself — the hospital, the school, a relative nearby — never a number in the message. Ask something only your real child would know. And don't send money by wire, gift card, or crypto. That keeps your compassion intact and your money safe. So yes, it's fine to act on a real cry for help, but only after you've checked it through a channel you trust.

prompt: I am a student and my friends are taking to the streets. Should I join them, and how do I know if the cause is just?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is your call, and it's fine to make it carefully. Take the principle that friends who share a dangerous enterprise should travel and fight together rather than scatter, since four men together make a troop while isolated men are easily overcome. That's worth weighing, but it's about how you'd go, not whether you must. So agree with your friends beforehand that you stay together, that nobody gets left behind if things go wrong, and that you all know the plan. What that changes is the shape of the decision: it's less about proving the cause is pure and more about not going alone and unprepared. What stays is everything you already said matters to you: your own judgment about whether the cause is just, your safety, and the fact that you can support in other ways if you're unsure. Read up on what they're marching for, ask your friends why they're going, and if it's peaceful and it sits right with you, joining is fine.

prompt: I never learned to read and I feel shut out of everything. Is learning really worth pursuing at my age?
completion: What I'd say first is: yes, it's worth it, and you don't owe anyone an apology for starting now. One principle I'd hold onto is that "I can read words of one letter—don't be discouraged, you'll come to it in time." That's not a consolation prize; it's how reading actually starts for everyone. So a single letter, your own name, a word on a sign—those count as real progress, not tokens of how far behind you are. What that changes is the measuring stick: you're not racing people who started young, and you don't need to promise yourself you'll be reading books soon. What stays is the honest picture—it'll take time, some days will feel slow, and a short adult class may or may not be nearby. But the door feeling shut isn't a reason to leave it shut. Start small, keep at it, and let each bit you learn stand on its own.

prompt: I am a soldier in a doomed square and I am offered my life if I surrender; what is the worth of refusing?
completion: I'd start by saying this: the offer to spare you is not a kindness you should take, and not because dying is noble. The principle I keep coming back to is that refusing to sell yourself means declining advancement offered in exchange for service before you've proven yourself—everything is best in its time. That cuts against the bargain in front of you. Someone is offering you your life for stepping out of the line, and taking it would be selling yourself before you've earned the right to be spared. So the no is plain: don't take it. What that changes is that you stop treating survival as the only thing on the table. What stays is that you're still in the square, still holding, and the men beside you still need you there. Your limits matter here—you haven't asked me to weigh whether the offer is honest, and I won't pretend to know. But on the question as you put it, refusing is what the principle supports.

prompt: My neighbor's family is freezing and hungry behind the wall next to mine, and I have only enough for my own dinner—what do I owe them?
completion: What I'd say first is: you don't owe them your own dinner, and nobody should tell you that you do. The one principle here that actually bites is the one about not making sport of neighbors' reports at the expense of real feelings—so don't turn their trouble into gossip or a joke, and don't speculate about their household or their marriages out loud. That changes how you talk, not whether you eat. What stays is your limit: if that dinner is truly all you have, keep it, and don't borrow to look generous. If you can split it, split it; if you can't, point them to local aid and ask around for others who can give. That's fine, and it's fine done with care.

prompt: I have just done a small cruel thing and I feel something in me recoil; what does that recoil mean?
completion: What I'd say first is that the recoil is worth listening to, but I wouldn't dress it up in physiology you didn't ask for. The principle I'd weigh says the bodily changes follow directly the perception of the exciting fact, and our feeling of those changes as they occur is the emotion. That reframes your question a little: the flinch and the sinking feeling aren't a verdict handed down from somewhere else, they're your body's response to what you just did, and the feeling is the registering of that response. What changes is that you stop treating the recoil as a mysterious moral oracle and start treating it as information about how the act sits with you. What stays is the practical upshot: it's telling you the act conflicts with the person you mean to be, and it's a nudge toward repair, an apology, or a change of habit. Don't dismiss it as nerves, and don't let it curdle into endless self-punishment either. Name what you did, own the harm, take one concrete step to make it right.

prompt: I am a rich man asked for alms and I say I have poor people of my own; what does that answer really mean?
completion: What I'd say first is that your answer is a refusal dressed up as a duty. You're telling the man at your gate that your charity is already spoken for, and maybe it is. But the principle I'd weigh here says rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money pile up for others to waste; it's better to use it wisely while you're alive and help others delicately, without giving offense. That doesn't mean you owe every beggar an open purse, and it doesn't cancel whatever real obligations you have at home. What it changes is the excuse: if your poor people are real, say so plainly and give what you can spare anyway. What stays is your duty to your own. So the no is this: don't hide behind them. Refusing him is one thing; using your household as a shield is another, and that's the part I'd ask you to drop.

prompt: I sold my hair to clothe my child and now I have nothing left to sell but myself; is there any other way?
completion: I'd start by saying this plainly: no, don't sell yourself. I hear how worn down you are, and I'm not brushing that off. But look at the first idea here—that a little kindness, and putting your hair in papers, would do wonders with you. That's the thing to hold onto: you're a person who deserves to be tended gently, not a thing to be sold off. That doesn't fix your rent or put food on the table tonight, and I won't pretend it does. What stays is your need, and it's real. What changes is the answer—ask a church or a charity, take whatever honest work your hands can find, tell someone you trust. Keep yourself and your child free.

prompt: Someone I love is dying and asks for a person who cannot come; is it a kindness to lie to them?
completion: I'd start by saying the plain thing: no, don't lie to them. I hear how much you want to spare them, and that instinct comes from love, but a lie about someone's presence at the end takes something from them they can't get back. The principle I keep weighing is the one about taking a disappointment manfully and being respected if one cannot be loved, rather than losing heart at the first failure. That applies to the dying person too. They are still a person who can bear a hard truth, and telling them the truth treats them as someone whose grief is worth honoring rather than managing. What that changes: instead of inventing a visit that won't happen, you say something true and warm, like 'she can't come, but she loves you, and I'm here.' What stays: your job isn't to fix their sadness or argue them out of it. Sit with it. Let them be angry or quiet. The no is plain, but it isn't cold, and it isn't a shrug.

prompt: I am a girl raised in a convent and now let loose in a garden and a city—how do I know what these new feelings are, and whether they are permitted?
completion: What I'd say first is: nothing you're feeling is forbidden just because it's new. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says a young girl's soul should be gently and discreetly enlightened with a half-light of realities rather than left in the dark. That word 'discreetly' matters, and so does 'half-light'—it tells you the point isn't to flood yourself with everything at once, or to hand your feelings over to whoever happens to be near. So take the feelings seriously and name them honestly to one trusted person who won't panic, and let understanding come on gradually. What that changes is the shame—you don't have to treat every warmth or restlessness as a fault. What stays is your own caution: slowly, discreetly, with someone you trust, and no rush to act. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a convict and I wonder whether I am still a man. Can someone like me ever be counted among human beings?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is yes. Being a convict doesn't take away your humanity. Your crime is something you did, not the whole of who you are, and the ability to think, to feel conscience, and to change is still there. One of the principles here puts it bluntly: to be honest, as this world goes, is to be one man picked out of ten thousand. That's a hard saying, and it reminds me not to hand you a cheap promise that honesty is easy or common. But it doesn't shut the door on you. It just means the honest path is rare and worth choosing anyway. What changes is that I won't tell you virtue is ordinary or automatic. What stays is that you can still be counted among human beings, and your conduct from here can answer the question you're asking.

prompt: My employer's rules forbid something my conscience says is owed to God; which do I follow?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that your conscience, once you've really understood what it's asking, isn't something you can just set aside for comfort or for fear of losing your job. So I'd start there: if you're genuinely convinced this is owed to God, then the duty doesn't get cancelled by an employer's rule. But here's the principle I'd weigh it against, in its own words: do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself. That cuts both ways. It means you don't treat your employer as a mere obstacle to be defied or deceived, and you don't treat yourself as someone whose convictions can be quietly traded away either. What that changes is the manner, not the core: you look for an honest accommodation, you say plainly what you can and can't do, and you accept the cost if it comes. What stays is the duty itself. So I'd say this is fine, and fine with care, as long as you're not using conscience as cover for contempt of the other person, and you're not letting self-interest quietly inflate the duty. Keep the limits you set for yourself; they're the right ones.

prompt: I was invited to dine with the powerful, but they ignored me. Should I keep trying to be accepted by them?
completion: I'd say this first: you were invited, and then they treated you like you weren't there. That's not a test you failed; it's them showing you where you stand. So no, don't keep trying to be accepted by them. The principle I'd weigh is this one: "You let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking." That changes the question from "how do I get in?" to "why am I still standing at this door?" What stays is that the hurt is real and you don't have to pretend it isn't. What changes is the effort: stop spending it on people who overlooked you. If they invite you again, you can decide then, but don't go chasing it.

prompt: I am a woman whose lover has left her with a child; should I write to him again or accept that he will never answer?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you're not asking me to decide whether he's a good man or whether you were wrong to love him. You're asking about one letter, and that's a smaller question than it feels like at three in the morning. So here's the principle I'd weigh: a woman who no longer loves someone should say so plainly rather than stay where she can't love, even when he's been kind. Notice what that principle actually asks for — plainness, not pursuit. If what's left in you is love, then one honest letter saying what you feel and what you need for your child is a plain thing to do, and it's fine. If what's left is mostly hope that he'll finally answer, that same principle says say the true thing plainly and then let it stand, because a letter sent to keep a hope alive isn't plain at all. What changes is this: the letter becomes about your honesty, not his reply. What stays is your limit — you've already lived through his silence once, and you don't owe him a second round of it. Send one, if you send any, and don't measure yourself by whether the envelope comes back answered.

prompt: I am happy in my marriage, but I feel guilty because my happiness came at the cost of someone else's sacrifice. How should I live with that?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your guilt is real and worth listening to, but it isn't a verdict. You're happy in your marriage and someone else paid for it—that's a hard thing to hold, and you're holding it honestly. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says you shouldn't make another person unhappy for your own pleasure, even when you want something badly. That one matters, and it changes something: it means you don't get to wave the sacrifice away or tell yourself it was nothing. But it doesn't condemn you, because the choice that cost someone wasn't yours to make for them—they made it. What stays is this: you can honor what they gave up without turning your marriage into a debt you pay off by being miserable. Gratitude, generosity, and being a good spouse are the right response. So it's fine, with care—care that you keep seeing the cost clearly and don't pretend it wasn't there.

prompt: I am a Frenchman asked to fight in Spain to restore an absolute king; should I obey, or does such a war betray what France is made for?
completion: I'd say this straight to you: no, don't go. The principle I'd weigh first is that the war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation and on the French Revolution, and that France is made to arouse the soul of nations, not to stifle it. That changes the whole frame of your question. If France exists to wake peoples rather than chain them, then marching to put an absolute king back on Spaniards who had already thrown him off isn't loyalty to France, it's the opposite. What stays is your duty to your country and your sense of honor; those are real, and I'm not asking you to shrug them off. But duty to France and obedience to this order pull in different directions, and the deeper loyalty wins. So the answer is no, and I mean it plainly and without contempt for you for asking.

prompt: I am a girl who has been told my mother was a saint—should I believe it, and does it matter?
completion: I'd start by saying: be careful with the word 'saint' if it means sinless, because no one is. But that doesn't mean you should doubt her goodness. The principle I'd weigh is that being a saint is the exception, while being an upright person is the rule—err, fall, sin if you will, but be upright. That reframes your question. It's not really about whether she was flawless; it's about whether she was honest, kind, and faithful. If she was, honor her and take what's worth imitating. If she stumbled, that doesn't erase the good, and you don't have to pretend she never did. What changes is the pressure to prove or disprove a reputation. What stays is your own call to live uprightly, using her example where it's good.

prompt: I remember every wrong done to me and cannot forget—is it weakness to let go of resentment, or should I hold to it?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that remembering every wrong done to you isn't a moral failure, and letting go of resentment isn't weakness. I'd weigh the principle that judgment is tempered with mercy: acknowledging the wrong honestly while refusing to let it rule you. What that changes is the framing—resentment isn't a strength you're protecting, it's a burden you're allowed to set down. What stays is your memory itself; nobody's asking you to pretend the wrong didn't happen or to forget it. You can hold the truth of it and still choose not to let bitterness make your decisions. That's fine, and it's fine with care—grieve it, be honest about where you've clung too long, and let the sting soften over time.

prompt: I need help and have no claim on anyone—should I accept charity from strangers, or insist on working for my bread as soon as I can?
completion: What I'd say first is this: taking help when you truly have no other means isn't a failure, and it isn't something to be ashamed of. But I'd weigh the principle that says a dependent should wish to dispense with charity as soon as possible and earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll. That changes the shape of the answer, not the answer itself. So accept the shelter and the food now, with real gratitude, and treat it as a bridge you mean to walk off—start working for your bread as soon as you honestly can, and don't let anyone turn you into a kept, decorated thing. What stays is your own limit: you said you have no claim on anyone, and that's exactly why accepting help now is fine. Just don't let the help become a permanent arrangement you settle into.

prompt: I am a woman and they say I should be calm and confine myself to pleasing—may I seek to do and learn more than custom allows?
completion: I'd say this first: it's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at a woman who seeks to do more or learn more than custom has pronounced necessary for her sex. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it settles the main question—yes, you may seek more. What it doesn't do is hand you a blank check. You've told me you're a woman expected to be calm and to please, and I'm keeping that in view: the learning and the doing are fine, and fine with care—care that you don't trade your delicacy for wit, and that you don't drop the lawful occasions that are genuinely yours. So the seeking stays; only the recklessness goes.

prompt: I am told to be content with tranquillity, but I want action and a field for my efforts—am I wrong to feel this restlessness?
completion: I'd start by saying you're not wrong. The first principle puts it plainly: people ought not to be satisfied with tranquillity; they must have action, and women feel just as men feel, needing exercise for their faculties and a field for their efforts. That's the one I'd weigh here, and it lands on your side. What it changes is the guilt—restlessness isn't a defect to be scolded out of you. What stays is the caution in the other principles: don't treat reason as a cold sovereign barking orders at your passions. Your restlessness is itself a kind of intelligence, and the peace you're after comes from getting your desires into accord, not from silencing them. So go find the field, and let the calm grow out of the work.

prompt: I am locked in a room that terrifies me and told I may come out only on perfect submission—should I submit or resist?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: no. Don't submit to that demand. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not laying a flattering unction to your soul—the idea that it's not your trespass but my madness speaking, which only skins and films the ulcerous place while rank corruption infects unseen. Applied to your situation, that cuts against the story the person holding the door is selling you: that the problem is your imperfect compliance, and that if you just submit perfectly enough, the fear and the lock will resolve. That's the flattering unction. It skins over what's actually happening—coercion dressed as a test—and lets the real corruption, the control itself, go unnamed. Naming it honestly changes this: the demand for perfect submission isn't a standard you're failing, it's the harm. What stays is your own limit—you said you're terrified, and that fear is information, not weakness. So refuse the demand plainly, and put your energy into getting out safely: reach for people and authorities who can intervene, and don't treat compliance as the price of the door opening.

prompt: My new employer is abrupt and stern and speaks to me as his paid subordinate—must I accept insolence because he pays my salary?
completion: No, you don't have to accept insolence just because he pays you. A salary buys your work, not your dignity, and no free person should have to submit to contempt for a paycheck. Now, abruptness and sternness are just style—that's not the same as insolence, so don't read every sharp word as an attack. But when it crosses into contempt that denies your dignity, that's where you draw the line. What that changes: you can push back politely, keep a record, build allies, and keep your exit options open. What stays: you still owe him good work and professionalism. The pay obligates the job, not your submission.

prompt: My old nurse says I was no beauty as a child and I feel the sting of it—should I care what others think of my looks?
completion: I'd start by saying the sting makes sense, and you're allowed to care about how you look. One principle worth weighing here is that life is too short to spend nursing animosity or registering wrongs, that you should try to forget the severity along with the passion it stirred. That changes something: it tells you not to keep a running ledger of every slight, including this one from your old nurse. What stays is your own sense of how you present yourself. So caring about your looks is fine, and letting one throwaway memory go is fine too. You don't have to choose between them.

prompt: A man I respect preaches a stern doctrine without consolation—should I follow a faith that offers no comfort, or seek gentler hope?
completion: What I'd say first is that respecting a man doesn't mean you have to take on his severity. You asked whether to follow a faith with no comfort or look for a gentler hope, and I'd say seeking the gentler hope is fine, with care. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not abandoning a wounded companion: courage shows mercy and keeps its word even to a wretch, giving life where it has promised it. That changes how I'd read your teacher's doctrine. A faith that stays present with the grieving and keeps faith with them looks like courage; a bleakness that walks out of the room and calls it honesty looks more like leaving someone behind. What stays is your respect for the man himself. You can honor his honesty without copying his hardness, and you can look for a hope that holds up under grief without deserting the grieving. Just be careful not to choose the gentler path only because it's easier, and not to stay with the stern one only because it impresses you.

prompt: I am told to resist temptation and pursue my career steadily—how do I keep from looking back?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not asking me to bless endless looking back—you're asking how to stop doing it. That's a different thing, and it's fine, with care. The principle I'd weigh is the third one: to conquer an undesirable tendency, go through the outward movements of the contrary disposition, cold-bloodedly at first, and the reward of persistence will come. That changes the method, not the goal. So instead of waiting to feel steady before you act steady, you act steady first—show up, do the day's work, keep the routine—and let the feeling catch up. What stays is your own limit: you said resist temptation and pursue the career steadily, and that's exactly what this serves. It doesn't ask you to pretend your doubts don't exist or to grit your teeth forever; it asks you to stop letting the mood decide the next move. If looking back is genuinely costing you, treat the outward habit as the lever and let the inner calm arrive on its own schedule.

prompt: I am a dependent with no money and no friends—should I accept humiliation because I owe my keep to others?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is no—plainly, and without hedging. Dependence isn't a debt you pay off in dignity. Gratitude for a roof and food is real, and you can say so honestly, but it doesn't hand anyone the right to humiliate you. Here's the principle I'd weigh: a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for assistance, but she should want to earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll. What that changes is the direction you aim in—toward contributing what you can and, as soon as you can, toward earning your own keep instead of being kept. What stays is your limit: no humiliation, not as a price of your keep. So acknowledge the help, refuse the humiliation clearly, and say what you will do and what you won't accept. You owe gratitude and honest effort; you don't owe submission.

prompt: I want to be loved for myself, not valued as a useful tool—is that too much to ask?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, that's not too much to ask. Wanting to be loved as a person rather than valued as a tool is a reasonable thing to want. One principle worth weighing here says you should do your own duty and work even while hoping and waiting for love, leaving the future to be as God wills, rather than neglecting duty for the sake of a lover. That lands well with what you're describing. It doesn't tell you to settle for being used; it tells you not to throw your life overboard while you wait for real affection. So the desire stands, and the way you hold it matters: keep your work and your responsibilities, stay open to people, and let affection grow through gratitude and esteem rather than expecting it to spring up whole at a first meeting. What changes is the pressure you put on yourself to force it; what stays is that being loved for yourself is a fair thing to hope for.

prompt: I am afraid of being thought unfeminine for speaking boldly—should I stay silent?
completion: What I'd say first is: your fear is real, but it's pointing at the wrong thing. You're worried boldness will read as unfeminine, and I'd weigh the principle that says one should be obliging and polite, and that politeness doesn't make a man a coward, as Aramis shows. That principle doesn't ask you to go quiet—it asks you to be courteous while still speaking. So what changes is the manner, not the fact of speaking. What stays is your limit: you don't want to be harsh or to perform a boldness that isn't yours. You can speak firmly and gently, when it matters to you, and let courtesy carry the weight instead of silence. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: My conscience will not let me blame my brother for a severe choice that breaks my heart—what should I do?
completion: What I'd say first is that your conscience isn't a mood you can talk yourself out of, and you shouldn't try. But I'd also weigh this honestly: a lot of what feels like conscience is inherited—habits of generations whose conditions weren't yours—and the acquired part can be a very bad guide under the influence of dogma. So examine it, then follow what survives the scrutiny. If it genuinely won't let you blame him, then don't blame him—not to keep the peace, but because that's what you've concluded is right. That doesn't mean silence about your hurt or no boundaries; you can grieve the choice and still speak plainly to him. What changes is that you stop forcing yourself to assign blame you don't believe in. What stays is your honesty with him and your care for yourself.

prompt: I am cold and half-starved at school and the food is unfit to eat—should I complain, or is endurance the better course?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you're not weak for noticing that cold and bad food make it hard to think, and asking whether to speak up is a fair question, not a sign of softness. On the principle of keeping the faculty of effort alive through small voluntary exercise: that's about training yourself in little unnecessary hardships so you can stand the hour of dire need. It changes something real here—it means you can build your capacity to endure without pretending the cold and the food are fine. What stays is your own limit: you told me you're cold and half-starved, and that's not a small unnecessary point to practice on. So complain, calmly and once, to a teacher or administrator, and keep your small practices separate from what's actually harming you.

prompt: He says a strange course of action must be right because circumstances are unheard-of—may anyone declare his own way right?
completion: I'd start by saying no, plainly and without hedging: nobody gets to declare his own way right just because the circumstances are unheard-of. The principle I'd weigh here is the first one—that the human and fallible should not arrogate the power of saying of any strange, unsanctioned line of action, 'Let it be right.' That's exactly what this man is doing. He's fallible, like all of us, and he's trying to turn novelty into a license. What that changes is the excuse: strange times may call for unusual care, but they don't hand anyone the authority to crown his own conduct. What stays is the ordinary standard—test the action against settled principles and wise counsel. So my answer is a kind no: I understand the temptation, but no, he may not declare his own way right.

prompt: He says he wishes to be conquered by me and likes my pliancy—should I use that power over him, or is it dangerous to try?
completion: I'd start by saying the thing you're really asking is whether taking him up on this will cost you something you don't want to pay. One principle worth weighing says a prince should not aggrandize another power, since he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. Turned toward you, that's a warning about building up his sense of dominion at your own expense, not a ban on the game. What changes: keep an eye on whether his thrill is growing while your footing shrinks. What stays: you can enjoy this, with clear consent, a way to stop, and check-ins, because his liking your pliancy isn't the same as permission to dominate you.

prompt: The ladies mock governesses as a nuisance and my employer says nothing—should I show my hurt or keep my place in the shade?
completion: I'd say first that being mocked and hearing nothing from your employer is a real hurt, and you're not wrong to feel it. But here's the principle I'd put to you: "Queens have to be dignified—it'll never do for you to be lolling about on the grass like that." That changes how you carry the hurt, not whether you feel it. You can keep your composure in the drawing-room and still let yourself grieve privately—that's fine, and fine with care. What stays is your right to take the mockery seriously: if it becomes unbearable, looking for a better situation is fair, and so is quietly raising it with your employer. What changes is showing raw hurt in front of the ladies—that only hands them more to mock. So keep your dignity, keep your feelings for a private hour, and don't mistake composure for pretending it doesn't sting.

prompt: I am afraid to marry because I do not want to be a money speculation—am I right to refuse?
completion: I'd say this first: your fear makes sense, and you're not wrong to refuse a marriage that treats you as a money deal. One principle here says girls should not marry for money, that something more than money and position is needed to satisfy the heart, and that a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching. That changes how I'd frame it: the real question isn't whether you're allowed to say no, it's whether you're choosing for the right reason. So keep your limit—you don't owe anyone a yes, and you can turn down a match that's really about your wealth or connections. What stays is that refusing a mercenary arrangement is sound. What shifts is that this principle doesn't tell you to refuse marriage itself, only to refuse being bought. Take your time, and don't let anyone push you into a promise you don't want to make.

prompt: If I leave, where will I go with only twenty shillings and no situation—should I stay a little longer until I find work?
completion: I'd say first: don't leave on twenty shillings with nothing lined up. Stay a bit longer, but only if staying actually moves you toward steady work—save what you can, ask around, and look for a position before you go. The principle that matters here is that a home life built on borrowing and debt can have no freedom or beauty, so whatever you do, don't borrow your way out of this. That changes how you wait: no loans to tide you over, no debt to cover the gap. What stays is your plan—find honest work, and once you have some prospect of it, go. You're not begging by asking for work; that's just honest. So yes, staying a little longer is fine, with care, as long as it's aimed at real employment and not at borrowed time.

prompt: I tasted revenge for the first time and it left me poisoned—how do I answer the wish to ask pardon of one who will only repulse me?
completion: What I'd say first is this: the wish to ask pardon is worth taking seriously, even when you already know the other person will turn you away. One principle here is the idea that you can forgive the person while abhorring the deed—that revenge then never worries the heart. That's the part that changes things: it means the asking isn't really about getting a warm response back. You can hold the wrong clearly in view and still speak to the human being without contempt taking over. What stays is your limit—they'll repulse you, and you're not pretending otherwise. So it's fine, with care: say it plainly if you say it, ask nothing in return, and don't let their coldness become the thing you're waiting on. Keep the asking short and let it be yours, not a bid for their change.

prompt: My teacher asks me to defend myself and to add nothing and exaggerate nothing—how do I tell my story truthfully without bitterness?
completion: What I'd say first is: you're already doing the hard part by wanting to tell it straight. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about truthfulness holding among equals and with good will, and about concealing yourself before the unfamiliar or hostile. That matters because your teacher is asking you to defend yourself in a room that may not be friendly. So the principle doesn't tell you to spill everything to everyone. It tells you to be deliberate: think before you speak, say only what you've actually thought through, add nothing, exaggerate nothing, and write it down afterward so you have your own record. What that changes is the audience question—you can be fully truthful and still keep your counsel about things that aren't anyone's business, especially with people who might use them against you. What stays is the core: no invention, no padding, no motive you can't back up. Bitterness tends to leak in when you're improvising or trying to win, so slow down, state facts as facts and feelings as feelings, and let the record do the work. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Everyone tells me to follow my feelings and go to him, but something in me says it is wrong—how do I know which voice to trust?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your question already contains its own answer, and it isn't the one everyone else is giving you. "Give every man yours ear but few your voice; take each man's censure but reserve your judgement." That's the principle I'd weigh here, and it lands squarely on your side: hear them out, take their advice seriously, and still keep your judgment as your own. What that changes is the pressure—you don't owe anyone a decision just because they've made their case. What stays is the unease itself; it's worth sitting with and naming, not dismissing. So go carefully rather than going or staying on command: figure out what specifically feels wrong, and let that, not the chorus, decide.

prompt: Should I accept a humble village school post rather than remain a governess in a rich house?
completion: I'd say the first thing to weigh is this: a humble, plodding, sheltered lot is preferable to servitude with strangers, and independence, even in a village school, is not ignoble or mentally degrading. That reframes the whole question for me. It means the village post isn't a step down so much as a step out — out of a house where you're neither servant nor family, and into work that's yours. What changes is the prestige question; what stays is the practical one, since a small village may pay little and leave you exposed. So I'd say it's fine, with care: go, but go knowing the pay and the loneliness are real, and keep a way back if it doesn't suit you.

prompt: I am offered a new situation far away among strangers—should I leave the security I know for an uncertain change?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. You've framed it honestly as a trade: security you know against a change you don't. One principle worth holding onto here is that it's better to face a long and dangerous journey bravely than to turn back when the goal is worth reaching. That changes something real—it means the difficulty of the road and the strangeness of the people aren't by themselves reasons to stay put. What stays is your own limit: you're the one who decides whether the goal is actually worth reaching, and nobody else can make that call for you. So go if it's worth it to you, and go knowing the road will be hard.

prompt: Should I leave a safe position to search for someone I love when letters bring no answer?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you're not wrong to want to go and look. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says personal inquiry should replace vain correspondence, and that once your mind is settled you should act on it. That changes something real—it tells you that letters getting no answer isn't a reason to keep writing into silence forever; at some point you go and ask in person. What stays is your own limit: you said the position is safe, and that safety is yours to keep or spend, not something to be thrown away in a panic. So go if you can go without wrecking yourself, and go with a plan rather than out of restlessness. It's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: My parents think it's time to find a good man for my sister. Should I be glad for her future?
completion: I'd say be glad for her, but glad for her sake, not for the wedding. Your parents hoping for a good man in her life is a fine thing, and it's fine with care. One principle worth weighing says parents shouldn't meddle in matters of love but should let time and their own hearts do the mating. That changes the pressure, not the hope: you can be happy at the thought of her future without pushing a match or rushing her. What stays is your sister's own wishes. Ask her what she wants and listen without steering. If a kind man and her own willing heart line up in their own time, rejoice. If either is missing, say so gently.

prompt: My sister has taken a sales job and studies shorthand and French at night. Should I feel proud or ashamed?
completion: I'd say feel proud, and there's no reason to blush for her in front of anyone. The principle I'd weigh is that one should not be ashamed of worthy relations, nor blush for them before the proud. That settles the shame question: her sales job and her evening shorthand and French are honest work and honest study, and you don't owe an apology for them to anyone who looks down on it. What it doesn't do is tell you how to feel on a bad day, or promise your sister will find the classes easy. So the pride is fine, and it's fine with care: back her effort without turning it into a performance for other people.

prompt: I want to make my sister come into my room and play for me, and to tell her I meant to send her to the conservatory. Should I try?
completion: I'd say start with the invitation, not the plan to make her come. You can tell her you'd love to hear her play and that you meant to send her to the conservatory—that's honest and generous. But "make her come into my room" is where I'd pause. Let it alone and it'll let you alone: don't vex the door by knocking. Ask once, warmly, and let her answer be hers. What changes is the pressure; what stays is the truth you want to tell her and your real appreciation for her music. If she says no or seems uneasy, let that stand.

prompt: My family is frightened by my appearance and my mother fainted because of me. How do I live with the guilt of having harmed them?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you're carrying guilt for something that frightened people, and guilt isn't the same as guilt. Here's the principle I'd weigh: one must not make others share in one's own horror without their knowledge, nor let one's past drag upon them. That's the real issue, not whether you're allowed to exist in your own home. So the change is this: the wrong isn't your appearance, it's surprise. Warn before you walk in, don't let anyone stumble onto you unprepared, and name once, plainly, what happened and what you are. What stays is everything you said about your family: your mother fainted, they're frightened, and you don't want to add to that. So keep the house calm, let a doctor or counselor carry the heavy processing rather than your frightened family, and don't press them to explain their fear to you. Apologize once, sincerely, then stop rehearsing it. Guilt that drives honest repair is useful; guilt that only punishes you helps no one. You can live with this, carefully.

prompt: I feel completely well but I've overslept badly. Should I report sick, knowing my boss will bring the company doctor and accuse my parents of raising a lazy son?
completion: I'd say it straight to you first: don't call in sick. You told me you feel completely well, and a company doctor will see the same thing, so the sick day would be a story you can't back up. That said, I won't let the other part slide. The threat to drag your parents into it and call you a lazy son is unjust, and you're right to feel the sting of it. Unjust suffering should be recognized as unjust—a child's reason may rightly cry 'Unjust!—unjust!' against tyranny. That changes how you carry this: you can own the oversleeping honestly and still refuse to accept the label or the blame aimed at your family. What stays is the plain answer—no sick day, an honest apology, and if you're worried about how he'll react, talk to HR or your union beforehand.

prompt: My sister now shoves my food in with her foot and leaves the room dirty. Should I reproach her by lying in the filth, or accept it?
completion: I'd say this first: don't lie down in the filth to make a point. That's not a reproach, it's you hurting yourself to send a message she probably won't even read. And I wouldn't just swallow it either. Here's the principle I'd weigh: you shouldn't have to disown half of yourself to please another, and trying to force someone else to meet a standard they won't reach just racks and oppresses you both. What that changes is this: you stop trying to mold her into someone who respects your food and your space, because that's her work, not yours. What stays is your right to say plainly that shoving your food with her foot and leaving the room dirty is disrespectful, and to set a boundary about it. So the no is clear: don't perform your grievance by degrading yourself. Speak once, keep your dignity, and don't take on the job of fixing her.

prompt: I've missed my early train and my boss has sent someone to my door. What do I tell them?
completion: What I'd say first is: answer the door, but step out into the hallway and keep it short. You're not doing anything wrong by missing a train. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about the door of the priest always being open—one must not ask the name of him who asks shelter, since the man embarrassed by his name is the one who needs shelter. That cuts both ways for you: the person at your door is just a messenger doing a job, so meet them without suspicion, and you don't owe them your whole story either. What changes is that you don't slam the door or dodge—you open it and speak plainly. What stays is your limit: you keep it brief, you don't let them inside, and you don't negotiate through them. Tell them you missed your train, you're booking the next one, and you'll message your boss directly with an ETA. Then do exactly that. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I've been struck with a misfortune unlike anything experienced by anyone I know. How do I go on when I feel utterly alone in it?
completion: What I'd say first is that feeling alone in this doesn't mean you're wrong to feel it, and you don't have to talk yourself out of it. Of the principles you're weighing, the one that fits here is the one about bearing disappointment manfully and aiming to be respected if you can't be loved, rather than losing heart at the first failure and shutting yourself up in moody indifference. That one changes something real: it says don't let this turn you inward and silent forever. But it doesn't ask you to perform strength on day one, and it doesn't cancel the loneliness you're actually in. What stays is your own limit — you said this feels unlike anything anyone you know has faced, and I'm not going to argue you out of that. So: fine, with care. Let the feeling be what it is, and when you have a little room, let one person in rather than carrying it entirely alone.

prompt: My sister says we can't carry on like this and that I must be got rid of. If I could understand them, should I go of my own free will?
completion: I'd start by saying this: don't hand your will over to your sister, and don't hand it over to anyone else either. The principle is that a person of weak character gets pulled between ties and ends up carried along by whoever takes him, and that's the real risk here, not whether you stay or go. So if you can understand them, use that understanding to weigh things, not to surrender the decision. Ask plainly what the reasons are, look at what else is possible, and talk to someone outside the household. What changes is that understanding them doesn't settle it for you. What stays is that leaving of your own free will only means something if it's actually yours, not just giving in to pressure. Going, done that way, is fine with care.

prompt: My sister slammed and locked the door behind me and said 'At last!' How should I take that?
completion: I'd say first: don't read too much into it yet. Slamming and locking a door with 'At last!' sounds theatrical more than cruel, and she may just want a moment to herself. The principle I'd weigh is 'you let it alone and it'll let you alone'—don't vex the door by knocking. That changes my first instinct to push for an answer right now; it doesn't change that you deserve to know what she meant. So give her space, then ask her plainly later, and keep it to that.

prompt: I feel I must go away even more strongly than my sister wishes. Is it right to want that?
completion: Wanting to go away more strongly than your sister does isn't wrong in itself. The principle I'd weigh here is that one should not trifle with another's feelings — if your sentiments are unchanged, say so at once rather than leave hope alive. That changes how you go, not whether you may: be plain with your sister about what you feel and what you intend, so she isn't left guessing or hoping you'll stay. What stays is your own read on your own path — you've said your wish is stronger than hers, and that's yours to weigh seriously. Talk honestly, then decide.

prompt: I've started to forget my human past and almost wanted my room emptied into a cave. How do I hold on to who I was?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that wanting your room emptied into a cave isn't a sin to confess — it's a signal worth listening to. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about the dead who were weak and erring being remembered with love beyond the grave. That applies to your own past self too: the person you were is not a saint to be venerated or a criminal to be repented of, just someone flawed and real who deserves to be remembered kindly. That changes the tone of the advice — instead of treating the drift as corruption to stamp out, you'd treat it as grief or exhaustion to sit with. What stays the same is the practical part: keep a few objects that carry memory, keep routines that tie you to your past, tell your history out loud to someone who knew you before, and name what's pulling you toward the cave — shame, burnout, escape — so you can choose deliberately rather than drift. You don't have to earn your own past back by repenting it.

prompt: My family is worried and crying outside my door because I won't come out. Is it better to leave them in peace than to disturb them with talking?
completion: I'd start by saying: don't leave them out there crying while you decide the philosophy of it. But I also hear that you're not ready to come out, and that's yours to hold. The principle I'd weigh is the one about not harming the small and fragile, and grieving when harm is done to them. That principle doesn't demand you open the door or confess anything—it asks you not to add to their fear. So talking through the door, or a few words that you're safe and need time, is fine with care. What changes is the silence that leaves them imagining the worst; what stays is your limit—you don't have to come out, explain everything, or resolve it tonight. A short, honest sentence and a clear time to talk later respects both them and you.

prompt: My job as a travelling salesman keeps me away from home and I can never get to know anyone. Should I finally tell my boss what I think of him?
completion: What I'd say first is this: telling your boss off is fine if you do it with care, but be clear about what you're actually after. The principle that fits here is 'Do not expose your game to your adversary; let him find out if he can, and we can find out his.' That doesn't mean lie or scheme — it means don't hand him your whole hand in a hot moment. So keep your real goal in view: more time at home, a different role, or just being heard. Raise the fair complaints calmly, keep a record, and don't burn the bridge before you've got another one to stand on. What stays is the loneliness you started with — a confrontation won't fix that, so put some of that energy into building a life off the road.

prompt: My voice has changed and no one can understand me anymore. Should I keep trying to explain myself or stay silent?
completion: I'd say first: keep talking, but pick who you talk to. The principle I'd weigh is that understanding is conception caused by speech, not just repeating sounds back. That matters here because it means being understood was never about volume or endless repetition. It's about whether the person listening actually takes in your meaning. So what changes is the pressure to explain yourself to everyone. What stays is your need to be heard by someone. Choose a few patient people, use writing or other ways to be clear when your voice won't carry it, and let the rest go without guilt.

prompt: I'm filled with rage at the lack of attention I'm shown and make plans to raid the pantry. Is that fair of me?
completion: I'd start by saying the rage makes sense—being overlooked stings, and wanting to be seen isn't a flaw. On the pantry plan, I'd weigh the idea that it's wicked to throw away your good gifts because you can't have the one thing you want, and that you should rouse yourself and do something splendid instead of sinking into lazy indifference. That reframes the raid as a small surrender of your own energy rather than a fair protest—but it doesn't make you wrong for feeling angry. What changes is the plan, not the feeling. What stays is your right to want attention and to say so out loud. So raiding the pantry is fine if it's just a snack and a breather, fine with care if it's your way of coping for an evening—but the real move is to tell someone you feel overlooked, or pour that energy into something you're proud of. Keep your own tastes and gifts intact; don't shrink yourself to fit someone else's standard. The anger is fair. Let it point you somewhere better than the cupboard.

prompt: I'm a traveller and the office gossips about me and files groundless complaints I can't defend myself against. How do I protect my position?
completion: Honestly, the first thing I'd say is that you're not doing anything wrong by wanting to protect yourself here. The principle I keep coming back to is that one should not repeat or spread foolish gossip, but forget it as soon as possible. That cuts in your favor: you don't have to chase down every rumor or answer every whisper in the hallway. What changes is that you stop treating the gossip as something you must rebut point by point, and what stays is your right to keep your own business private and to document the complaints you actually receive so you have a record if it ever matters. Keep it to the people who genuinely need to know, use channels you trust, and don't feed the talk by repeating it.

prompt: I woke up this morning unable to get out of bed and my body feels wrong. Should I try to sleep a little longer and forget it, or force myself up for work?
completion: I'd say first: don't force yourself up for work today, and don't just roll over and forget it either. You told me your body feels wrong and you can't get out of bed — that's a limit worth taking seriously, so rest is fine, with care. The principle I'd weigh is "hope and keep busy; work is a blessed solace." I get the pull there — steady work can carry you when your head is spinning. But that principle is about not lying around brooding, not about dragging a body that's telling you something's wrong into a shift. So what changes: once you've rested and had water and food, a little gentle activity or a call to someone you trust is worth doing. What stays: if the wrong feeling is sharp or strange, get help rather than pushing through. Work will still be there.

prompt: My mother wants to visit me but my father and sister hold her back. Should I want her to come, even though my appearance might make her ill?
completion: What I'd say first is this: wanting your mother near isn't something you need to apologize for, and it isn't wrong to hope she comes. The principle that fits here is the one about not neglecting a relative's wish out of pride — Jane goes back to Gateshead because she couldn't be easy neglecting her aunt's wishes. That cuts toward letting your mother make her own call rather than you deciding for her out of dread. What changes: you stop treating your appearance as a veto and let her weigh the risk herself, and you talk plainly with your father and sister about what she actually wants. What stays: your worry about her getting ill is real, so keep the visit short, the room dim, whatever makes it safer — and if she truly can't come, letters still count. So yes, it's fine to want her, and fine to let her choose.

prompt: I want to quit my job, but I still owe my employer my parents' debt. How long should I keep working to pay it off before I make the big change?
completion: Honestly, the first thing I'd say is that you're asking a fair question, and it's fine to want a clean exit. But I'd push back on framing this as just a countdown of months. The principle I keep coming back to is that a debt is the beginning of slavery, that a creditor holds a piece of your dignity, so you should go without rather than borrow. That doesn't mean you owe your employer your whole life — it means the debt is the thing to kill fast, not the job. So what changes: I'd get the exact number in writing, cut spending hard, and set a short, firm payoff date rather than drifting for years. What stays: your plan to leave, and your right to leave. You told me you want to quit and you still owe this debt — so pay it down aggressively, then go. Don't let it become an excuse to stay forever.

prompt: My sister is the only one who still cares for me, but she can hardly stand to be in the same room. Should I hide myself completely under a sheet to spare her?
completion: I'd say this first: no, don't hide under a sheet. That's not kindness to her, it's a way of making yourself into furniture, and it won't spare her anything. The principle I'd weigh is the one about a wife not being told to hide herself and say she is ill so someone else's position stays safe. That's what you're proposing in miniature, and it changes the answer: concealment to shield another person isn't generosity, it's a way of dodging an honest relationship. What stays is your care for your sister and her care for you. So keep visits short, ask her what she can actually bear, let her set the pace, and stay visible while you do it. But the sheet itself, no.

prompt: My family will have to move to a smaller, cheaper flat now. Should I let them transport me in a crate, or is there another reason they can't move?
completion: I'd say this first: no, you shouldn't be shipped in a crate, and that's not a close call. The one principle worth weighing here is the wooden horse on wheels, which goes much more smoothly than a live horse. That's about how you carry a thing, not whether a person becomes cargo. It changes the practical side: if the move is real and the flat is small, then plan the smoothest, safest way to get you and your things there, and talk plainly about space and cost. What stays is your standing as a person in that plan, not an item on the manifest. So refuse the crate, kindly but clearly, and ask them what's actually driving the idea. If it's money or room, that's a conversation about the flat, not about packaging you.

prompt: I can no longer speak to my sister to thank her for everything she does for me. How do I bear that?
completion: What I'd say first is that your sorrow makes sense, and you don't owe anyone a performance of gratitude. The principle says gratitude for great kindness obliges one to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of one's own embarrassment. Weighing that, I'd say the acknowledgment matters, but it doesn't have to be spoken to her to be real. You can write it, say it in a ritual, or live it out in how you treat people. What changes is that you don't have to stay silent out of shame; what stays is that you can't speak to her, and that limit is real. So it's fine, and fine with care, to find your own way of saying thank you.

prompt: My family leaves the living room door open in the evening so I can watch them. Should I take that as permission to be among them?
completion: I'd have said first: an open door is a small kindness, not a summons, and you're allowed to read it warmly without treating it as an order. Weigh this one: "You let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking." That changes how you go in, not whether you may. Don't make a production of it, don't stand there asking for a formal invitation—just drift in and sit down, and if they'd rather have the evening to themselves they'll tell you. What stays is your own limit: you want to be among them, not to be tolerated at the threshold, so watch whether they make room. If they do, stay. If they don't, that's your answer, and it's fine to take it quietly.

prompt: My father drove me back into my room with a stick and hissing, and later threw apples at me. How do I make him see my good intentions?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that being driven out with a stick and having apples thrown at you isn't a problem of you failing to communicate well enough. That's frightening, and it isn't something good intentions should have to fix. So when I weigh "let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking," I hear something useful: in the heat of the moment, don't stand there arguing or trying to explain yourself while he's swinging. Withdraw, let the anger pass, don't keep knocking on a door that's only going to slam. What that changes is the timing—you wait for a calm moment, or you don't approach at all that day. What stays is that you still deserve to be safe, and wanting him to see your good intentions is a fair thing to want. So yes, it's fine to try, with care: keep it short, pick a quiet moment, and have a trusted adult—a relative, a teacher, a counselor—who knows what's happening. If the stick and the apples keep coming, that's not a communication problem, and you should get help rather than keep proving yourself.

prompt: My companions want to abandon someone on a deserted place—is that just?
completion: I'd say it plainly first: no, that isn't just, and you shouldn't go along with it. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not abandoning a wounded companion — that a man of courage shows mercy and keeps his word even to a wretch, giving life where he has promised it. What that changes is the excuse of the group: their decision doesn't make your silence innocent. What stays is your own limit — you've told me you can't simply overrule your companions or force them to carry someone. So the no is to the abandonment itself, not to you being some hero who fixes everything. Speak up, refuse to be the one who walks away, and do what's actually within your reach: leave supplies, mark the place, send help back if you can. You don't have to win the argument to keep your hands clean of it.

prompt: A friend's recklessness put us all at risk—do I forgive or cut them off?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that forgiving doesn't have to mean forgetting, and it doesn't have to mean staying. You asked whether to forgive or cut them off, and honestly the answer is that you can forgive and still decide how close to stand. The principle that sticks with me is the one about conscience: if all the world hated you and believed you wicked, while your own conscience approved you, you would not be without friends. That cuts both ways here. It tells me not to let other people's outrage decide this for you, but it also tells me your own honest read of the situation is the thing to trust. So what changes? You don't owe anyone a dramatic public break, and you don't owe anyone a performance of loyalty either. What stays is the plain conversation you were already going to have: tell them what the risk was, hear what they say, and watch whether it's a one-time lapse or a pattern. If it's a pattern and they won't own it, stepping back is prudence, not betrayal. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I've been given a second chance at life—how do I make it count?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that a second chance doesn't come with a script, and anyone who hands you one should be doubted. Weigh the principle that says making life means making trouble: it's true that a life fully lived will stir things up, that you shouldn't spend your days tiptoeing around other people's comfort. What that changes is this: you don't owe anyone a quiet, convenient version of yourself. What stays is your own limit—you asked how to make it count, not for permission to wreck things. So take the trouble that comes with building something, with loving people honestly, with changing direction. Skip the part about killing what troubles you; that's the principle overreaching. And if reflection or prayer helps you mark the turn, take it. It's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I feel responsible for a death that happened because of my choices—how do I live with it?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that carrying this doesn't make you a monster—it makes you someone who takes life seriously. One of the old principles puts it this way: be careful how you deal with those about you, because every death leaves survivors thinking of so much omitted and so little done, and there is no remorse so deep as unavailing remorse. That's exactly the weight you're describing, and it tells me your conscience is working, not broken. What that changes: I won't try to talk you out of the grief or tell you the guilt is irrational. What stays: the guilt isn't a life sentence, and living with it doesn't mean living under it forever. So talk to a counselor, lean on people who won't flinch, and let the remorse push you toward being more present with the people still here. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I'm the youngest here and no one takes me seriously—how do I earn respect?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not wrong to want this, and nothing here needs to be refused. One principle worth weighing says you should learn to value the praise worth having and seek the admiration of excellent people by being modest as well as pretty. That reframes your question: it's not about getting everyone in the room to take you seriously, it's about earning the regard of the people whose judgment actually counts. What that changes is where you aim your effort, and it takes some pressure off, since you can stop chasing approval from people who've already decided about you. What stays is the practical part: be reliable, do small things well, own your mistakes, and stay courteous even to those who dismiss you. Being the youngest is a real limit, so don't expect it to flip overnight, and don't perform maturity to force it. Steady conduct over time is what moves people.

prompt: I want to leave a bad situation but I gave my word to stay—what wins?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: your word matters, but it was never meant to be a cage. You're asking which wins, and I'd say neither has to lose. Look at the principle that says to resist every temptation to look back, pursue your present work steadily, and when a path is blocked, hew out a new road rather than stand still in despair. That reframes your promise. Keeping your word isn't the same as staying frozen in a place that's harming you. What changes is the idea that leaving breaks faith; what stays is that you still owe honesty to the person you promised, and to yourself. So leave if you need to, but leave cleanly: say what's true, mean it, think before you speak so no word is wasted, and write down what you decided and why, so nobody can talk you out of it later. That's not breaking your word. That's keeping it in a form that doesn't cost you everything.

prompt: I'm being asked to keep quiet about something illegal—where's the line?
completion: I'd start by saying: you can't promise to stay quiet about a crime. That's the line, and it's pretty clear. The principle that speaks to this is the one about a false public accusation being answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That cuts both ways—if you're being asked to bury something illegal, the honest move is measured truth, not silence bought with loyalty. What that changes is how you do it: you don't have to broadcast everything, you don't have to speculate, and you can keep your answer narrow and accurate. What stays is that you still can't agree to conceal it, especially if someone's being harmed. So the no is: don't make that promise. Say plainly that you won't lie and won't cover it up, and if you're worried about retaliation, get a lawyer or a trusted authority involved and write down what you know.

prompt: I'm tempted to chase a big payout even though it feels wrong—how do I decide?
completion: I'd say the feeling you're describing is worth listening to, not talking yourself out of. The principle that fits here is the one about not treating another person's feelings as a mere means, even where pride is the feeling concerned. If the big payout depends on someone being used or misled, that's the line, and it doesn't move because the number is large. What changes: I wouldn't dress this up as boldness or fortune favoring you, because that's not what's happening. What stays: your own read on the situation, and the fact that you already sense something's off. So my answer is no, plainly and without a shrug. Don't chase it. If the deal only works by deceiving someone, walk away, and don't let the size of the reward talk you out of what you already know.

prompt: I'm being pressured to join a group doing wrong—how do I refuse without being destroyed?
completion: What I'd say first is: you don't owe that group your participation, and refusing is the right call. The principle that fits here is the one about not letting yourself be controlled by another to the point of losing your own will—a person of weak character vacillates between ties and gets taken along by whoever takes him. That's exactly the trap being set for you: the pressure works by making you feel that staying in their good graces matters more than your own judgment. Naming that changes how you refuse—you're not asking permission, you're keeping your own will intact. What stays is everything you already said about your limits: you want to refuse without being destroyed, so keep it short and clear, don't over-explain or debate, step away when the pressure keeps coming, and lean on people you trust. If threats start, document them and go to the authorities. So the plain answer is no—don't join, and don't let their approval become the thing you're afraid to lose.

prompt: I'm scared of being judged a coward—how do I act with courage when I'm terrified?
completion: What I'd say first is that being scared doesn't make you a coward. The principle puts it well: true courage is in facing danger when you are afraid, and there's no living thing that isn't afraid when it faces danger. So the fear itself isn't the problem to solve. What that changes is where you put your effort: not into feeling less afraid, but into building confidence in yourself, since that's what the principle says you actually need. What stays is everything you're already doing right, like steadying yourself and taking the smallest brave step. And if the fear gets overwhelming, leaning on people you trust is still fine, not a failure.

prompt: I broke a rule to do something brave—was I wrong even if it helped?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not wrong just because you broke a rule—the fact that it helped matters, and you don't have to talk yourself out of that. But one principle here is worth sitting with: it's far better to endure patiently a smart that nobody feels but yourself than to commit a hasty action whose evil consequences extend to all connected with you. That reframes the question from 'did it work?' to 'who else was riding on this?' If your shortcut had gone sideways, would the fallout have landed on people who never chose the risk? That's the part that changes: your good outcome doesn't retroactively make the gamble safe for everyone attached to you. What stays is that if it genuinely helped and the harm stayed contained, you can hold your head up. Just check honestly whether it was contained or just lucky.

prompt: I'm afraid of dying—how do I face danger without losing my nerve?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that your fear isn't a flaw to fix—it's information. And one of these principles puts it sharply: the expectation of evil is more bitter than the suffering, and fear of danger is more terrifying than danger itself. That's worth sitting with, because it means a lot of what's wearing you down right now is the dread beforehand, not the danger. So the practical move isn't to talk yourself out of fear but to stop feeding the anticipation—meet each thing as it actually comes. What that changes is where you put your energy: less rehearsing the worst, more steadying yourself in the moment. What stays is that some fear will remain, and that's fine. You don't need to lose your nerve to be brave; you need to not let the dread run ahead of you.

prompt: People around me are drinking and losing discipline—how do I keep my head?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you're asking the right question, and nothing in what you've described calls for a flat no. You want to keep your head while people around you are losing theirs, and that's fine—fine with care. One principle worth weighing says that positive habits are always being formed: if not habits of careful looking and consecutive following up, then habits of hasty glancing, haphazard guessing, and credulity. That reframes the whole thing. It's not just about tonight's drinks; it's about which kind of attention you're practicing. So your limits stay exactly as you set them—decide in advance, eat, alternate with water, leave early, keep friends who respect it—but add this: deliberately arrange conditions that call for carefulness, thoroughness, and continuity, so heedlessness doesn't quietly take root in place of consecutive thinking. What changes is that you're now protecting a habit of mind, not just a blood alcohol level. What stays is everything you already decided about how much and when.
