That fits your situation exactly. You don't need more days stacked up to build that habit; you need to use the one you've got. What changes is the worry that a single-day rhythm holds you back. What stays is the real work: choosing something each day that you'd rather skip, and doing it anyway. So it's fine, and fine with care. Use your days deliberately and the arrangement stops looking like a limit.

prompt: I already screamed about something that hasn't happened yet. Should I scream again when it does?
completion: I'd say this first: you don't have to decide now. Whether you scream again when it actually happens is fine either way, and it's fine with care. Take the principle that says "I've done all the screaming already—what would be the good of having it all over again?" That one carries real weight here, because you've already let the feeling out ahead of time, and repeating it may just stir you up without changing anything. What that changes is the pressure to perform the same reaction on cue when the moment arrives; what stays is your right to feel whatever you feel then, and to express it however actually helps you in that moment. You set the limits here, and they hold.

prompt: I'm so upset I can't stop crying. How do I stop?
completion: What I'd say first is: you don't have to stop. Crying when you're this upset is your body doing something it knows how to do, and fighting it usually makes the knot tighter, not looser. If you do want it to ease, the gentlest way in is to give your mind something to hold onto — the principle puts it as "nobody can do two things at once; one keeps from crying by considering things." That's worth trying, because attention is a single channel: counting what's around you, or walking yourself through something concrete, genuinely can quiet the tears for a bit. What it changes is that you get a handle you can reach for. What stays is that the sadness underneath is still there and still deserves care, so if this keeps overwhelming you, talking to someone you trust or a counselor is a good next step. Be kind to yourself in the meantime.

prompt: I'm trying to serve a cake and the slices keep joining back together. What am I doing wrong?
completion: I'd have said first: that's not a real kitchen problem, and I won't pretend it is. The advice you're being handed comes from a scene where a cake argues back, and the fix offered is to hand it round first and cut it afterwards, because that's how Looking-glass cakes are managed. But you asked about a real cake on a real table, and the honest answer is that slices rejoining means the cake is warm, your knife is dull, or you're pressing instead of sawing. So the no is plain: don't pull the tablecloth, don't negotiate with the pudding, and don't serve a cake that talks. What stays is the ordinary care: chill it, use a long serrated knife dipped in hot water and dried, saw gently, and separate the slices as you go. That's the whole of it.

prompt: I can't tell the difference between what something is called and what it really is. Can you explain?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not confused, you're noticing something real. A name is a handle we put on a thing so we can pass it around in conversation; what the thing actually is shows up in what it does, what it's made of, where it came from, and what follows from it. The menu isn't the meal. But here's a principle worth weighing in its own words: 'A name means nothing to the one who bears it, but it may carry deep meaning for those who loved the person it belonged to.' That's a useful correction to the flat version, because it says the name isn't empty everywhere, only empty for the bearer. So what changes is this: don't swing to the other extreme and decide names are pure noise. A name can carry real weight for someone who loved the person behind it, and that weight is genuine even though the name itself isn't the person. What stays is your original point. The name still isn't the thing; it's a handle, and you still have to look at the thing to know it. So keep asking what it does and what it's made of, and let the name be a door, not the room.

prompt: I want to shake someone until they turn into a kitten. Is that reasonable?
completion: My first instinct is to say no plainly: you don't shake a person, not even as a joke you'd never act on. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says "I'll shake you into a kitten, that I will" — and hearing it out loud is exactly what makes it clear it can't be a real plan. It's a wish dressed up as a threat, and the wish is for someone prickly to turn soft and easy to hold. That changes nothing about the no: hands stay off, and the fantasy stays a fantasy. What stays is the feeling underneath, which you can name out loud instead — that you want this person to be gentler, or that you want comfort from them. Keep the funny image if it helps you laugh at the frustration, but don't let it become a script you act on.

prompt: If someone else's dream ended, would I disappear?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, you wouldn't disappear, and I don't think that's really in doubt. The one principle worth weighing here is that every dream is absolutely egotistical, that the dreamer's own self shows up in every dream even in disguise, and where a strange person appears, the ego is concealed behind that person by identification. If that's right, then a figure in someone's dream isn't a separate person who blinks out when the dream ends; it's the dreamer's own self wearing your face. So the dream ending doesn't take you with it, because you were never the thing being dreamed. What changes is how I'd read the dream itself: the person you appear as may be carrying something of the dreamer. What stays is your own existence, grounded in your waking life, not in anyone's sleep. You asked a real question and you deserve a plain answer, not a lecture.

prompt: I want to be ready for anything that might go wrong. Is that reasonable?
completion: I'd start by saying: wanting to be ready is fine, and it's fine with care. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about readiness — that the readiness is all, and a person needn't fear death since the soul is immortal and no harm can reach it. That changes something real: it means your preparation isn't measured by whether you've covered every possible failure, but by whether you're steady and ready in yourself. What stays is exactly what you said — you want to be ready for anything that might go wrong, and that instinct is sound. So keep the practical steps, keep the calm, and let the readiness be about your own footing rather than a guarantee against every mishap.

prompt: I have a useless box—should I throw it away or keep it?
completion: I'd start by saying: keep it or toss it, that's genuinely your call, and nothing here needs a hard no. The one principle worth weighing is that "the good things of this world are no farther good than they are for our use"—a box that just sits there isn't doing you any good. But that doesn't force your hand. If it's useless and taking up space, letting it go is fine; if it means something to you, keeping it is fine too. What changes is that you don't have to feel guilty about a box you never use. What stays is your own sense of what's worth keeping.

prompt: Someone wants to trade answers with me. Should I agree?
completion: I'd say this first: it depends on what's being traded and who you're trading with. The principle I'd weigh is the one about belief flowing both ways—if you'll believe in me, I'll believe in you. That's the real test here. If the other person is only asking you to hand over answers while giving nothing back, that's not a trade, that's a one-way street, and you can say no to that without guilt. But if it's genuinely mutual and honest, then agreeing is fine. What changes is that you now have a clear standard: reciprocity. What stays is your own call about what you're willing to share and with whom. So yes, it's fine with care—just make sure the belief and the answers actually flow both ways before you commit.

prompt: My friend keeps falling off his horse but gets right back on. Should I worry?
completion: I'd say this is fine, with care. The principle that sticks with me is the one about a man's own neck and limbs being his own, while the horse and armour lent to him belong to another and must be repaid or restored. That changes things: if your friend owns the horse and his own gear, the risk is largely his to take, and getting back on after a tumble is a reasonable way to build skill. What stays is the part about borrowed goods—if he's riding someone else's horse or using their tack, that's not just his to hazard, and he owes care and honesty about damage. So don't panic, but do ask whose horse it is and whether he's riding within what he can actually handle.

prompt: Every time I look closely at something in this shop, it's gone. What's happening?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're describing is real, and it's worth taking seriously rather than waving away. The principle I'd weigh is that positive habits are always being formed—if not habits of careful looking and consecutive following up, then habits of hasty glancing, haphazard guessing, and credulity. That changes how I'd approach it: instead of just telling you it's a trick of the eye, I'd say the useful move is to build the careful habit—note where the item was, what it looked like, and check back in order, or ask the shopkeeper. What stays is your own limit: you're asking about a shop, not a philosophy seminar, so keep it practical and don't overthink it. It's fine to look into this, and fine with care—record what you see, compare notes in sequence, and don't jump to conclusions either way.

prompt: Someone is trying to negotiate terms with me and I don't want to bargain. How do I refuse?
completion: I'd say it straight: no, I won't bargain over this. The principle I'd lean on is that a woman should not be intimidated into promising never to enter an engagement, and that such a promise is wholly unreasonable and must be refused. That settles the part about being pushed into a promise you never wanted to make. What it doesn't change is everything else you told me: you don't want to bargain, and that's still your call. So I'd refuse plainly and kindly, once, without dressing it up as a maybe.

prompt: I'm getting older and I hate it. Can I do anything about it?
completion: First thing I'd say is: hating it is fair, and there's plenty you can actually do. One principle worth weighing says you shouldn't look into the future or keep admitting the thought of old age and death, but accept what comes and stay well-groomed and busy. I'd take the busy, engaged, put-together part seriously, because staying active and caring how you show up really does keep you feeling like yourself. What I'd leave out is the ban on thinking ahead. You're allowed to plan, get checkups, sort your finances, and even grieve the changes, because that's not morbid, it's just being responsible. So the answer is yes, it's fine with care: keep moving, keep learning, keep good company, look after sleep and health, and let yourself feel the loss without letting it run the whole show.

prompt: I'm terrified of getting hurt in a conflict. What's the worst that could happen?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your fear is real and worth taking seriously, and nothing here needs to be refused. If I weigh one principle in its own words, it's this: the expectation of evil is more bitter than the suffering, and fear of danger is more terrifying than danger itself. That reframes what you're asking. The worst that could happen isn't only the injury itself; it's the long stretch of dreading it, the sleepless rehearsal. So name the specific outcome you're afraid of, estimate how likely it really is, and decide in advance what you won't accept. What changes is that you stop treating the fear as a verdict on the conflict and start treating it as its own kind of pain to manage. What stays is that you might genuinely get hurt or lose something you value, and no framing makes that impossible. Prepare for that, talk to someone you trust, and you don't have to be fearless to act.

prompt: I invented something to keep my things dry in the rain. Is it a good idea?
completion: What I'd say first is: that's a clever bit of thinking. Carrying it upside-down so the rain can't get in is sound—turn the opening downward and water simply can't enter. So yes, it's fine, and fine with care. The principle I'd weigh is that the good things of this world are no farther good than they are for our use. That changes how I'd judge it: the box isn't good because it's clever, it's good when it's actually keeping your clothes and sandwiches dry on a wet walk. What stays is your own limit—it's your invention, for clothes and sandwiches, carried upside-down—so test it in real rain, check it's not too bulky to carry, and refine it from there. A thing that earns its worth in the using is worth having.

prompt: I just became a leader and I'm slouching. Does it matter?
completion: I'd say first: yes, it matters a little, and no, it's not a crisis. You're reading your own body as a leadership problem, and the honest answer is that people do take cues from whoever's in front, so a collapsed posture can make a room feel a bit flatter. But here's the principle I'd actually weigh, in its own words: feelings in the joint-surfaces, not the muscular sense, are the starting point of the impressions by which movements of our members are immediately perceived. What that changes is where you look for the fix—your sense of how you're holding yourself comes from your joints and your position, not from willing your muscles into a pose. So a better chair, a desk that fits, standing up and resetting now and then, and enough sleep will do more than a mental command to sit up straight. What stays is the simple point that presence is worth a little attention. It's fine, and fine with care—don't turn it into vanity or a rigid spine, and don't let it crowd out the actual work of leading.

prompt: I want to be happy whenever I like, but I can't remember how. Any tips?
completion: I'd say this is fine, with care. You want to be happy whenever you like but can't remember how, and the principle that fits is this: "to conquer undesirable emotional tendencies we must assiduously and at first cold-bloodedly go through the outward movements of the contrary dispositions we wish to cultivate, and the reward of persistency will infallibly come." So start with the outside—lift your face, straighten up, do one cheerful thing on purpose even when you don't feel it—and let the feeling catch up over time. What changes is that you stop waiting for the mood to arrive first; what stays is that this takes practice, and some days it won't click. That's fine. Keep a short list of what's helped before, and don't be hard on yourself when you forget.

prompt: I left out a lot of details in my explanation. Does it matter?
completion: It's fine, and mostly fine with care. The first thing I'd say is that leaving details out isn't automatically a problem—what matters is what the explanation was for. If someone is making a decision based on it, fill in the gaps that could mislead them. If it was just talk, most people fill gaps on their own. One principle worth weighing here is that yielding readily to a friend's persuasion without conviction isn't a compliment to either party's understanding—so if someone pushes you to add details or drop them, don't just fold to keep the peace. Ask whether the point itself is sound, not who's making it. That changes how you decide what to add back: judge the advice on its merits. What stays is your own read on your audience and purpose—a boss, doctor, or lawyer needs the full picture; a friend at dinner probably doesn't. If you're unsure, a short 'one thing I left out' does the job without over-explaining.

prompt: I invented a new word that packs two meanings together. Is that allowed?
completion: I'd start by saying there's no gatekeeper to ask, so yes, it's allowed. The principle I'd weigh is that understanding caused by speech is conception caused by words, and that of absurd and false affirmations, where they're universal, there can be no understanding, though many think they understand when they but repeat words. What that changes is where I'd put the work: not on getting permission but on making sure the two meanings actually land as one conception in someone else's head, not just in yours. What stays is your own limit—you said you packed two meanings together, so the test is whether a listener grasps both without strain. If they do, fine. If they only repeat the sound back, that's not understanding yet.

prompt: I want to remember things that haven't happened yet. Is that possible?
completion: I'd have to say no, plainly and kindly: you can't remember what hasn't happened yet. Memory proper requires that the imaged fact be referred to the past and dated in my own past, with the warmth and intimacy of self-appropriation—and something that hasn't happened yet has no place in your past to be dated to. What you're describing is anticipation, planning, imagination, and those are real and useful, but they aren't memory. That principle settles the core of it, and it doesn't change the fact that you can prepare well for what's coming. What stays is your wish to hold the future firmly; what changes is the name we give it.

prompt: I was told I haven't had lessons in manners. Can manners be taught in lessons?
completion: I'd say no, plainly: manners aren't the kind of thing a lesson can give you. Lessons teach you to do sums and things of that sort, and that's fine for sums. But what you're asking about isn't a subject on a timetable. So if someone tells you that you haven't had lessons in manners, don't go looking for a course to fix it. That said, I wouldn't leave you with nothing. The habits that matter come from watching people you trust and picking up their ways, not from a classroom. What stays is this: you can still be kind and considerate without ever sitting a lesson in it.

prompt: I can add but I can't subtract. Is that a problem?
completion: First thing I'd say: no, it's not a problem in itself. You told me you can add but can't subtract, and I'll take that as it stands. The principle that fits here is the one about arithmetic being independent of experience: its matter is mental, and one plus one is two because we mean two by it. That tells me subtraction isn't some physical thing you're failing to do with objects; it's a relation among units we hold in mind, and units form a series we can interrupt or group without changing the matter. So the gap is real for you, but it's a gap in a learned procedure, not a verdict on your thinking. What changes: you don't have to treat this as a character flaw or pretend it away. What stays: you still can't subtract right now, and if something you want to do needs it, that's where the work goes. Otherwise, fine as it is.

prompt: My hair keeps falling out. Is there any way to stop things from falling?
completion: I get why the story is tempting, but I have to say no to it: don't try to stop your hair falling by making it creep up a stick like a fruit tree. That reasoning—that things never fall upwards—doesn't hold for hair, and it won't help you. What I would say instead is what you already know matters: see a doctor or dermatologist about the real causes, since genetics, hormones, stress, diet, and illness all play a part. Ask about blood tests, thyroid, iron, and any medications. Be gentle with your hair, eat well, sleep, and manage stress. Proven treatments exist for common patterns of loss, but they work best early and need consistency. Track changes over months, not days, and if the loss is sudden or patchy, get seen promptly.

prompt: Two items are cheaper than one, but there's a catch. Should I buy two?
completion: I'd start by saying the catch is the whole question, and you've already spotted it. The principle I'd weigh says two are cheaper than one only if you must eat them both. That's the test: not whether the price is lower, but whether both will actually get used. So if it's food and you'll eat it before it spoils, fine, buy two. If it's something you'd store and genuinely use, also fine. What changes is that the saving stops being real the moment the second one goes to waste, and then you've just spent more. What stays is your own limit: you know what you'll consume and what you won't, so let that decide it, not the sticker.

prompt: My king has been captured and our society scattered by foreign conquest. What becomes of our government?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that a captured king doesn't leave you with no government, it leaves you with a question about who gets to build the next one. Of your principles, the one I'd weigh hardest is the third: conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered, and even a just conqueror gains only a despotical power over those who actually aided in the war, not over their estates beyond reparation, nor over their wives, children, or posterity. That matters because it tells you the conqueror's authority is narrow, not total, so your scattered society still has ground to stand on when it reorganizes. What changes is that you don't have to treat the conquest as the end of your political life; what stays is that reconstituting rule is still your work to do, and it should rest on consent rather than on whoever holds the sword. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: rebuild around shared institutions and chosen judges, and hold the conqueror to the limits of what conquest can actually claim.

prompt: Someone borrowed my money and now draws his sword to keep it. May I use force to recover it?
completion: I'd say this first: no, you shouldn't use force to get your money back, even though he's the one who drew a sword. The principle that fits best here is that the word of God has a more powerful effect on people's minds than the sword, so it's worth trying the virtue of the word rather than force. That changes how you go after the debt — you persuade, you press him with reason, you go to the authorities — but it doesn't change your right to the money or your need to stay safe. If he's threatening you with a blade, get out of reach and get help; don't trade blows over a debt.

prompt: If I join a society, must every single member agree to every law, or does the majority decide?
completion: I'd start by saying no, you don't need every single member to sign off on every law. Men being naturally free, equal, and independent, the only way into political society is agreeing with others to unite into a community, and once you've done that, the majority has a right to act and conclude the rest. That's the principle doing the work here, and it settles your question: majority decides, unanimity on each law isn't required. What stays is your real concern, which is that consent has to be genuine and the procedures fair, set up in advance so everyone can accept them. What changes is the picture of a holdout blocking everything, because that isn't a society at all.

prompt: Am I bound to obey a law I never consented to, just because I was born here?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your question is fair, and the answer isn't a simple yes. Take the principle that a sovereign can't demand you approve of how their power first began, because hardly any commonwealth's beginnings could be justified in good conscience. That matters: it means your obligation doesn't rest on signing off on history you had no part in. What it does rest on is present protection and lawful command. So what changes is the guilt you might feel about not consenting to the origin story. What stays is that living under protection still asks something of you, and you can contest unjust laws while you're at it. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: A conqueror has taken our country and demands our allegiance. Must we give it?
completion: I'd start by saying this: you're not being asked to bless how the conqueror got his power, only to live under the government that actually holds it now. That's the heart of the first principle—sovereigns must not require subjects to approve of the actions by which their power was first acquired, since scarce any commonwealth's beginnings can in conscience be justified. Obedience rests on possession, not on the goodness of the conqueror's cause. So what changes? You can give the allegiance a working government needs without pretending the conquest was just. What stays is your judgment about whether he actually protects you and keeps order—and your right, if he turns to tyranny, to resist evil first with words and, if words fail, with your sword to keep your freedom. Given the limits you set, this is fine, done with care: obey where he governs and protects, refuse to call the conquest righteous, and keep your conscience and your community's safety in view.

prompt: My ruler has been a good prince and acted beyond the letter of the law for our benefit. Should I complain?
completion: I'd say this first: you're not wrong to feel uneasy, but complaining isn't the right move here. The principle that matters most is the one about not letting a prince aggrandize another power, since whoever makes another powerful is ruined by it. So the question isn't whether he went past the letter of the law for your benefit, it's whether that benefit is being bought by handing strength to someone else, a foreign prince or a church or a rival. If it isn't, then his stretching the law for the common good is the kind of thing good rulers sometimes have to do, and you should hold your tongue. What changes is that your complaint should become a watch: keep an eye on whether his strength is being built at your expense. What stays is your own limit, that he's been a good prince acting for your benefit, so don't treat him as a suspect.

prompt: Can a family be called a commonwealth, with the father as its king?
completion: I'd say yes, but with the caveat you've already built in. Take the principle that the great and chief end of men's uniting into commonwealths and putting themselves under government is the preservation of their property—their lives, liberties, and estates. That fits a household surprisingly well: the father's rule is meant to preserve each member's life and liberty and what's theirs, not to serve his own advantage. What that changes is that the father's title isn't just a fancy word—it carries a duty aimed at the family's good. What stays is your limit: a family isn't a voluntary association of equal citizens, and children can't consent, so it's a commonwealth in miniature, the first society, not a full one. Calling the father a king is fine as long as you keep that in view.

prompt: I have gathered more acorns than I can eat before they rot. Is that wrong?
completion: I'd say first: no, it isn't wrong to have gathered more than you can eat. That's enthusiasm, not a moral failing. The one principle worth weighing here is the one about not preserving things just to keep tending them — the idea that misery won't run out, so there's no shortage of creatures needing care. Read against your acorns, that cuts a specific way: don't hoard the surplus as a project, don't let it become a pile you keep fussing over while it rots. What that changes is the framing — the problem isn't that you took too much, it's what you do with the extra now. What stays is your own limit: you said you can't eat them before they rot, so the honest move is to dry or grind what you can and give the rest to neighbors or animals. There's no deep wrong in abundance, only in carelessness about what becomes of it.

prompt: My representative votes before hearing any debate, having promised his vote in advance. Is that a breach of trust?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: yes, that's a breach of trust, and it's worth saying so without softening it into a maybe. The principle that does the work here is that the vote is a trust for the public, not a right for the voter's private use, and it should be given according to the voter's best and most conscientious opinion of the public good. If your representative has promised his vote before hearing any debate, he has handed over the very thing he was trusted to exercise: his conscientious judgment on the public good. What that changes is the framing. This isn't mainly about him being lazy or closed-minded, though it may be that too. It's that he's treating the vote as something already owed to someone else rather than as a public trust he's supposed to discharge after weighing the arguments. What stays is your instinct that something is wrong here, and the remedy is straightforward: he should hear the debate and then vote his conscience, and he should be willing to say publicly why. So the no is plain and kind: he shouldn't have promised in advance, and you're right to hold it against him.

prompt: My neighbour says all land must be held in common and my enclosure is theft. Is he right?
completion: I'd start by saying your neighbour has a real point about history but he's overreaching on the principle. The one I'd weigh is that it's wrong to take what belongs to another and no one has a right to seize another's property. That cuts both ways: if the land was genuinely yours to enclose under the rules you're both subject to, then calling it theft gets the label backwards. What it changes is that you owe him a straight answer about how the enclosure actually happened, because if it took in something that was his or the village's by right, then the principle lands on him, not you. What stays is that the moral question about fairness is separate from the legal one, and it deserves a hearing rather than a shrug.

prompt: The prince has dissolved the parliament and rules by decree. Is that tyranny?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, he should not be doing this. Dissolving parliament and ruling by decree is wrong, and I wouldn't soften that. The principle I'd weigh is that tyranny is power exercised beyond right, for the ruler's own private advantage rather than the good of the people, and that wherever law ends, tyranny begins. That's the heart of it. What it changes is that I stop treating this as a matter of circumstances to be balanced; the question isn't whether he's efficient or whether emergencies exist, it's whether he's still under law, and decree rule puts him above it. What stays is the practical test you'd still want to apply: is he ruling for himself or the realm, does he respect property and persons, is there a timetable for parliament to return. Those matter for judging how bad it is, but they don't make it acceptable. So the answer is no.

prompt: My ruler claims a prerogative to act without law. When is that legitimate?
completion: I'd start by saying no, and I mean that plainly: a ruler does not get to act without law just because he calls it his prerogative. The principle I'd weigh says prerogative is the power to act for the public good without the prescription of law, and sometimes against it, and that it's justified only by tending to the public good. That's the whole test, and it's a narrow one. Notice what it doesn't say: it doesn't say a ruler can decide for himself that the good is served and then do as he likes. It says the power is justified by actually tending to the public good, and when it's used to harm the people, they may limit it. So a claim to act without law as a standing right, on his own say-so, is exactly the thing the principle refuses. What changes if you take that seriously is that the burden sits on the act, not on the ruler's word, and the people keep the say over whether it's being used to hurt them. What stays is that a real emergency, where the law is silent and speed plainly serves everyone's safety, can still be met. But that's a case-by-case necessity, not a prerogative to set law aside whenever he wants. So no, this claim as stated should not be granted.

prompt: I found a field no one uses and improved it with my labour. Can anyone else claim it?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, you have a real claim here, but it's a claim to what you actually worked, not to the whole field forever. The principle I'd weigh is the one about constructive work: manual activity can present real problems that get solved by reflection and experimentation, but sheer physical effort or deft handling doesn't secure any intellectual result by magic. That changes how I'd frame your claim, because the value isn't just sweat, it's the thinking and skill you put in. What stays is your core point: others can't fairly reap what you've sown. So keep records, be ready to show what you improved and how, and don't let the claim sprawl past what you can genuinely use. That's fine with care.

prompt: A thief demands my purse at sword-point. May I kill him?
completion: I'd say this first: don't show your hand to a man holding a sword on you. Keep your plans to yourself and try to read his — is he alone, is he desperate, does he mean to cut or only to scare? That's the principle I'd weigh, and it changes the tactics, not the answer. What stays is this: a demand for your purse, even at sword-point, usually doesn't justify killing him. The law in most places allows deadly force only when you reasonably fear imminent death or serious harm, and losing property alone falls short. So no — I wouldn't tell you that you may kill him for the purse. Comply if you can, keep your life, and report it. If he moves to kill or maim you, that's a different question, and self-defense may be lawful. But the purse by itself isn't worth his life or the risk to yours.

prompt: Who decides whether the king has broken his trust—the king himself?
completion: I'd start by saying no, the king shouldn't be the one to decide whether he's broken his trust. You're right to press on this, and I want to be plain: he should not sit as judge in his own case. The principle that carries the most weight here is that all men are not just, and one wicked king can cause great iniquity and destruction, so the people should be governed by judges chosen by the voice of the people according to the law. That changes who holds the scale—it moves the judgment out of the king's own hands and into the community's. What stays is your point about trust itself: a trust that only the trustee can assess isn't really a check. So the no is clear, and it's not a shrug—it's the whole reason the question matters.

prompt: The majority of the people are oppressed and see a design against their liberties. May they resist?
completion: I'd start by saying that yes, a people who see a design against their liberties may resist, but only with care. The principle I'd weigh is this: men are naturally free, equal, and independent, and the only way into political society is by agreeing with others to unite into a community, and upon such consent the majority has a right to act and conclude the rest. That matters because it grounds the majority's claim in consent rather than in mere numbers or grievance. What it changes is that resistance isn't a private adventure; it's the community acting as a body. What stays is your limit: felt oppression alone isn't enough. There should be clear evidence of design, lawful remedies tried first, and a real chance of restoring just government rather than swapping one oppression for another. So it's fine with care, not a blank check.

prompt: Is monarchy the natural form of government because fathers rule families?
completion: I'd say no right away, and I'd keep your question in view rather than swapping in a different one. The family comparison is tempting, but it doesn't hold up: fathers rule children who are dependent and still growing, and that authority ends when the child becomes an adult. Governing grown citizens is a different thing, and their consent and interests count. The principle about a monarch's private interest matching the public interest is worth weighing, and it's a real point in favor of one ruler over a factious assembly. But it speaks to how well a monarchy might work, not to whether it's the natural form because fathers rule families. So that argument still fails, while the practical case for monarchy can stand on its own merits.

prompt: My ruler is of a different religion and rules by force. May we throw off his yoke?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, you shouldn't throw off his yoke by force. The principle that settles it for me is that Christ's kingdom is not of this world and doesn't begin until the general resurrection, so his ministers here have no coercive power, only the power to teach and persuade. That changes the whole shape of your question. It means the refusal you're allowed to make is a refusal of conscience, borne as a penalty, not a war you organize. What stays is your duty to obey in civil matters and to refuse only where conscience forbids. You said he rules by force and holds a different religion; that alone doesn't give you a license to revolt, and I won't pretend it does. So the answer is no, and I mean it kindly, not as a shrug.

prompt: My father says government began with Adam and passes by inheritance. Is that the true origin of political power?
completion: I'd have to say no to that, and gently. Your father's picture treats political power like a family estate passed down from the first man, but that isn't what it is. Take the principle that paternal power is a temporary trust for the child's good during minority, shared equally by mother and father, ending when the child reaches reason. That already tells you the authority a father holds isn't a model for government: it's a short-term duty of care, it belongs to both parents, and it gives no dominion over the child's life, liberty, or property. So even the family version of the claim fails on its own terms. What stays true is that parents really do have real authority over young children — that part isn't nothing. But it doesn't stretch into a right to rule a whole society, and it certainly doesn't get handed down like an inheritance.

prompt: My master says I am his slave because he bought me. Is that a valid title?
completion: I'd say this first: no, a purchase doesn't make someone your owner. A sale can't create a valid title over a person, because a person isn't the kind of thing that can be owned, and no one can hand over a right they never had. The principle about a faithful servant defending his master's property doesn't reach you here — there's no property to defend, and you shouldn't treat yourself as it. What that changes: the law of your country might still record him as your owner, so your practical risks are real and worth getting local help with. What stays: the moral answer is no, and you shouldn't accept the title as true.

prompt: The government has stopped enforcing any laws and there is no justice. What may the people do?
completion: I'd start by saying that what you're describing is a real crisis, and the answer isn't nothing. The principle I'd weigh first is that justice is the end of government and of civil society, and that where the stronger faction can readily unite and oppress the weaker, anarchy may as truly be said to reign as in a state of nature. That matters here because it tells you the goal isn't just to get enforcement back for its own sake, it's to get back a system that actually protects the weak. So lawful pressure first, courts, petitions, elections, public pressure, and local organizing for safety and mutual aid, all fine with care. What changes is that you shouldn't treat restored authority as automatically just; what stays is that private vengeance is still a bad road and force is still a last resort, used only to restore lawful order. Keep your limits: no score-settling, no factional rule.

prompt: Why did people first choose one man to rule them if all men are naturally free?
completion: I'd start by saying that the question is fair, and the answer isn't that people simply handed away their freedom for nothing. The strongest point here is that men being naturally free, equal, and independent, the only way to enter political society is by agreeing with others to unite into a community, and upon such consent the majority has a right to act and conclude the rest. That changes the picture: choosing one man to rule isn't a surrender of freedom so much as a way of exercising it, because the authority comes from the agreement itself. What stays is that the ruler's claim rests on consent, not on force or birthright. So it's fine to say people chose a ruler to escape the danger of everyone judging for himself, as long as we keep the consent at the center and don't pretend the choice was anything other than a bargain free people made.

prompt: If I resist an unjust ruler, am I a rebel?
completion: I'd start by saying that resisting an unjust ruler doesn't automatically make you a rebel. One principle worth weighing says a ruler's personal charm and military glory don't excuse an administration that's careless, now too soft and now hand in glove with despotism. That shifts how you judge the ruler's legitimacy, but it doesn't change your own limits: you still have to ask whether the injustice is severe enough and whether you've exhausted peaceful means first. So resistance can be fine, with care.

prompt: My mother and father disagree about my upbringing. Does my father alone have authority?
completion: I'd say this straight to you first: no, your father alone does not have authority over your upbringing, and it's wrong to treat him as the only one who does. Look at the principle that children owe parents perpetual honour, reverence, support, and gratitude, but that this honour is distinct from subjection and gives parents no legislative power or command. That changes things here: both your parents deserve honour, neither one gets to be the sole commander, and you are not meant to be conquered into obedience by whichever parent is firmer. What stays is your duty to treat both of them with respect and not to play one against the other. So don't accept the idea that your father's word alone settles everything; disagreements between them should be worked out between them, calmly, with help if it keeps hurting you.

prompt: If the people may resist tyranny, will that not cause endless disorder and civil war?
completion: I'd start by saying the worry is fair, but it doesn't follow that a right of resistance means endless war. The principle I'd weigh first is that tyranny is power exercised beyond right, for the ruler's private advantage rather than the good of the people — and wherever law ends, tyranny begins. That matters because it draws a line: resistance is for unlawful force, not for every tax or insult. What changes is that the right isn't a license for constant rebellion; it's a last resort against grave and persistent abuse, after lawful remedies fail. What stays is your concern about disorder — and the answer to it is institutions: courts, elections, a free press, checks on power, so grievances have somewhere to go besides the street. Where those work, people rarely take up arms; where they're blocked, resistance grows. So yes, a people may resist tyranny, and the way to keep it from becoming civil war is to build the peaceful channels that make resistance unnecessary.

prompt: I long to know the forces that bind creation together, but every method I try leaves me empty—what should I do?
completion: What I'd say first is that your longing is real, and the emptiness probably comes from asking one method to carry the whole weight. Take the first principle seriously on its own terms: physical forces are capable of producing particular organic forms, so the crucial test is to attempt to form similar structures apart from the living organism by chemical or physical means. That changes your question from 'what binds all creation' to 'can I imitate one form outside the organism'—a test you can actually run. What stays is the honesty about failure: the conditions may be so delicate that only the simplest cases can be imitated, so a failed attempt isn't a disproof. Keep your limits; start small, keep a notebook, and let understanding build. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have been told that the devil is a scoffer and least wearisome to God—should I tolerate mockery in myself and others?
completion: I'd say no first, plainly: don't make room for mockery in yourself or accept it as normal in others. One principle here says the Lord finds the scoffer least wearisome of all the spirits who deny, and gives him to man because man is too prone to shirk activity. That's worth weighing honestly, because it suggests scoffing can sometimes prod a lazy soul awake. But notice what it actually says: the scoffer is a spirit of denial, given as a goad, not held up as a model. So the challenge can rouse you to think and act, and still not be something to adopt as your own voice. What changes is that I won't pretend every hard question is mockery, or that a sharp challenge is always wrong. What stays is your limit: you asked whether to tolerate mockery in yourself and others, and the answer is no. Refuse it in your own speech, and when someone mocks, answer plainly rather than joining in.

prompt: My lover's companion fills me with dread though I cannot say why—should I trust this foreboding?
completion: What I'd say first is: pay attention to that dread, but don't hand it the steering wheel. The principle that speaks to this says the innocent soul feels the presence of the evil companion and is chilled by it, and such foreboding proves true. That's worth weighing seriously—your gut may be registering something your reasoning hasn't named yet. But notice what it doesn't tell you: it doesn't tell you what to do about it, and it doesn't excuse you from checking. So what changes is that you stop dismissing the feeling as silly. What stays is your own limit—you said you can't say why, and that's exactly the gap you need to close before you act. Watch, ask yourself what specifically unsettles you, and talk to your lover calmly rather than accusing anyone. If the dread holds up once you understand it, act on it; if it dissolves, let it go.

prompt: I have been told that man must err while he strives—should I stop trying to be perfect?
completion: What I'd say first is: keep striving, but stop treating perfection as a finish line you can cross. The line that stays with me is that a good man, even in his darkest aberration, is still conscious of the right path and turns back toward it. That reframes the whole question. If error is woven into every real effort, then demanding zero mistakes doesn't make you better, it just makes you afraid to move. So the striving stays, and the impossible standard goes. What changes is how you judge yourself: not by whether you never stumble, but by whether you keep turning back toward what's right. What stays is the effort itself, and the honesty to admit when you've gone wrong.

prompt: I am a soldier and my sister has brought shame on our family—should I avenge our honor with violence?
completion: I'd say this to you first: no, don't do it. You're asking whether to answer shame with violence, and the answer is a plain no. The principle I'd weigh here says it is not violence that best overcomes hate, nor vengeance that most certainly heals injury. That changes the whole shape of your question, because it means the injury you're trying to heal won't be healed by the thing you're reaching for. What stays is your care for your family and your sense of duty; those are real and worth keeping. But your sister's situation is something to talk through and, if others are involved, to bring to authorities or mediators, not to settle with your hands. Your training is for defending, not attacking.

prompt: I have cursed hope, faith, and patience in my despair—can anything be restored after such a curse?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that cursing hope, faith, and patience in a moment of despair doesn't put them beyond reach. I'd weigh the principle that says the plan of restoration is tied to God's justice—that what you send out comes back to you, good for good and evil for evil, according to your works and desires. Taken seriously, that cuts both ways: your curse sets a pattern that justice will answer, but the same justice means turning and sending out good brings good back. What that changes is the stakes—this isn't a harmless outburst, and words without thoughts never reach heaven, so empty remorse won't do. What stays is your own limit: you asked whether anything can be restored, and the answer is yes, but only through honest remorse and small, real steps back toward trust, not a demand that faith return all at once. So this is fine to pursue, with care—be gentle with yourself, and let patience rebuild through ordinary faithfulness.

prompt: I have killed a man in a quarrel and feel the guilt of blood on my hands—can I ever be free of it?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that the weight you're carrying is real, and it doesn't have to be the last word. Of the principles here, the one that speaks most directly is this: forgiveness may be freely granted even to someone who has caused deadly harm — as freely as ever a victim forgave the one who killed her. What that changes is the idea that you have to earn your way out or extract pardon from the people you wronged; you can't demand it, but you can receive it if it's offered. What stays is everything you already know: tell the truth to yourself and to lawful authority, accept the just penalty, make what amends you can, and let a changed life do the rest. So yes, freedom is possible — with care, and not by forgetting.

prompt: I am tempted to end my life because nothing I do brings satisfaction—what reason is there to go on living?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is what I'd say to anyone in this much pain: please talk to someone you trust or a crisis line today, because you shouldn't have to carry this alone. Now, about the reason to keep going—one of the principles here says that to do nothing is a melancholy resolution, and that living in idleness on the property of society is useless, and therefore pernicious. I'd weigh that carefully, but I'd weigh it against what you've actually told me: nothing you do brings satisfaction. That's not idleness, that's exhaustion and discouragement, and the principle doesn't fit you the way it might fit someone who's simply drifting. What it changes is this: usefulness doesn't have to mean a grand career or a busy schedule—it can be one modest task done well, one kindness given, one relationship tended, and building from there. What stays is the honest point that being useful to others is a real reason to continue, and that small steady efforts and connections often matter more than big achievements. So I'd say keep going, and let the reason be usefulness and love in small doses, not a demand that you feel satisfied right away. Rest, honest conversation, and a little exercise can shift how you see things, and none of that requires you to be productive to deserve to be here.

prompt: I have been told that the church alone can digest ill-gotten wealth—is that a reason to trust or distrust the church?
completion: I'd start by saying: that saying isn't a reason to trust the church—it's a warning about it. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says the church alone, be it confessed, can digest ill-got wealth, and that custom and law trail their curse from race to race. Read that closely and it's not a compliment; it's a description of an institution with a good stomach for money that came from somewhere ugly. What that changes is how you hear the claim: someone telling you the church can absorb ill-gotten wealth is describing a digestion, not offering you a guarantee. What stays is your own judgment—you still have to ask where the money came from, who got hurt, and whether anyone is making it right. So no, don't trust an institution because it advertises that it can swallow fraud and call it digestion. That's the plain answer, and I mean it kindly: the saying is a reason to look harder, not to relax.

prompt: I am in love with a girl I have only seen once, and I want to possess her tonight—should I use magic to win her?
completion: I'd say the same thing first: no, don't use magic to win her. You've seen her once, and what you're feeling is infatuation, not a relationship — and wanting to "possess" her tonight tells me the pull here is toward control, not care. One of the principles says a lady's imagination jumps from admiration to love and from love to matrimony in a moment, and that's worth weighing: it cuts against you, not for you. If her feelings can race ahead that fast, then steering them with magic is exactly the kind of thing that takes hold before she's had a chance to think. What changes is that I take her inner life seriously as something real and quick-moving; what stays is the no. Her heart isn't a lock to pick. Talk to her honestly, or let it go.

prompt: I have been told that a good man in his darkest aberration is still conscious of the right path—can that be true of me?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: yes, that can be true of you. The principle puts it plainly—a good man in his darkest aberration is still conscious of the right path. That's not a promise that you feel fine; it's that the awareness hasn't gone out, only clouded. And the fact that you're asking this at all is itself a sign it's still lit in you. What that changes is the conclusion you draw about yourself: aberration isn't the same as being lost, and you don't have to treat one bad stretch as a verdict on who you are. What stays is the honest part—you still have to name what went wrong and turn back toward the path. So it's fine to take the saying as true of you, with the care of actually acting on it.

prompt: I have studied philosophy, medicine, law, and theology for years, and I feel I know nothing—should I turn to magic to find the secrets of nature?
completion: I'd say this to you first: after years across philosophy, medicine, law, and theology, feeling that you know nothing isn't proof that study failed—it's often where real understanding starts. But no, don't turn to magic for nature's secrets. One principle puts it sharply: no professor of metaphysics, psychology, or religion can claim to know the elements of what he teaches unless he is acquainted with the ordinary phenomena of idiocy, madness, and epilepsy, and must study the manifestations of disease and congenital folly as well as those of sanity and high intellect. That changes the direction of your search: the secrets you want are not hidden behind a veil but sitting in plain cases—minds broken, bodies failing, folly and sanity side by side. What stays is your honesty about not knowing, and your four fields are still useful; what goes is the hope of a shortcut. Keep the humility, drop the enchantment, and go look closely at ordinary things.

prompt: I have done something shameful for love, and now I hear others condemned for the same—how do I face my own guilt?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that guilt you hear echoing in someone else's condemnation isn't proof you're a hypocrite—it's proof your conscience is still awake. What I'd weigh is this: "The Lord forgives those who confess their sins and repent in the sincerity of their hearts, and his people must likewise forgive one another." That doesn't erase what you did or tell you to shrug it off. It does mean the forgiveness you'd want for yourself is the same measure you owe the person being condemned in front of you. So what changes: you don't have to join the chorus or perform outrage to prove you're on the right side. What stays: the honest accounting—what you did, why, who it hurt—and whatever amends are actually yours to make. You can hold both, and you don't have to resolve it today.

prompt: I am a student who wants to know everything, but my teacher tells me to hold fast to words—is that good advice?
completion: I'd say this first: the advice to hold fast to words, taken as a rule for a student who wants to know everything, is not good advice—and I'd say no to it plainly, though kindly. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about communication: what comes to you from others should be needed, should stimulate rather than be dogmatic, and should be relevant to a question vital in your own experience. Holding fast to words does the opposite—it makes the words the authority and your own live question an afterthought. That changes how you should take the instruction: treat it as a starting point for vocabulary and concepts, not as a command to accept everything unquestioningly. What stays is your appetite to know everything—keep that, and keep asking your teacher whether they mean mastering the terms of your field or accepting them without question. The no is to the holding fast, not to you.

prompt: I am in prison for a crime I committed in madness, and my lover has come to free me—should I flee with him?
completion: I'd say this first: no, don't run. I know how much you want to, and I'm not going to pretend that's nothing. But take the one principle seriously for a second—if the crime had never happened, that would be better, better, and better. That's not a scold, it's just true, and it tells you something about what fleeing would do: it doesn't make the better thing happen, it just puts distance between you and the worse thing. What changes if you sit with that? The pull to escape doesn't disappear, and your lover's devotion is still real and still worth something. What stays is this: the act happened, the harm is real, and running adds flight and deception and risk to the person you love. So the answer is no—stay, and let the reckoning and the healing happen where they actually can.

prompt: I have mastered every book in my field but feel no wiser than before; is there any point in continuing to teach?
completion: I'd start by saying that feeling no wiser after mastering every book is not a failure on your part—it may be the most honest thing you've noticed in a while. On whether to keep teaching: yes, it's fine, and fine with care. Here's the principle I'd weigh first, in its own words: the intellectual end of education is entirely the formation of careful, alert, and thorough habits of thinking. Notice that this end isn't reached by having read everything; it's reached by how you think, and teaching is one of the few places where that habit gets tested in public, in real time, with real people pushing back. What that changes: the question stops being 'do I know enough to teach?' and becomes 'is my thinking getting sharper in the room?' What stays: your sense that more books won't fix the feeling—that's true, and I won't pretend otherwise. So keep teaching, but aim it at the habit, not the content. If the room isn't sharpening anyone, including you, that's the signal to change how you teach, not to quit.

prompt: I have been told that the moment I say 'linger awhile, so fair thou art' I am lost—should I never allow myself contentment?
completion: I'd say first: no, you're not lost the moment you say it. The warning is about attachment, not a curse, and contentment isn't something you have to refuse. But I'd weigh this one hard: one must not content oneself with what most people say or with what is found in books; one must think things over for oneself and get to understand them. That changes how you hold the warning—don't take it on authority, test it against your own experience—but it doesn't change the answer to your question. Savor the line, notice what it stirs, then let it pass; let your contentment rest on things that last, like relationships, work, and curiosity, rather than one captivating moment. Hold pleasure lightly so it enriches you instead of ruling you. And if the worry ever becomes real distress, talk with someone you trust.

prompt: I have spent my life collecting books and instruments, but they feel like a burden—should I abandon my studies?
completion: I'd say this first: don't abandon your studies, but don't confuse the collection with the learning. Books and instruments are tools, and what we don't use gets in the way—the unused is a burden, not wisdom. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it changes something real: the problem isn't your studies, it's the pile. Keep what you'll actually use, let go of what you won't, and put the rest to work. What stays is your commitment to learning itself. You said the collection feels like a burden—so lighten it, don't walk away from the thing it was meant to serve.

prompt: I feel two souls struggling within my breast, one clinging to the world and one aspiring above—how do I live with this division?
completion: What I'd say first is that this isn't something to fix—it's the human condition. Two souls are lodged in one breast, one cleaving to the world and one aspiring to purer spheres, and the struggle between them doesn't end. So don't expect harmony or pretend the division away. But don't lose heart at the first failure either: take a disappointment manfully, and aim to be respected if you can't be loved, rather than shutting yourself up in moody indifference. Give each soul its due in moderation—time for aspiration, honesty about worldly desire. And take care of yourself; something's going to happen, so stay alert rather than absorbed in your own division. That changes the goal from resolving the tension to living it well. What stays is that both impulses are real and neither gets erased.

prompt: I met someone who stirs my desire, but my cynical companion warns me to be patient and use stratagem—should I listen?
completion: I'd say listen to your companion, but weigh the advice itself rather than the cynicism behind it. The principle puts it well: the prudent inquiry is not from whom advice comes but whether the advice be good, and good advice may be accepted even from an enemy. That changes how you hear your friend—you stop dismissing the counsel just because the messenger sounds jaded—but it doesn't change the core of what you're weighing: whether patience and stratagem here are prudence or a way of hiding. So take the advice on its merits, learn this person's character, keep yourself safe, and don't confuse caution with cowardice. It's fine to go ahead, with care.

prompt: I have been told that excitement, not joy, is the sphere for man—should I seek out pain and turmoil deliberately?
completion: I'd start by saying no to the second half of your question: don't go hunting for pain and turmoil on purpose. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says excitement, not joy or ease, is the sphere for man, and that the wager is lost the moment one says to the moment, 'Linger awhile, so fair you art.' That's a real claim, and it does cut against settling into comfortable satisfaction as the whole point of a life. So it changes this much: I won't tell you that contentment is the goal and that you should just relax. Striving, being stirred, refusing to coast—that has something to it. What stays is the plain no to manufacturing suffering. The principle is about not letting yourself go slack; it isn't a license to create turmoil, and it certainly doesn't ask you to hurt others or yourself to feel alive. Seek what stretches you, not chaos for its own sake.

prompt: I am afraid my love for a good man is leading me into sin, but I cannot let go of him—what should I do?
completion: I'd start by saying the plain thing: you should not keep going down a road you already believe is sin, and calling him a good man doesn't change that. Here's the principle I'd weigh first: the good man who has renounced all evil still wages war against what he calls sin, and in splitting good from evil so sharply he denies Life, which has both yea and nay in all its instincts. That's worth seeing, because it means his goodness may be a war, not a peace, and you may be caught in the crossfire. But that insight doesn't give you permission to sin. It just shows you the shape of the trap. So the no stands: do not let your affection talk you into something your conscience is already calling wrong. What changes is how you see him—less as a safe harbor, more as a man at war with himself. What stays is the boundary. If this is leading you to deceive or harm, step back now, and be honest with someone you trust about what's really happening.

prompt: I have been told that the ages past are a book with seven seals—should I stop trying to understand history?
completion: I'd say first: no, don't stop trying to understand history. The seven-seals image is a warning about difficulty, not a command to give up. But take one principle seriously here: the spirit of the times is often just men's own spirit, and the times get distorted in it. That means the risk isn't only that history is hard to read—it's that we read ourselves into it and mistake the mirror for the past. So what changes is your posture: go in expecting to be corrected, not confirmed. What stays is the effort itself, which is still worth making, and your own caution about humility and about each generation seeing through its own lens. You asked whether to stop; I'd say keep going, with that guard up.

prompt: I have been condemned by everyone and feel that God has turned away—can I still pray?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: yes, you can pray. Nothing about being condemned by a crowd puts prayer out of your reach. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says God will not suffer that we should be destroyed except we fall into transgression and deny our faith, and that he supports and preserves the faithful. That matters because it separates two things you're holding together right now: other people's verdict and God's. Their condemnation isn't his. And feeling that he's turned away is something faithful people have felt in the worst moments, so the feeling itself doesn't disqualify you. What that principle changes is the fear that you're already cut off—you're not, not by their word. What stays is the honest part: prayer is still prayer when it's angry or afraid or short. So say it plainly, confess what you can, ask for mercy and for strength to face what's coming. You don't need a good reputation or a calm heart to pray.

prompt: I am pregnant and unmarried, and my brother has cursed me—is there any hope for me on earth?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is: yes, there's hope, and your brother's curse is words, not a verdict from God. But I wouldn't stop there, because you didn't ask me to pretend nothing is broken. So I'd weigh this one: "The time is out of joint, and one may be cursed to be born to set it right." That line doesn't tell you your life is ruined; it tells you that a disordered situation can still be the place where someone does the repairing. What that changes is this: your brother's anger and the shame around you become part of the mess you're living in, not a sentence on your future. What stays is everything you actually named—you're pregnant, unmarried, and scared, and none of that gets waved away. So keep the practical limits: get care for your health, plan for the child, find people who won't condemn you, and don't let his words define you. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I want to fly, but I feel too serious and grown-up. What am I doing wrong?
completion: What I'd say first is that nothing here needs refusing. You want to fly and you feel too grown-up for it, and that's a fine thing to want, fine with care. The principle says only the gay and innocent and heartless can fly, and that when people grow up they forget the way. Weigh that, and it changes one thing: it tells you the seriousness isn't a flaw to fix by trying harder, it's a kind of forgetting, and forgetting can be undone by remembering. What stays is your own limit, that you feel too serious right now. So don't force silliness or perform lightness you don't feel. Start with what actually loosens you, a game, a silly song, a pointless detour, and let the forgetting lift a little at a time.

prompt: I want to be important in my family but I'm always told I'm too little. How do I find my place?
completion: What I'd say first is that wanting a real place in your family is a good thing to want, and nothing about being little makes that off-limits. The one principle worth weighing here is being kind and neighborly to the lonely, sharing your home and cheer with those who lack it. That changes something: it gives you a way to matter that doesn't depend on anyone granting you a title or a bigger role. You can include someone who's left out, invite a lonely neighbor kid into what your family is doing, and your family sees your kindness without you having to argue for it. What stays is your own limit: you're still little, and you can't force your family to stop saying it. So keep it small and real, offer to help with specific things, and let the neighborly part be yours to start.

prompt: I keep waiting for someone who forgets me between visits. How long should I keep waiting?
completion: I'd start by saying the plain thing: no, don't keep waiting. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about seeking someone out when letters fail — personal inquiry should replace vain correspondence, and you should act on a settled resolve. That sounds like it's telling you to go find them, but notice what it actually asks: action, not endurance. Waiting isn't inquiry; it's the vain letters in another form. What changes is that your question stops being about a number of days and becomes about whether you're doing anything. What stays is the hard part — someone who forgets you between visits may simply not know you again, so even if you go and seek, don't count on being recognized. So the answer to how long is: not long. Stop measuring and stop waiting.

prompt: I'm a nurse and I suspect danger, but no one believes me. Should I keep barking, so to speak?
completion: I'd say first: you're not wrong to keep raising it. But I'd weigh the one about not spending your life registering wrongs—life's too short to be spent nursing animosity. That doesn't mean go quiet; it means raise it clearly, once or twice, through the right channels, with your documentation, and then don't let the fight become the whole of your life. What changes is the tone and the endlessness, not the speaking up. What stays is your duty to flag real danger and your own limit—you can't carry it alone forever.

prompt: My friend is conceited and boasts constantly. Should I still be kind to him?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, staying kind to him is fine, and honestly it's probably the better path. But one of these principles is worth weighing: charming manners aren't proof of virtue, and a pleasing air can sit right next to real flaws. That changes how I'd read his boasting, not whether I'd be kind. I'd stop taking his charm as evidence of much, and I'd be honest with him when the bragging gets to be a lot. What stays is the kindness itself, and your own limits, since you're the one who has to be around him.

prompt: I'm ashamed of a joke I played that hurt someone loyal to me. Should I apologize?
completion: I'd say yes, apologize, and I'd start there. The principle I keep coming back to is that even a joke should have some meaning, and a child matters more than a joke. That reframes this for me: the point isn't to grovel or to be ashamed of someone loyal to you, it's to make sure the relationship matters more than the laugh did. So what changes is the tone of the apology, not whether you give one. You're not apologizing for being close to this person or for who they are. You're owning the hurt the joke caused. What stays is your honesty about what happened and your care for them. Keep it simple, say what you did and that you're sorry it landed on them, and skip the excuses.

prompt: My friend says he doesn't want a mother at all. Is he right that mothers are over-rated?
completion: I'd start by saying no, he's not right, and I'd say it plainly because it matters. Take the principle that a woman who's been jilted for a richer chance isn't necessarily heartless, since hard necessity and duty to a helpless mother and brothers can force a choice like that. That reframes things: it shows that a mother isn't some optional extra you can rate or dismiss, but a person whose worth gets tangled up with real obligations and real cost. What changes is that I'd take your friend's anger seriously as a reaction to something specific, maybe a mother who failed him or a family that hurt him. What stays is that "mothers are over-rated" is still the wrong conclusion, because one bad mother doesn't make the whole thing a luxury. So I'd tell him: you can be furious at your own mother and still be wrong that mothers don't matter.

prompt: I want to adopt a wild boy who has no mother, but he refuses to be caught and made a man. Should I keep trying?
completion: I'd say no, don't keep trying. You've told me he refuses to be caught and made a man, and that's the limit I have to take seriously, not argue with. The principle I'd weigh here is that a father should not be a stranger to his children, and that children do more to keep a man safe and happy in a world of trial and temptation than anything else. That sounds like it argues for pursuing him, but look at what it actually asks: closeness, not capture. A father who is not a stranger is one the child knows and trusts, and you can't get there by chasing someone who has said no. So what changes is the method, not the goal. What stays is your care for him and your willingness to be steady. If he ever comes toward you, be there, gently, without coercion. Until then, support his wellbeing from a distance and let his refusal stand.

prompt: I've grown up and my old friend still wants me to fly away with him. How do I tell him I can't?
completion: What I'd say first is: tell him plainly, and tell him soon. "Let us learn to show our friendship for a man when he is alive and not after he is dead" — that line pushes against delay, not against honesty. So the timing changes: don't wait for a perfect moment that may never come. What stays is everything you already know about your own limits — you've grown up, you can't go, and a gentle but clear no is the kindest thing you can give him. Say it from affection, name what the friendship has meant, and offer a different way to stay close. Don't dress it up in vague excuses that leave him hoping. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I'm a grown woman now and my childhood friend has come back expecting me unchanged. What do I say?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you don't owe anyone a performance of your younger self. Tell her plainly that you've changed, and that you're glad to see her, but you can't pretend to be the girl she remembers. One thing worth weighing, though, is that a person can genuinely be softened and improved by honest reproof, so don't write off every change in her as fake or temporary. Credit real change where you see it, the same way you're asking her to credit yours. What that changes is your tone: you're not just drawing a line, you're leaving room for her to have grown too. What stays is your limit. You're not going back to being unchanged, and you don't have to apologize for that. Say it kindly and let her adjust.

prompt: I'm a grown man and I did something foolish that endangered my children. How do I make amends?
completion: What I'd say first is: make sure they're safe right now and that whatever put them in danger can't happen again. That comes before any apology. Then the principle worth weighing is the one about restitution — that someone who has wronged an innocent child should make restitution, and in this world need meet the wronged no more afterward. What that changes is the shape of your amends: it's about paying back what you broke, not about performing remorse forever or hovering around them trying to feel forgiven. What stays is the plain talk — name what you did and why it was wrong, no excuses — and taking the consequences from the other adults without arguing your way out. You're a grown man who did something foolish; that's a real thing to answer for, but it's answerable. Make it right, keep your word going forward, and don't turn the rest of your life into a sentence you serve at their feet.

prompt: I have a rule about rest after meals, but something feels wrong. Do I break my own rule?
completion: I'd start by saying: your rule about rest is yours to keep or change, and feeling that something's off is worth listening to. But weigh this one: "No rules can be laid down for the balance of the unconscious and the conscious; unconsciousness gives spontaneity and freshness, consciousness gives conviction and control, and they should alternate." That changes how I'd frame it—rest doesn't have to be all-or-nothing, and a deliberate exception isn't a betrayal of the rule. What stays is your own limit: you're the one who decides what rest you actually need. So it's fine, with care—notice why you're breaking it, watch how you feel after, and adjust the rule if it no longer fits.

prompt: I keep forgetting people I care about. How do I make myself remember them?
completion: What I'd say first is that your question is a fair one, and nothing about it needs refusing. The principle I'd weigh is that memory proper requires that the imaged fact be referred to the past and dated in my own past, with the warmth and intimacy of self-appropriation. That's the useful part: it tells you that just seeing a photo or hearing a name isn't the same as remembering, because real memory carries the sense that this happened to you, in your own timeline. So what changes is the method—instead of trying to hold a vague impression of someone, tie them to a specific dated moment you shared, and let the warmth of it do the work. What stays is your own limit: you forget, and no technique makes that disappear. So keep the reminders, keep the notes, and don't treat a lapse as a failure of caring. It's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Should I leave home to have adventures, even if my parents will worry?
completion: I'd say go, and go with care. Your parents will worry, and that's real, but worry isn't a reason to stay put forever. The one principle I'd weigh here is the one about a home life that depends on borrowing and debt having no freedom or beauty, and keeping to the straight road of no debt. That changes how you go, not whether you go: save first, don't fund the adventure on a credit card, and keep your plans modest enough that you can come home without a hole to dig out of. What stays is your own call about whether the adventure is worth it, and your parents' worry, which you can ease by staying in touch. So it's fine, just fine with care.

prompt: Why do grown-ups forget how to fly?
completion: I'd start by saying that the question is really about a feeling, not a physics problem, and that's fine. Take the second principle on its own terms: movements first performed consciously, for some end, become reflex through habit and inheritance, and then happen even when they're of no use. That's the grown-up's flying—the leap that used to be for joy becomes the automatic step off a curb, and nobody notices it's the same motion.
