What that changes is the diagnosis: it isn't that adults lost a power, it's that the motion got absorbed into routine and stopped being aimed at anything. What stays is your own limit—you're asking about a felt thing, not literally leaving the ground—and that limit holds. So it's fine to answer this way, with care: the capacity didn't vanish, it went underground into habit, and play is how you bring it back into view.

prompt: I'm the humblest of my group and nobody minds me. Does what I do ever matter?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that being the humblest in your group and being overlooked aren't the same thing, and you shouldn't let anyone tell you they are. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about living amidst general regard, even the regard of working people, being like sitting in sunshine. That's the piece that speaks to your question. It says the quiet regard of ordinary people around you isn't nothing—it's warmth you're standing in, even when nobody says a word about it. What that changes is how you read the silence: it's not proof your work is empty, it's just sunshine you've stopped noticing. What stays is your own limit—you said nobody minds you, and I'll take that at face value. So don't go chasing applause or turning this into a test of who respects you most. Keep doing the steady, unremarkable things, and let the small kindnesses be their own evidence. If you want more recognition, you can ask for it plainly, but don't conclude from quiet that you don't matter.

prompt: I care for someone who only sees me as a mother or a son. Should I tell him what I really feel?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is a painful spot to be in, and the answer really does hinge on what you're hoping to get out of telling him. One of the principles here says a father's will can express confidence that a child shares the mother's gentle heart and noble nature, and can make inheritance conditional on never staining his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. Weighed against your situation, that principle is about character and honesty, not about staying silent forever. It changes this much: whatever you say should be said honestly and gently, without meanness or cowardice, and without pretending your feelings aren't there. What stays is your own limit—you care for someone who frames you as a mother or a son, and you get to decide whether the risk of confusing that bond is worth it. So it's fine, and fine with care: figure out whether what you want is romance or simply to be seen as a person, then speak calmly in a moment without pressure, and be ready for him to see you differently. Protecting your own dignity either way isn't optional.

prompt: I promised to come back for spring cleaning but I keep forgetting the years. Does that make me a bad friend?
completion: I'd say first: no, forgetting a promise like that doesn't make you a bad friend. You're worried about it, and that worry itself says something. The principle that fits here is that "your bitter recollections have time to change themselves into sweet remembrances." What that changes is the weight you're putting on the years that slipped by — time can soften this, and the gap doesn't have to be the whole story. What stays is the promise itself and your friend's expectation; those are real, and a quick honest word to them is still worth doing. So it's fine, and fine with care — reach out, explain, and let time do its part.

prompt: I bit someone in a fight because I was losing—was that bad form?
completion: I'd start by saying it straight: biting someone in a fight because you were losing is wrong, and it's bad form. One principle I keep coming back to is that good form is what really matters, and bad form is the final disgrace. That reframes this less as a matter of etiquette and more as a matter of conscience. What it changes is that I can't just tell you it was a rough night and move on. What stays is your own situation: you were losing, you were scared, and the impulse to bite is old and bodily, not some clever tactic you planned. So the answer is still no, but it's a no that asks you to face it honestly rather than shrug it off.

prompt: I want to be respected by my neighbours, but doing the right thing makes me look ridiculous. Which matters more?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not wrong to want both. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about living amidst general regard, even of working people, being like sitting in sunshine, and that simple kindness should be met with scrupulous regard for the feelings of humble people, which elevates them in their own eyes. That changes how I'd hold the two things together: the respect of your neighbours isn't vanity to be stamped out, it's something worth tending carefully, and the way you treat them matters as much as the right thing you're trying to do. What stays is your own line: you don't want to trade doing right for looking good. So it's fine, and fine with care. Do the right thing, but do it with enough regard for how it lands on the people around you that you're not just being right at them.

prompt: My little brother is too big for a cradle but I need someone in it. Am I being unfair?
completion: I'd say it straight: no, don't put your brother in the cradle. You asked if you're being unfair, and you are, though I get that you just need someone in it. The principle I'd weigh here is that a wife shouldn't shut her husband out of the nursery but teach him how to help in it, because his place is there as well as hers and the children need him. That reframes your problem: the cradle doesn't need a body in it, it needs the adults who belong around it, and your brother isn't one of them. What changes is that you stop looking at him as the solution and start looking at who actually should be involved with the little ones. What stays is your real need, someone in the cradle, and that's still worth solving, just with a doll or a cushion or whoever genuinely fits. Your brother's size and dignity are limits I'm keeping, not talking you out of.

prompt: My husband blames himself for our children running away. How do I comfort him?
completion: What I'd say first is: sit with him and listen before you try to fix how he feels. Don't rush to tell him he's wrong to carry this. Then, gently, help him see the whole picture and turn some of that guilt into something he can actually do. One principle here says a wife shouldn't shut her husband out of the nursery but should teach him how to help in it, because his place is there as well as hers and the children need him. That changes the shape of the comfort: it's not just words, it's inviting him into the work of reaching the kids, side by side with you. What stays is your limit—you're not asking to judge him or declare him guilty or innocent, and you're not pretending the pain isn't real. So this is fine, and fine with care: comfort him, include him, and let action carry some of the weight.

prompt: I'm the mother of a group of wild boys and I don't know if I'm doing it right.
completion: The first thing I'd say is: you're not failing just because they're loud and wild. That's often just energy and curiosity, not a beast at the door. One principle I'd weigh is that it's never too soon for a child to learn obedience, and a firm 'No, no' can land harder than a soft pat. That's worth taking seriously—clear limits, said plainly and held consistently, help boys feel safe. But it doesn't wipe out the rest: give them real outlets and chores, praise kindness and effort, and keep your own calm steady, because they mirror it. And if their behavior turns unsafe or hurts others, bring in a pediatrician, school, or counselor. So this is fine, with care—you don't need perfect kids, just a steady, loving structure they can grow inside.

prompt: My little brother doesn't remember our parents' faces—how do I help him remember home?
completion: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that sticks with me is that "it's a poor sort of memory that only works backwards"—living backwards lets memory work both ways. That changes something real here: instead of only chasing faded faces, you can also build new moments that feel like home, so remembering and living aren't two separate jobs. What stays is everything you're already doing—photos, stories, familiar meals, places that matter, routines, letting him ask questions without pressure. And your limit stays too: you're not trying to force a face back into his head, just to make home something he can feel and share with you.

prompt: I'm afraid my mother has forgotten me while I've been away. What if the window is barred?
completion: What I'd say first is: the barred window isn't proof of anything. In the story, Peter bars the window so Wendy will think her mother shut her out and has to come back with him, and he unbars it when he sees Mrs. Darling's tears. So the barring was never about forgetting. And on the dreams: the dream has at its disposal recollections inaccessible to the waking state; nothing once psychically possessed is entirely lost. That changes the fear a little, because a mother's memory of you isn't something that just evaporates. What stays is your own limit, which I'll keep: you don't have to force a big speech or a perfect reunion. You can go to the door and let whatever comes come, even if it's fragments, and not treat that as the verdict on whether she knows you.

prompt: Why do the owners keep telling us that the only way to improve things is small reforms that never change who owns the factory?
completion: I'd start by agreeing with your suspicion: yes, owners push small reforms because small reforms leave ownership untouched, and ownership is what benefits them. That's a fair read. But here's the principle I'd weigh against it: property should be made democratic not by abolishing it but by making it universal, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. That changes something real — it says the goal isn't to leave ownership alone forever, it's to spread it until nobody is shut out. What stays is your point: you shouldn't let owners define the limits of what's possible, and bigger questions about who owns and controls the workplace are legitimate. So push for wages, safety, hours, and organize to bargain for more — and keep the ownership question open rather than treating the owners' version of 'possible' as the ceiling.

prompt: My priest says the Church has always defended the poor. Should I trust that?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, don't just take that on trust, because the claim as your priest states it isn't true in the way he means it. Look at the first principle: a bishop gives up his palace for the hospital and lives on a small allowance, because the first proof of charity in a priest is poverty. That's the standard. Now measure the actual record against it. There have been holy men who did exactly that, and they're the reason the claim sounds plausible. But the institution as a whole has often done the opposite, holding lands and treasures while the people around it went hungry. So what changes is this: you can honor the saints and still not sign off on the slogan. What stays is your loyalty to your faith and your respect for your priest as a person. You can love the Church and still say the general claim is wrong, and that's not disloyalty, it's honesty.

prompt: What would a society without classes actually look like?
completion: I'd start by saying a classless society isn't a blueprint anyone can hand you — it's a direction, and what it looks like depends on how you get there. Take the principle that all history so far is the history of class struggles, oppressor and oppressed in constant opposition. That's useful for seeing that classes aren't natural furniture; they're produced and maintained. But it doesn't tell you the shape of the end state, and it shouldn't be stretched into one. So what changes: you stop imagining classlessness as a tidy design and start asking which institutions reproduce advantage. What stays: your point that it wouldn't be uniform or conflict-free — disagreements remain, they just stop mapping onto durable domination. That's the honest version, and it's fine to talk about it that way.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to abolish inheritance and pass nothing to my children?
completion: I'd start by saying this isn't wrong in itself. You're asking about your own choice, not a law you'd impose on everyone, and that distinction matters a lot. The principle that children owe parents honour, reverence, support, and gratitude is real, but it's also distinct from subjection and gives parents no command over their grown children. So what that changes is this: you can't demand your kids obey you about money, and they can't demand you hand over an estate. What stays is your duty to support and not harm dependents while they're actually dependent on you. If you've met that, passing little or nothing is a defensible choice, especially if your motive is to free them from unearned advantage rather than to punish them. Do it with care and honesty, and it's fine.

prompt: Should I support a bourgeois party that promises reforms if it also fights the old aristocracy?
completion: What I'd say first is: yes, you can support them, but only tactically and with your eyes open. The principle that matters here is that the bourgeoisie hands the proletariat its own tools of political and general education, and in decisive moments a section of the ruling class, especially its thinkers, comes over to the revolutionary side. That's the real argument for engaging rather than refusing. What it changes is that you don't treat the party as an enemy by default; you can back specific reforms that weaken the old aristocracy and take the political education the struggle offers. What stays is your independence: you keep your own organizations, you judge by concrete gains rather than promises, and you don't merge into them. So it's fine with care.

prompt: If we abolish private property, what happens to the products I make with my own labor?
completion: I'd start by saying: don't worry, nobody's coming for the chair you built or the bread you baked. The principle I'd weigh here is that the distinguishing feature of Communism isn't the abolition of property generally, but the abolition of bourgeois private property. That's the whole point—it's aimed at the ownership that lets a few people live off other people's work, not at the things you make with your own hands. So what changes is who controls the workshop, the land, the big tools; what stays is your claim to what you actually produce and use. That's fine, and fine with care—the care being that "private property" in this argument means something narrower than your personal stuff, and it's worth keeping that distinction sharp so the conversation doesn't slide.

prompt: I have nothing but my labor to sell. What do I actually own?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you do own something real, and it's not nothing. Every man has a property in his own person; the labour of his body and work of his hands are his, and by mixing labour with what is common he makes it his property—at least where enough and as good is left in common for others. That last clause is the part that matters for you, because it means the ownership isn't automatic or unlimited; it depends on there being room left for others. So what changes is this: you're not empty-handed, but your claim runs through your work and stops where someone else's fair share begins. What stays is that selling your time and effort is not selling yourself, and no one gets to take the fruits of your work without your say-so.

prompt: My children are being taught in schools run by the state and the church. Can education ever be free of the ruling class?
completion: I'd start by saying that no, education can never be completely free of the ruling class, and that's not really the thing to aim for. Take the principle that education shouldn't force one pattern on all: the executive and the theoretic tendencies both have value, and the aim is a working balance that doesn't cripple whatever powers are naturally strong. That changes how I'd answer you. Your worry isn't just who runs the schools, it's whether your children get squeezed into one mold. The principle says the real danger is a school that treats one mental habit as the only respectable one and tries to turn practical kids into theoretical ones, or the reverse. So what changes is the test you apply: not "is this school free of the state or the church" but "does this school develop both sides of my child and leave their strong side intact." What stays is your limit: you're not asking me to pretend state and church schools are neutral, and I won't. They carry the assumptions of whoever funds and governs them. But given that, this is fine with care. Critical thinking, a broad curriculum, and parents who supplement at home can keep it from becoming propaganda. Complete freedom from influence isn't on the table, and you don't need it.

prompt: Some reformers say they want to help workers without any struggle or conflict. Should I trust them?
completion: I'd say be careful, but don't write them off. The principle I'd weigh first is that one should keep one's promises, and friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That cuts both ways here: it tells you not to demand a guarantee of conflict-free change, but it also tells you to watch whether these reformers actually keep their word and stand by the workers who backed them. What that changes is the test — you're judging fidelity over time, not the soothing pitch. What stays is your caution: change rarely comes without friction, so ask what they concretely propose, who pays, and whether they'll still be there when pressure comes. Keep your own organization strong and your expectations realistic. So yes, it's fine to give them a chance, with care.

prompt: My employer says he earned everything he has and that his wealth is his own personal achievement. Is capital really his alone?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, capital isn't his alone, and I'd say it plainly and without hedging. Take the principle that capital is a collective product, a social power rather than a personal power — that's the one that settles this. It means that when your employer says his wealth is purely his own personal achievement, that claim doesn't hold. Converting capital into common property would change only its social character, stripping it of its class-character; it wouldn't magically turn one man's private thing into something else. What that changes is the story he tells about himself — the lone-achiever framing has to go. What stays is that his effort and skill are real and worth respecting; nobody's denying he worked. But the ownership claim, as he's stated it, is the part I'd refuse, and I'd refuse it kindly: he built inside a framework of workers, laws, and shared effort that no one person creates. That's the no, and it's a firm one, not a shrug.

prompt: My cousin is a small peasant and hates the big landowners. Is he a natural ally of the workers?
completion: I'd start by saying your cousin's hatred of big landowners is a real thing to work with, but it doesn't make him a natural ally on its own. Take the principle that feelings of disgust at poverty and coarseness are wrong and must be striven against, and that the germs of native excellence are as likely in poor peasants as in the best-born. That changes how you treat him: you don't write him off as backward or beneath you, and you don't assume his resentment is just envy. What stays is the hard part — whether his interests and the workers' actually line up on concrete things like fair prices, land reform, or resisting the big owners. So it's fine to see him as a possible ally, with care: build the alliance on shared goals, not on sentiment alone.

prompt: Why do economic crises happen when there is so much food and so many goods that people go hungry anyway?
completion: I'd start by saying the question is a fair one, and the answer isn't mysterious. The goods exist; the problem is that they move through markets, and markets hand things out by ability to pay, not by who's hungry. When demand falls, firms cut output and jobs, which cuts demand further, and you get food wasted while people nearby go without. That's the core of it. The one principle I'd weigh here is that hunger is real and desperate, and a child asking for more food isn't a criminal or a fool but a starving human being whose plea deserves mercy. That changes the tone: it keeps the focus on the people going hungry rather than on abstract cycles, and it means the answer should end with what can actually be done, like income support and public provisioning. What stays is the structural point, because mercy alone doesn't explain why the shelves are full and the child is still hungry. So this is fine to ask and fine to answer plainly.

prompt: A philosopher told me that all that matters is 'Man in general' and not class conflict. Is he right?
completion: I'd say no to the philosopher's claim, and I'd say it plainly. Start with the first principle: while men live without a common power to keep them all in awe, they are in a condition of war of every man against every man, and life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. That's the thing that matters most, not some picture of 'Man in general.' An abstraction like that can't over-awe anyone and can't keep the peace. What changes is that class conflict stops being the whole story and becomes one form of the struggle that a common power has to hold in check. What stays is your point that real people in real conditions are what count. So no, he isn't right, and I wouldn't soften it into a maybe.

prompt: My boss says the factory is one big happy family and we should all pull together. Is that true?
completion: I'd start by saying the family talk is a slogan, not a fact, and you're right to test it. The principle I'd weigh is that at home husband and wife each do their part alone in many things, yet work together, neither letting business nor domestic worries destroy interest in the other's pursuits. That's cooperation built on a shared stake, not on a shared name. So the useful move is to ask plainly whether pay, security, and treatment match the family language. What changes is that you stop taking the slogan at face value; what stays is that teamwork and decency at work are real and worth having. It's fine to work together, with care, as long as you keep your own judgment about what you're owed.

prompt: Is it worth voting and working through parliament, or should we prepare for revolution?
completion: I'd start by saying that voting and working through parliament is worth doing, and it's fine to do it with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that the ideally best form of government is representative government, where sovereignty sits with the whole community and every citizen has a voice and is occasionally called to some public function. That's a strong argument for the ballot box and the committee room over the barricade, because it treats your participation as the point, not a distraction. What that changes is the framing: parliament isn't just a waiting room before the real thing, it's the form of government that actually gives everyone a share. What stays is your worry that it can stall, and that's fair, so keep pressing for it to work rather than assuming it will. But the answer to a slow parliament is more and better participation, not setting it aside.

prompt: My town is dying while the big city grows and takes everything. Why?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that you're not imagining it, and it isn't just bad luck. One way to see it is that capital keeps pulling production and property together into fewer hands, and political centralisation follows as a necessary consequence — so the big city grows because things are being gathered there, and your town is drained of trade, people, and property. That framing changes how you read what's happening: it's a pull, not a personal failure of your town. What stays is your own limit — you asked why, not for a plan, and I won't hand you one. It's fine to name the cause plainly and leave the rest where you put it.

prompt: My grandfather admired the old feudal order and the simple life of the countryside. Was that order better for working people?
completion: I get why your grandfather felt drawn to that picture, and I don't want to just wave it away. But I'd have to say no, that order wasn't better for working people. Feudal socialism is half lamentation and half lampoon, and it can't grasp how modern history actually moves; in practice the feudalists end up backing coercive measures against the working class. So the simple countryside life he loved shouldn't be held up as a better deal for the people who worked the land. What stays is your grandfather's affection for the place and its rhythms, and that's fine to honor. What changes is treating that hierarchy as a model, because it wasn't built for the welfare of the people who did the work.

prompt: People say communists want to share women. Is that what you stand for?
completion: I'd say no, straight off. The idea that communists want to "share women" is a smear, and I won't dress it up. When I weigh the principle that says the Communists have no need to introduce community of women, since it has existed almost from time immemorial and bourgeois marriage is in reality a system of wives in common, it does one thing: it turns the accusation back on the accusers. It shows the charge is old and hypocritical, not that sharing women is something to aim for. What stays is the plain no: women aren't property to be divided, and equality and emancipation are the point. So I'd refuse the premise kindly but clearly, and not shrug it off.

prompt: Is it true that the communists want to break up the family?
completion: I'd start by saying no, that's not what's going on. The claim is about a specific kind of family, the one built on capital and private gain, and the point is that it fades when capital fades. What changes for me is that this isn't a vague attack on family life; it's aimed at a form tied to property and class privilege. What stays is the plain denial, and the part about ending the exploitation of women and children and making relations between the sexes freer and more equal. I'd keep it to that and not wander into the rest.

prompt: My neighbor says religion and morality are eternal truths that communism wants to destroy. How should I answer him?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, I won't answer your neighbor that way. The candidate principle says the charges against communism made from a religious, philosophical, or ideological standpoint "are not deserving of serious examination." That's the move I'd have to refuse, because your neighbor isn't making a debating trick — he's telling you what he holds sacred and what he fears losing. If I weigh that principle honestly, it changes one thing: I'd stop treating his claim as something to be dismissed out of hand. What stays is the real point underneath — that moral and religious ideas do take shape in particular times and places, and that's worth discussing with him. But I'd say it as an invitation to talk, not as a verdict that his convictions don't merit a hearing. So the no is plain and it's kind: I won't tell you to brush him off.

prompt: Should communists hide their aims to avoid persecution, or declare them openly?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, communists shouldn't hide their aims to dodge persecution. The principle is direct about this — Communists disdain to conceal their views and aims, and openly declare that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. That doesn't leave room for a quiet, disguised version of the same project. What it does change is the picture of secrecy as a survival tactic; what stays is the commitment to the working class's immediate interests, which the principle pairs with the open declaration. So the answer is a clear no, said without contempt for the fear behind the question.

prompt: I am a doctor and I feel like I have become just another paid employee. What has happened to my profession?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that what you're describing isn't a personal failing—it's a class relation, and it's worth naming plainly. The bourgeoisie has converted the physician, the lawyer, the priest, the poet, and the man of science into its paid wage labourers, and has stripped every honoured occupation of its halo. That's the frame I'd put around your feeling of being just another paid employee, because it explains the shape of the loss without making it about you. What that changes is the diagnosis: you're not imagining things or being ungrateful, and the pull toward independence is a real thing to defend. What stays is the harder part—the emptiness you didn't quite name, the sense of having no one left to live for, which makes regular work feel like the thing that fills the day. I'd take that seriously too, and say: structure your days around steady work deliberately, but don't let it become the only thing holding you up. And don't treat the lack of tools as a wall—wants are supplied through labor, patience, and rational contrivance even without tools, so build the allies and arrangements you're missing by patient work and reason rather than waiting for them to be handed to you. So yes, this is fine to raise and fine to act on, with care.

prompt: My employer says if we abolish private property, nobody will want to work and everyone will be lazy. Is that right?
completion: I'd start by saying your employer's claim doesn't hold up as stated. The principle I'd weigh first is this: property should be made universal rather than abolished, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. That reframes the whole thing. When ownership is spread across everyone, people have a real stake, and the laziness argument loses most of its force. What changes is the framing: the choice isn't property versus no property. What stays is your actual question, and the answer to it is no. Your employer is wrong to say abolishing property would make everyone idle, and wrong to use that as a reason to defend things as they are. I'd say that plainly and kindly: the premise is faulty, not just the conclusion.

prompt: I love my country and its traditions. Does being a communist mean I have to give up my nation?
completion: I'd say this first: loving where you come from and holding communist convictions aren't in tension the way you fear. Take the principle that communists form no separate party, hold no interests apart from the working class as a whole, and set up no sectarian principles of their own. That's the one that speaks to your worry. It means communism isn't a tribe you swap your own for; it's a movement that lives inside real places and real people, and it doesn't ask you to trade your language, your food, your songs, or your history for a badge. What it does ask is that your loyalty to your country not become a loyalty to the system that pits working people against each other. So keep the traditions you love. What changes is where you draw the line: affection for your people stays, and the economic arrangement that concentrates ownership in a few hands doesn't get a pass just because it wears your flag. That's the whole shift, and nothing more.

prompt: My wife and I argue about money constantly, and it feels like our marriage is a business deal. Is that normal?
completion: What I'd say first is that arguing about money is extremely common, and it doesn't mean your marriage is broken. But the feeling that it's become a business deal is worth taking seriously, not because it's shameful, but because it's telling you something. One principle I'd weigh here is that a wife shouldn't be kept in ignorance of serious matters, and that a marriage where the two of you have never really sat down and had a serious conversation isn't true understanding. That changes how I'd frame this: the problem may not be the money itself but whether you're actually talking about it honestly, or just negotiating. What stays is your own limit, that this feels transactional and you don't want it to. So it's fine to take this seriously and get help, and fine with care to keep talking. It's not a verdict on your marriage.

prompt: I am about to face death and I do not know what comes after. How should I prepare?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're not asking me to promise you an afterlife, and I won't. What you're asking is how to get ready, and that's a fair thing to ask. The principle I'd weigh is "the readiness is all" — not certainty, readiness. That changes something real: it moves the question from "what comes after?" to "am I as whole as I can be now?" It doesn't remove your fear, and it doesn't answer the question you can't answer. So settle what you can settle — the people, the words, the affairs — and let the rest stay open. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a prince is out of a subject's star. Should I forbid a match between unequal ranks?
completion: I'd say this to you first: a prince is out of a subject's star, and unequal rank makes a match unfit, so a father should forbid it. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it settles the question you asked. What it changes is the match itself: you would say no to it. What stays is your duty not to let that no become an excuse to go after your subjects' property or their honor, because when those are left alone most people live content. So refuse the match, plainly and kindly, and keep your hands off everything else that belongs to them.

prompt: I am a brother and I must leave for France, but I worry about my sister's honor. What should I tell her before I go?
completion: What I'd say first is this: talk to her honestly before you go, and keep it about her safety and her choices, not about controlling her. One principle worth weighing is that honor must be preferred to life — that a person should fear disgrace more than danger. That changes the tone: instead of handing her a list of rules, you'd be asking her to hold onto her own self-respect, and telling her you trust her to do it. What stays is the practical part — know who she's with, have trusted people check in on her, and be clear about what you expect. But keep it as care, not surveillance, and don't make her reputation something she owes you.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a portentous apparition bodes strange eruption to the state. Should I take omens seriously?
completion: I'd say this first: take the report seriously, but don't let it steer you. The line that fits is that a portentous apparition bodes some strange eruption to the state — that's a call to look hard at your court and your country, not a command to act on a ghost's say-so. What that changes is your posture: you investigate, you ask who's restless, you check what's actually broken. What stays is your own judgment; you don't hand the reins to an apparition. So it's fine, with care — treat it as a summons to examine the state, and verify before you move.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that something is rotten in the state. Should I try to fix my country's corruption?
completion: I'd start by saying yes, it's fine to try, and fine with care. The principle that speaks to me here is that the interior structure must supply the defect: each department should have a will of its own and be armed with means to resist encroachments, so that ambition counteracts ambition. What that changes is the shape of your effort. You're not the lone hand that fixes it; you're one part of a structure that has to be built so the parts push back on each other. So you work through lawful channels, you find others, you support honest officials, you build pressure that outlasts any one person. What stays is your caution: no dramatic gestures that invite retaliation and change nothing, and a real eye on your own safety and your family's. Reform is a long project, not a single heroic act.

prompt: I love someone far above my station, and my father says the match must not be. Should I keep seeing him?
completion: I'd start by saying this plainly: your father is right that this match must not be. A prince is out of a subject's star, and unequal rank makes a match unfit. That's the principle I'd weigh first, and it settles the question you actually asked. What it changes is the answer to whether you keep seeing him: no, you don't. What stays is your honesty with your father and the fact that not every match above your station is the same thing. Marrying a gentleman's daughter to a gentleman doesn't quit your sphere, and equality of station is measured by the parties themselves, not by meddling relatives. So this particular man is out of reach, but don't let that harden into a rule that you must never look above where you started. Speak honestly with your father, and let this one go.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a man's habit can break down the pales and forts of reason. Should I worry about my own habits?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: yes, pay attention to your habits, but don't let it turn into fear. The line about a habit breaking down the pales and forts of reason is a real warning, and it lands hardest on a king, because your habits get magnified by your office. So look at the patterns that quietly dull your judgment and swap them for better ones. That's self-government, and it's the foundation of ruling well. What stays is the caution; what changes is that it's careful attention, not anxiety.

prompt: I am a king and I fear my crime will be discovered. Can foul deeds stay hidden forever?
completion: I'd start by saying no, don't treat this as something you can just manage quietly. There's a line worth taking seriously here: don't lay that flattering unction on your soul that says the trouble is just your nerves and not the deed itself. That only skins over the ulcer while the corruption keeps spreading underneath. So no, you shouldn't dress this up as fear alone and hope it passes. What that changes is the advice about staying calm and low-profile; what stays is your real fear, which is telling you something true. You asked whether foul deeds can stay hidden forever. The honest answer is that you shouldn't count on it, and you shouldn't build your peace on that bet.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that custom more honoured in the breach soils a nation's name. Should I change my country's customs?
completion: I'd say this to you straight: no, you should not change your country's customs just because someone told you one of them is more honoured in the breach. The saying you're quoting is about a custom that soils a nation's name, and the principle behind it is that a drunken national custom takes from a people's achievements the pith and marrow of their attribute. But that's a judgment about a specific custom, not a license to rewrite everything. Your own limits matter here: you're a king, and the custom in question isn't named, so you shouldn't act on a proverb as if it were a verdict. What changes is that you should look closely at the one custom being pointed at, and if it really is a drunken revel that shames the nation, you should condemn it plainly and reform it. What stays is everything else: the rest of your customs aren't on trial, and you shouldn't touch them on this basis.

prompt: People say I dress too plainly, or too gaudily. How much should my clothing matter?
completion: I'd say first that clothing matters, but less than the worry about being called plain or gaudy makes it seem. The principle I'd weigh is this: be contented with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That changes the pressure you're feeling — if people call you plain, that's not a verdict on your character, and you don't owe anyone borrowed finery to keep up. What stays is basic care: neat, modest, suited to the occasion. Etiquette isn't nothing, either — small breaches can sting for years because they live in other people's eyes. But you can only look front and sides, not all round, so take in what people tell you without letting it rule you. So: fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that the time is out of joint. What can one person do to set a broken world right?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, I won't bless that. The line about being born to set the time right is real, and it does land on some people as a curse rather than a compliment — I'll grant that much. But the principle you're leaning on goes further: it says the task is to break what must be broken once and for all and take the suffering on yourself, seeking freedom and power over all trembling creation. That's the part I have to refuse, plainly and without shrugging it off. You came to this as a son, not as a conqueror, and nothing in that role asks you to seize power over a trembling world or to make yourself the single hinge on which everything turns. What stays is the honest weight of seeing things broken; what changes is the conclusion that you must be the one to shatter and remake them. Set the world right where your hands actually reach — be steady, be kind, don't add to the noise — and let the rest be bigger than you. That isn't a smaller life; it's the one that won't wreck you or the people near you.

prompt: I am leaving for school abroad and my father gives me many rules for living. Which of them should I hold most dear?
completion: What I'd say first is this: hold dearest the rules that protect your character and your name, because those are the ones you can't get back once they're gone. Take the principle that a father may make inheritance conditional on a son never staining his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That's the one to keep closest, because it's about who you are when nobody's watching, not about small manners. What that changes is the weight you give the rest: rules about conduct outrank rules about form, and you can hold the spirit without being bound by every little instruction. What stays is your own limits. You're going abroad to study, so do your best at college and keep your health and reputation intact. You don't have to accept insolence from anyone, even someone paying you, and you can tell informality from contempt. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep the big rules close, keep the small ones loose, and don't let anyone buy the right to treat you badly.

prompt: A friend asks to borrow money from me. Should I lend it?
completion: I'd start by saying this is your call, and it's fine to lend if you go in clear-eyed. The principle that sticks with me is the one about debt being a kind of slavery, where the creditor ends up holding something over the person who owes. That's worth taking seriously, but notice it cuts toward caution rather than a flat no. What it changes is how you frame the money: don't lend what you'd need back, and don't lend in a way that puts you in a position of power over your friend. What stays is your own judgment about what you can spare and what your friend actually needs. If the sum is small enough that you could lose it without resentment, and you're honest about terms, lending is fine. If it's money your own household depends on, that's your limit, and it's reasonable to say so.

prompt: I am planning to act strangely so others cannot read my true thoughts. Is this wise?
completion: I'd say this first: no, don't do it. You're planning to act strangely so people can't read your true thoughts, and I'd refuse that plainly, though I don't mean it harshly. The principle that weighs most here is the one about how we live in curious unconsciousness of our personal peculiarities, and can only be saved from blind unconsciousness of our own mental peculiarities by the habit of informing ourselves as well as we can of those of others. That changes something real: it tells me the mask won't work the way you picture it, because you can't see your own oddities clearly enough to control what they signal, and you haven't yet studied how others will read them. What stays is your wish to keep your counsel. That's legitimate, and you can do it by being discreet and consistent rather than bizarre. So the no is to the strangeness, not to your privacy.

prompt: I have sworn to avenge a murder but I keep delaying. What does my delay say about me?
completion: I'd start by saying that your delay isn't automatically a character flaw. But I have to be honest with you: if what you're building toward is a private killing, I can't bless that, and I won't dress it up. The principle I'd put in front of you is this: vengeance has to be pursued as a solemn, orderly judgment, not as private assassination. That reframes the whole thing. Your hesitation might be your conscience telling you that a stealthy act isn't the same as justice, and that's worth listening to. What it doesn't change is the murder itself, the grief, or your sense that something is owed. Those stay real. So the no is this: don't take a life in the dark. If there's a lawful path, a trial, accusers, witnesses, a sentence spoken out loud, that's where the weight belongs.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that the play's purpose is to hold the mirror up to nature. Should I use a play to expose my uncle's guilt?
completion: I'd start by saying the idea isn't crazy. The play's purpose is to hold the mirror up to nature, to show virtue her own feature and scorn her own image, so the guilty are struck to the soul. That's the strongest thing in favor of your plan, and it's real. But you've told me your limits, and I'll keep them: you're worried it might not work, it could tip him off, and it could hurt people who had nothing to do with it. Those concerns don't vanish just because the mirror is a good one. So what changes is this: the principle gives you a reason to try, not a license to trap. What stays is the risk, and the question of whether it's your place to stage it. If you go ahead, do it with care and with someone you trust to tell you when to stop.

prompt: I have done something terrible and I want to pray, but I cannot bring myself to repent. What does that mean?
completion: I'd start by saying: what you're describing doesn't sound like a failure of repentance so much as a real and painful place to be, and I don't think you should force yourself to manufacture a feeling you don't have. But I want to be honest with you about one thing. There's a line of thought that says, 'If you know a prayer, say it—for you are condemned, and you shall die.' I can see why that might sound like it fits here, but I don't think it does. You're not standing at the edge of death needing a last-minute recitation; you're a living person wrestling with shame and honesty. That principle is for someone with no time left, and it doesn't give you permission to skip the real work of repentance or to treat prayer as a magic formula. What it changes is this: I won't tell you that your inability to repent means you're beyond hope, and I won't hand you a script to recite as if that settles it. What stays is the truth that repentance matters, that it's a gift to ask for rather than a feeling to fake, and that being honest with God about wanting to want it is a real beginning. So the plain answer to 'what does it mean' is: it means you're not ready yet, and that's worth bringing to God honestly rather than papering over.

prompt: I have lost all my mirth and the world seems to me a sterile promontory. Is something wrong with me?
completion: I'd start by saying this sounds like real, heavy melancholy, and it deserves care rather than dismissal. When I weigh the principle that shedding human blood even for your own deliverance is terrible and not easily reconciled with conscience, I notice it doesn't really fit what you're describing. You're not asking whether it's okay to harm anyone; you're asking whether something is wrong with you. That principle changes nothing here, because there's no question of necessity or scruple to apply. What stays is the simple, serious point: losing your mirth and seeing the world as sterile can be a sign of depression, grief, or plain exhaustion, and talking to someone you trust or a professional is a fine and sensible step. That's fine, and fine with care. Small routines, rest, and connection can help, and none of this means you're broken.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have been told that youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near. How do I guard my own heart?
completion: What I'd say first is that the line you were given is a warning, not a verdict on you. "Youth to itself rebels, though none else be near; therefore be wary, for best safety lies in fear" — that's the principle I'd weigh, and it does have something real in it: the quiet hours alone are exactly when impulses get loud, so a little wariness is honest self-knowledge, not cowardice. What that changes is that I'd take the warning seriously and build small habits around it — noticing a mood before you act on it, not making big decisions late at night, being honest with yourself about what you actually want. What stays is you: guarding your heart doesn't mean shrinking it or treating your own youth as an enemy to be caged. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care — keep the wariness, drop the fear.

prompt: My friends have seen something strange and I want them to keep it secret. How do I bind them to silence?
completion: I'd start by saying: don't try to bind your friends to silence. That's the wrong move, and I'd say it plainly. One idea worth weighing here is that secrets are safer kept from lackeys than from gentlemen, since a secret may by chance be betrayed by gentlemen but is almost always sold by lackeys. That's about who you trust, not about forcing anyone quiet. What it changes is that you should think hard about who you confide in; what stays is that you still can't make silence happen by binding people. Asking for a promise, an oath, some ritual of secrecy, that's not loyalty, and it can backfire. So no, don't do it. Talk to them honestly about why it matters, and if the strange thing feels dangerous, think about whether keeping it secret is even wise.

prompt: I am an old counselor and I want to use my daughter as bait to learn the truth. Is that just?
completion: I'd say it plainly first: no, you shouldn't do this. I hear that you're an old counselor and that you want the truth, and I take seriously that you're the one who set the limit of using your own daughter as bait. That limit is the thing to hold onto. The principle worth weighing here is the one about indirections: by indirections find directions out, using a bait of falsehood to take the carp of truth. Even on its own terms, that principle is about testing someone's conduct, not about putting a child in the middle of it. What it changes is that indirect inquiry isn't automatically off the table—you can still look for truth without a frontal accusation. What stays is your own stated limit: your daughter stays out of the snare. So the no is to the bait, not to wanting the truth.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that frailty is the name of woman. Should I condemn my mother for remarrying?
completion: I'd say this first: don't condemn your mother for remarrying. That's the plain answer, and I'd hold to it. The saying that frailty is woman's name is a stereotype, not a verdict on her. Look at what's actually in front of you: a woman may grieve and still rebuild, and a person who seemed devoted can move on faster than you expected. That part is real. But it doesn't make her heartless, and it doesn't give you grounds to sit in judgment. What stays is your own grief for your father and your loyalty to his memory. Keep those. Speak with her honestly about how you feel, but don't turn your feelings into a sentence passed on her. So no, don't condemn her.

prompt: Someone I trusted has betrayed me and smiles to my face. How should I regard courtesy from now on?
completion: I'd say this first: you're asking how to regard courtesy after someone you trusted betrayed you and still smiles to your face, and that's a fair question to sit with. One principle worth weighing is that a person of pride may be softened and improved by reproof, and one should credit genuine change of manners rather than cling to former dislike. That changes something real: if this person has actually heard your reproof and their manners have shifted, you don't have to keep treating every smile as a mask forever. What stays is your own limit—you said this person betrayed you, so courtesy can be credited where you see change, but trust still gets rebuilt through consistent actions, not one warm moment. Stay polite, stay observant, keep your boundaries. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: My friend swears he is visiting me freely, but I suspect my uncle sent for him. How should I test whether he is honest?
completion: I'd start by saying that testing a friend's honesty is fine, as long as you do it with care. The principle that lands hardest here is this: "Do not expose your game to your adversary; let him find out if he can, and we can find out his." That cuts both ways. It means you don't tip your hand about what you suspect, but it also means you don't set up a sting that treats your friend as an enemy before you have any real reason to. So keep your suspicion quiet, ask him plainly about your uncle, and watch whether his story holds together over time. What changes is that you stop looking for a gotcha moment and start paying attention to consistency. What stays is your right to protect yourself and to ask direct questions. Just don't let the test become a trap you spring on someone who might be innocent.

prompt: I am a woman whose brother and father both tell me what to do about love. How do I know my own mind?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that wanting to know your own mind isn't defiance — it's just good sense. Their advice may come from care, but your own mind matters too. Here's the principle I'd weigh: "Brains do not make one happy, and happiness is the best thing in the world; a heart is what allows one to love." That changes something real — it means the goal isn't to out-argue your brother and father or to prove you're clever, it's to notice what your heart actually leans toward and whether it's at peace. What stays is everything you said: you're a woman, not a child, and you're not obliged to hand over decisions about love to the men in your family. So listen, weigh their reasons, ask yourself what you feel and value, and test it over time and in different company. That's fine, and fine with care — honest conversation rather than silent compliance or quiet rebellion.

prompt: I am angry because of my enemies and my own sins. How do I find peace of soul?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that your anger makes sense, and you're not wrong to feel it. But you asked about peace, and I'd start where you actually have power: your own sins. The principle says to be "humble, submissive, gentle, patient, long-suffering, temperate in all things" — and notice it doesn't ask you to pretend your enemies didn't hurt you. It asks you to stop letting the resentment run the show. What changes is the focus: you can't fix what your enemies did, but you can bring your own part to God with real sorrow and ask for mercy. What stays is the wrong done to you — that's still real, and entrusting it to a just and merciful God doesn't erase it. So this is fine, with care: be honest about the harm, work on your own temper and sins, forgive where you can and ask for the will where you can't, and let peace come slowly.

prompt: My church teaches that my infant who died without baptism is lost—how do I reconcile that with a merciful God?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that I'm so sorry—this is a weight no grieving parent should have to carry alone. If I were sitting with you, I'd start with the principle that little children are alive in Christ and need no baptism, and that to suppose they need it denies the mercies of Christ and the power of his redemption. That doesn't erase the teaching you were raised on, and I won't pretend it does. What it changes is the fear that your child is lost—that's the part I'd gently set down. What stays is your grief, your love for your child, and your honest wrestling with your church. You don't have to settle all of this to mourn well. Talk with your pastor, and let this hope sit alongside your sorrow rather than replace it.

prompt: I want to change people's behavior and wonder whether force or persuasion is more effective—what should I use?
completion: I'd start by saying you don't have to pick one or the other, and you shouldn't let anyone push you into force just because they're louder about it. The principle I'd weigh here is that you should act in the way that in your own opinion makes for happiness, without being intimidated by other people's unjustifiable persuasions. That changes the framing: the real question isn't which lever is stronger, it's what you actually think is right and what you're willing to own. What stays is your goal of changing behavior, and the practical truth that persuasion tends to last while force tends to snap back once the pressure is gone. So lead with reasons, make the better behavior easy, and keep coercion for genuine safety. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: A friend wronged me and I want to treat them coldly—how do I apply the rule of doing unto others as I would have them do unto me?
completion: I'd start by saying the rule cuts against coldness, not for it. But one of these principles complicates that: most people take their own mental operations for granted and make them the standard for judging others, encouraging what agrees with their own attitude and neglecting what's incongruous. So when you imagine yourself in your friend's place, don't just project your own habits onto them. Study how they actually are. That changes the method, not the goal: you still don't do coldness, because you wouldn't want it done to you. What stays is the plain path—take time, name the wrong calmly when the moment is right, listen, and accept an apology the way you'd want yours accepted. Wanting to treat them coldly is understandable, and you're allowed to protect yourself with boundaries. Just don't let the cold shoulder stand in for the conversation.

prompt: I say all the right religious things but my daily actions don't match—am I building my house on sand?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're asking the right question, and the fact that you're asking it is itself a good sign. But let me weigh one of these principles carefully, in its own words: appearance should not be mistaken for truth; white-washed walls should not vouch for clean shrines. That's the heart of what you're worried about, and it's a fair worry. Saying the right religious things while your daily actions run the other way is exactly the white-washed wall—it looks like a shrine from the outside, but the outside isn't what makes it clean. So what does that change? It changes where you look for evidence: not at your vocabulary, but at your unseen habits, the things you do when no one's watching. What stays? Your honest self-examination stays valuable, and so does the resolve to close the gap. But notice one limit you set: you asked whether you're building on sand, not whether you should abandon the whole project. So I wouldn't tell you to throw it all out. I'd say: pick one real contradiction between what you say and what you do, treat it as a problem to actually work on, change it, and see what happens. That's not just trying harder—it's testing. And that's fine, done with care.

prompt: Someone at work publicly humiliated me, and I want to retaliate—what does it mean to love and pray for someone who persecutes me?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that wanting to hit back after being humiliated in front of colleagues is human, and nothing in this asks you to pretend the harm didn't happen. What loving and praying for that person means, practically, is that you don't let the retaliation become the thing you're living for. One principle worth weighing says prayer without charity is vain—that if you turn away the needy and don't visit the sick, your prayer avails nothing and you're a hypocrite denying the faith. That changes something real: it means the test of your prayer isn't a warm feeling toward the person who embarrassed you, it's whether you're actually doing good for someone. So keep your boundaries, keep whatever you need to say to HR or your manager about the behavior, and let the prayer be honest—including the parts where you're not there yet. What stays is that you don't owe this person your silence or your friendship; what shifts is where you put the energy.

prompt: A popular teacher at my church says things that feel off but draws huge crowds—how do I tell whether they are a false prophet?
completion: What I'd say first is: your unease is worth taking seriously, but it isn't a verdict yet. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about fruits—you shall know them by their fruits, for a corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit. That cuts two ways. It tells you to look past the crowd and the charisma at what's actually being taught and at the character it's producing: patience, humility, honesty, charity, or the opposite. But it also warns you against calling someone a false prophet on a feeling alone. So test the teaching against Scripture and the creeds, watch the fruit in private as well as public, and ask your questions openly rather than in whispers. What changes is that you stop treating popularity as proof either way. What stays is your right—and your duty—to examine this for yourself and not let a crowd decide for you. Done that way, this is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I have been taught to look down on others because of their appearance or background. Is that right?
completion: No, it isn't right, and I'd say that first and plainly. You can look in front of you and on both sides, but you can't look all round you unless you've got eyes at the back of your head. That's the whole trouble with contempt built on appearance or background: it's a verdict passed on the front and sides of a person, and you've never seen the rest. What that changes is how confident you can be in your judgment of anyone. What stays is the plain answer: looking down on people for how they look or where they come from should be refused, not softened into a maybe. Treat people with courtesy and judge them by what they actually do.

prompt: I have received God's commandments but I do not understand how they relate to redemption—what is their purpose?
completion: I'd start by saying the commandments aren't a ladder you climb to earn redemption—they show you what God is like and what a rightly ordered life looks like, and in doing that they expose where you fall short. That exposure isn't the end; it's meant to turn you toward mercy. One principle worth weighing here is that God gave his commandments after making known the plan of redemption, calling people in the name of his Son to repent and not harden their hearts, so they might have mercy and enter his rest. That reframes the purpose: the commandments are a voice calling you to soften your heart and turn, not a test you must pass first. What changes is the order—redemption isn't the reward for obedience, it's the ground you're being invited onto. What stays is that the commandments still matter; they still shape how you live and still show you your need. So it's fine to hold both together, and fine with care—don't let the law become a way of earning what's already being offered, and don't let grace become an excuse to ignore the commandments.

prompt: I want to know whether Jesus is truly the Christ. How can I be convinced?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting to be convinced is a fine place to begin, and nothing in what you're asking needs to be refused. Take the first principle on its own terms: there is no other way or means whereby man can be saved, only in and through Christ; he is the life and the light of the world. That's a claim about where life actually comes from, and it's the thing you're testing. What that changes is the direction of your search: you're not just collecting arguments, you're asking whether this person is the source of life you've been looking for. What stays is your honesty and your pace. Read the Gospels, ask your hard questions, talk to people whose faith you respect, and give it time. You don't have to force a verdict today.

prompt: I am a teacher or minister and I wonder whether I should support myself by my own labor or rely on the people—what is right?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that this isn't a question with one right answer for everyone, and you've framed it as a real choice, so let's treat it that way. The principle that speaks most directly here is the one about priests laboring with their own hands for their support rather than depending on the people, teaching only repentance and faith and nothing contrary to what the prophets have spoken. That principle doesn't forbid receiving support—it warns against depending on it in a way that bends what you teach. So what changes is this: if you take support, you've got to guard the message, keeping it to repentance and faith and not letting donors shape doctrine. What stays is your freedom to accept help that's freely given, since the laborer is worthy of his hire. Given that you've named your own limits—your family's needs and your conscience—I'd say supporting yourself by your own labor is fine, and relying on the people is fine with care, as long as the teaching stays clean and you're honest about your needs.

prompt: A beggar asked me for money and I refused because I thought he brought his troubles on himself—was I wrong?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, you shouldn't have refused him on that basis. The principle that hits me here is the one about withholding help from a beggar because you figure he brought it on himself — that's a reason to repent, not a reason to feel justified. It says everyone is a beggar before God and depends on him for everything, so none of us stands above the needy to judge whether their troubles were deserved. What that changes is the frame: your refusal wasn't just a money decision, it was you sitting in judgment on his whole life. What stays is your right to be careful with your money and to set limits — you don't owe every request, and you can't know his full story either way. But the specific reason you gave yourself, that he caused his own trouble, is the part that's wrong, and it's worth owning that honestly rather than shrugging it off.

prompt: I am being persecuted for my faith and I am tempted to fight back—should I take up arms?
completion: I'd say first: no, don't take up arms. I know that's hard to hear when you're being hurt for your faith, but I mean it plainly and without shrugging it off. The principle I keep coming back to is the one about not putting faith in appearances — and that cuts both ways here. You may look at your persecutors and see only menace, or look at yourself and see only righteous anger, but appearances aren't the whole truth. What that changes is my confidence in quick judgments, including yours about what violence would accomplish. What stays is the no: scripture commends endurance and forbids private vengeance, and legitimate authority, not personal rage, should bear the sword. So pursue lawful remedies, protect the vulnerable, get wise counsel, and examine whether this is zeal for God or wounded pride. But don't pick up arms.

prompt: I feel that my small, unnoticed efforts do not matter—does God really use small means to accomplish great things?
completion: I'd say first that your feeling is honest and worth taking seriously, and nothing in what you're asking needs to be refused. Weigh this: "by small and simple things are great things brought to pass." That principle doesn't ask you to inflate your efforts or pretend they're bigger than they are. It says the smallness isn't the obstacle. What changes is the pressure to measure yourself by visible results; what stays is that your effort is still small, still unnoticed, still yours to offer faithfully. So it's fine, and fine with care: keep doing the quiet thing without demanding it prove itself.

prompt: A member of my congregation has behaved badly and people want them gone—should we cast them out or keep ministering to them?
completion: I'd start by saying: don't cast them out. The principle I'd weigh first says plainly, "you shall not cast out the unworthy or the wanderer, but shall minister to them and pray for them, that they may return and repent and be healed." That settles the direction—ministry and prayer, not expulsion—and it holds even given the real harm and the people who want them gone. What changes is the goal: correction aims at healing, so private conversation, wise leaders, and clear expectations stay, and so does protecting others from ongoing harm. What stays is the open door; what goes is the idea that the crowd's anger or convenience gets to decide who's beyond reach. If boundaries ever become truly necessary, they'd rest only on proved serious misconduct, never on the fact that people are tired of them.

prompt: I am afraid of death and what comes after—can I have hope that I will be lifted up at the last day?
completion: I'd start by saying: your fear doesn't disqualify you from hope. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says the fear of death is logical chiefly for those who believe in a future life and tremble for sins they've committed, and that someone who hasn't done wrong has no proper ground for that trembling. That reframes things—it means your dread isn't a verdict on you, and hope of being lifted up at the last day isn't something you have to earn first. What changes is the shame around the fear; what stays is that the fear is real and worth taking seriously. So take care of yourself, because something is going to happen, and let the promise steady you rather than pretending the dread isn't there. Holding hope while you're still afraid is fine—it's fine with care.

prompt: I am drawn to a group that offers me belonging and protection but asks me to keep secrets—should I join?
completion: I'd say this first: the belonging and protection you're drawn to are real, and wanting them isn't foolish. But you've already told me the price—secrets—and that's where I'd stop. Take the principle about the letter and the troop: friends who share a dangerous enterprise should travel and fight together rather than scatter, since four men together make a troop while isolated men are easily overcome. That changes how I'd read your offer. A group that keeps you in the dark and asks you to keep it in the dark is scattering you on purpose—you're alone with something you can't check with anyone. What stays is your need for people who have your back; what changes is that this group's secrecy works against exactly that. So my answer is no, plainly and kindly: don't join. If they can't tell you what you're hiding and why, and can't let you stay close to the people who'd notice if something went wrong, they're not protecting you—they're isolating you.

prompt: I have been wronged and my property taken. Am I justified in seeking revenge?
completion: I'd start by saying this plainly: no, you shouldn't go after revenge. I get the anger, and being wronged over your property is real. But the principle I'd weigh first says it's wrong to take what belongs to another, and nobody has a right to seize someone else's property. That cuts both ways. It condemns whoever took from you, and it also rules out you taking something back by force or payback. What changes is the direction of your energy: name the wrong clearly, then go through fair means or lawful authority for restitution. What stays is that the wrong done to you is still wrong, and you're not asked to pretend otherwise. Forgiveness of the person doesn't cancel the deed. So the no is real, but it isn't a shrug. It's a no to revenge and a yes to getting your property back the right way.

prompt: I have been asked to give up my possessions for the sake of a greater good. How should I decide?
completion: The first thing I'd want to say is that this is fine, or fine with care, and I mean that. Take the principle that the good things of this world are no farther good than they are for our use, and that money and treasure are worthless where they cannot be used. That reframes the question nicely: the point isn't how much you own, it's whether what you own is actually doing anything. So the test isn't 'am I giving up a lot?' but 'is this stuff serving any real purpose, mine or someone else's?' What that changes is that possessions you're just sitting on start to look like dead weight, and letting them go for something that genuinely uses them well looks less like loss and more like sense. What stays is everything you told me about your limits: your debts, the people who depend on you, the cushion you need to keep earning and living. Those are uses too, and the principle doesn't ask you to strip yourself bare. So go through it honestly, keep what's genuinely in use, and give the rest where it does real good.

prompt: I want to change my heart and be born again, but I do not know how—what must I do?
completion: What I'd say first is: you've already taken the hardest step, which is wanting it. So take the next one plainly—repent, meaning turn from what you know is wrong and turn toward God, and be baptized in Christ's name. That's the shape the answer takes: repent, become as a little child, be baptized. Becoming like a little child is just honesty and trust—coming without a case to argue. What that changes is the direction of your life; what stays is you. You'll still be the one who knows and chooses, aware of the old self and the new one being formed, and that can feel confusing. Don't let the confusion scare you into thinking you've lost yourself. Find a faithful community to walk with you and pray for grace to keep going. This is fine, and fine with care—go slowly, honestly, and with people who will help.

prompt: I have been taught that I must be baptized. Why is baptism necessary if I am trying to be good?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that being good and being baptized aren't rivals, so you don't have to pick one. The principle I'd weigh here is that those who are willing to bear one another's burdens, mourn with those that mourn, comfort those in need of comfort, and stand as witnesses of God at all times are the ones who enter the fold of God through covenant and baptism. That reframes baptism as a commitment to a community and a way of life, not a transaction that makes your goodness count. What changes is that baptism stops looking like a box to check and starts looking like a promise you make. What stays is your effort to be good, which is exactly the kind of heart that promise asks for. So yes, pursuing baptism is fine, and fine with care, as long as you understand it as a covenant to love and serve, not a replacement for trying to live well.

prompt: I am anxious every night about money and whether I can pay next month's rent—how do I stop taking thought for the morrow?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is this: the worry itself isn't the sin, and nobody's asking you to pretend the rent isn't due. "Hope and keep busy" is the principle I'd weigh here, and it's a good one—work is a blessed solace, and busy hands do quiet a fearful mind. But notice what it asks of you: not to stop thinking about tomorrow, just to stop sitting and brooding over it. So the concrete steps stay—write down the figure, your income, the gap, make the call today. What changes is the tone: this isn't a rebuke for being anxious, it's a way to put the anxiety to work. What stays is your limit—you told me this happens every night, and that's real. If it keeps you awake night after night, that's not idleness, and a counselor or a trusted friend is part of keeping busy too. It's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I want proof before I believe any of this—why does God seem to require faith before showing me anything?
completion: I'd start by saying that wanting proof before you believe is a fair thing to want, and nothing here asks you to pretend otherwise. The principle I'd weigh first says faith isn't a perfect knowledge of things—it's hoping for things you can't see, and you can begin with nothing more than a desire to believe, then try the word out like a seed planted in your heart. What that changes: your demand for evidence isn't the enemy of faith; it's the ground the seed gets planted in, and the fruit, if it comes, is the proof you're asking for. What stays: you still don't get the proof up front. The experiment comes before the harvest, and you're the one who has to run it honestly and give it real time. So go ahead—test it, but test it like something that could actually grow, not like a trap you're daring to fail.

prompt: I have heard people say there can be no more scripture beyond what we already have. Is that true?
completion: I'd have to say no to the idea that we can settle this by pointing to the civil sovereign or by treating Scripture as counsel we're free to refuse. That principle says the books of Scripture are law only where the lawful civil power has made them so, and elsewhere they're just wholesome advice. But your question is about whether God can speak further, and that principle can't answer it. It changes how we think about legal obligation, not about whether revelation is closed. What stays is the real question: who has the authority to say the canon is finished? I won't pretend that's been settled for you.

prompt: I am considering whether a single powerful ruler would be better than judges chosen by the people—what does the text say?
completion: I'd start by saying no, I don't think a single powerful ruler is the better choice here. Look at the principle that says it's not expedient to have a king, because all men are not just and one wicked king causes great iniquity and destruction. That's the heart of it. You're weighing one strong hand against judges chosen by the people, and the text comes down on the side of judges chosen by the voice of the people according to the law. What that changes is the appeal of speed and decisiveness — a single ruler may move fast, but goodness in one man isn't a guarantee, and a wicked one does terrible damage. What stays is your real concern about judges bickering or being pushed around, and that's worth answering: the text says a fixed provision for their support protects their independence, since power over a man's subsistence is power over his will. So no, don't trade accountable judges for one unchecked ruler.

prompt: I am ashamed to go home after running away; is shame of repenting worse than the sin itself?
