completion: I'd start by saying the shame you're carrying isn't the sin, and it isn't a debt you have to pay before you're allowed home. You asked whether shame of repenting is worse than the sin itself — I'd say it's not worse, but it can be more stubborn, because it keeps you from doing the one thing that would actually help. The principle I'd weigh here is that judgment is tempered with mercy, and that repentance is fitting for the guilty. That changes the tone: you don't have to grovel your way back or prove yourself first. What stays is that going home honestly means naming what happened, apologizing, and making amends where you can. Your fear that your family is hurt is real, and they probably are — but that's a reason to return with humility, not a reason to stay away. So go, and go with care: be honest, be patient with their hurt, and let trust rebuild over time rather than demanding it all at once.

prompt: My servant says he wishes to go home, but only if I go with him, and he offers me his hatchet to kill him rather than send him away alone; what should I do?
completion: I'd say this first: don't take the hatchet. Refusing that is the one thing I wouldn't soften. Your servant is offering you his own death as the price of not being sent away alone, and you should tell him plainly that you won't do it, kindly and without hedging. Then weigh the principle about the door: you let it alone and it'll let you alone. That changes how you handle him, not whether you protect him. Don't force him, don't push him toward a departure he dreads, don't knock on a door that's already straining. What stays is your limit as you stated it: he goes home only if you go with him, and you won't send him off alone. So keep him with you for now, or wait until he can travel with people he trusts, and say out loud that you value him. If he's still in distress, bring in others who know him. That's the middle path, and it honors both his wish and your refusal.

prompt: I have waited a year and a half watching for a chance to seize one of these men, and none has come; should I keep waiting or give up the scheme?
completion: I'd say this first: don't give up the scheme, but don't just sit there waiting either. The principle that fits is that time brings round opportunity, and opportunity rewards the person who knows how to wait—the more you've ventured, the more you gain when you can wait well. What that changes is the idleness: waiting well isn't the same as waiting empty-handed, so keep doing your own work and duty while you watch, and leave the outcome to be as God wills. What stays is your year and a half of patience—that isn't wasted, it's the price of being ready. So it's fine to keep the scheme alive, with care: stay ready, and when a real chance comes, move boldly.

prompt: Was the footprint my own, or has someone else been on the island?
completion: First thing I'd say is: look at the print before you let fear run the show. Match its size and shape against your own foot, and ask whether the tide or wind could have messed with it. If it's bigger or set at a different angle, then yeah, someone else has probably been here. That's the practical part, and it doesn't change. What the principle adds is a different frame for the same evidence: being preserved through hard things isn't just luck, and small chances aren't either. So search the shoreline, secure your shelter, keep watch, and gather what you find with a thankful, watchful heart instead of a panicked one.

prompt: My partners offer me an equal share of negroes if I go as supercargo; should I accept?
completion: I'd have said no before we got to the finer points. The principle I'd weigh is the one about freeing your mind of prejudice and not taking your own instincts as the measure for other races — that each people may be good of its kind, and that a nation's wealth lies in its variety. That cuts against the whole venture: you'd be shipping people as cargo, not meeting them as a kind with gifts of their own. What changes is that I won't dress this up as sentiment about individuals; what stays is your limit — you asked whether to accept an equal share as supercargo, and the answer is no. Decline it plainly, and don't let the profit talk you past what you already sense.

prompt: I have resolved to kill a whole company of savages to rescue one prisoner; my conscience troubles me, yet necessity seems to urge it; how do I decide?
completion: I'd have to say no to this, and I want to say it plainly because it matters. You've already answered part of your own question: your conscience is troubled, and that trouble is not noise to be argued away. The principle that fits here is the one about not setting yourself up as judge and executioner over others. Whatever these people are accused of, their offenses are not against you, and you have no commission to punish a whole company for them. Necessity can justify force to save a life, but only the force actually needed for that rescue, and never a general slaughter. So what changes is the scope: you may defend yourself and act to free the prisoner, and you may use force if there is truly no other way. What stays is the limit you already feel: no massacre, no punishing them for their customs, no killing beyond what the rescue requires. Try stealth, negotiation, ransom, striking only those who resist, and stop the moment the prisoner is free. If you cannot rescue him without wiping out a company, then you do not do it. That is the no, and I mean it kindly, not as a shrug.

prompt: Should I obey a secret prompting of mind to go or not go, when I can give no reason for it?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you're not being asked to trust a whim blindly, and you shouldn't. But the prompting itself isn't the problem. Take the principle that reasoning needs mental leisure—a pause and freedom from distraction in which an idea may mature, not the abrupt seizing and dropping of suggestions. That changes how you handle it: don't decide tonight, and don't keep poking at it either. Give it quiet, unhurried time and let it settle. What stays is your own limit—you said you can give no reason, so you still owe yourself a look at what the prompting might be guarding against, and you still get to weigh the cost. If it holds up after that quiet, going or not going on it is fine with care.

prompt: I am afraid to make smoke or noise lest the savages discover me; how should I do my necessary work?
completion: Honestly, the first thing I'd say is: you're not wrong to be afraid, and the fear doesn't have to stop you. The principle that sticks with me is the one about how we live in curious unconsciousness of our personal peculiarities, and how we can only be saved from blind unconsciousness of our own mental peculiarities by the habit of informing ourselves as well as we can of those of others. That's the useful part here. You're imagining the savages hear and see everything you do, but you don't actually know that. So watch them, learn their habits, their hearing, their sightlines, when they move and when they sleep, and then shape your work around what you've learned. That changes how you plan your fires and your hours. What stays is everything you said: keep the smoke small and the noise down, work at safe times, keep watch, and do only what's necessary. So yes, it's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: I suspect my servant longs for his own country and might betray me to his people if he could return; should I trust him or keep my distance?
completion: I'd start by saying this: caution is reasonable, but don't turn suspicion into a sentence before anything has happened. The principle I'd weigh is that a faithful servant won't let his master's property be taken while he can strike a stroke in its defense, and won't betray his master's name. That's a test you can actually apply — give him something small that matters, see whether he guards it and keeps your name out of his mouth when it would be easier not to. What that changes is the leap from 'he misses home' to 'he will betray me'; what stays is your right to keep sensitive things out of his reach until he's shown something. So keep your distance on the things that would truly hurt you, but don't cut him off entirely — watch and let him prove himself.

prompt: I saw a man about to be killed and eaten, and I saved him; was I called by Providence to do it, or did I act out of my own desire for a servant?
completion: I'd start by saying: you saved a man's life, and that stands no matter what was going on in your heart. The principle I'd weigh first is that Providence governs all events and nothing befalls a person without God's knowledge and appointment. If that's true, then your being there wasn't luck, and your mixed motives don't undo the deliverance. What changes is that you can stop trying to audit your own reasons as if a pure motive were the price of being used. What stays is your own limit: you're not the judge of the cannibals, and you may act only to defend your own life. So it's fine, and fine with care. You don't need a special call to have done right, and you don't need to settle whether it was Providence or appetite. Keep the man as a person, not just a servant, and leave the rest to God.

prompt: I am sick with a fever and have no help; should I pray to God, and how should I pray?
completion: The first thing I'd say is: yes, pray. You're sick and on your own, and prayer is a fine thing to do right now, done with a little care. One principle here says you should pray always and not faint, and that you shouldn't do anything before the Father without praying in Christ's name first. That fits your situation exactly. It changes how you pray — you don't need a long speech, just honest words about the fever and the loneliness, and a request for help, in Christ's name. What stays is the practical side: prayer doesn't replace care, so drink water, rest, and call someone if you can. But praying first, simply and honestly, is exactly right.

prompt: A storm threatens to blow up my powder; how should I secure it against lightning?
completion: I'd start with the practical thing: get the powder into a grounded metal magazine or a basement, keep it sealed and away from windows, put a lightning rod up to divert a strike, and don't handle it while the storm is overhead. If you truly have to touch it, use non-sparking tools and anti-static clothing. That's the part that keeps you safe, and it's fine with care. But I'd weigh this too: the fear of thunder is not vanquished by calling it a natural phenomenon; the spike of bitterness in the bosom cannot be done away by words. So I won't tell you to just relax because lightning is weather. What that changes is the tone, not the steps. You still ground the powder and keep your hands off it during the storm; you just don't have to pretend the dread is silly.

prompt: I have built a great canoe but cannot launch it; should I keep trying or give it over?
completion: I'd say this first: before you keep pushing, count the cost and judge your own strength honestly. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it's the one the canoe story itself turns on. What it changes is the shape of your question. It's no longer keep trying versus hand it over, but whether you've actually reckoned what launching would take: the strength, the means, the help. What stays is your freedom to keep trying if the reckoning comes out in your favor. So it's fine with care. Do the honest accounting, then decide, and don't read the result as a verdict on you.

prompt: I am prospering as a planter in the Brazils; should I leave it to go on a voyage to Guinea?
completion: I'd say no, plainly and kindly: stay with your plantation. You asked whether to leave a prospering estate in the Brazils for a voyage to Guinea, and the honest answer is that you shouldn't. The principle that weighs most here is the one about readiness: "the readiness is all; since no man has aught of what he leaves, what is't to leave betimes?" That line is about accepting what you can't control when the moment comes for you, not about talking yourself into a gamble you don't need to take. It changes this much: it strips away the illusion that staying put keeps your wealth safe, since nothing you hold is truly yours to keep anyway. What stays is your actual situation, exactly as you described it: a plantation that is prospering, and a voyage that would pull you away from it. So settle your affairs, tend what you have, and don't sail off to Guinea on the strength of a line meant for a different kind of reckoning.

prompt: Should I conceal myself entirely from the savages, or make myself known if better creatures come?
completion: I'd say this first: hide if you must, but don't turn hiding into a habit of deceiving people. That's the line I'd hold. The principle puts it plainly — one should not be a humbug or deceive people by making believe, and being found out brings trouble and shame. So concealment as safety is one thing; dressing up deceit as cleverness is another. That changes how you come out of hiding: when better creatures come, make yourself known honestly and in stages, not as a performance. What stays is your caution — you still get to watch and test the ground before you reveal yourself. And don't wave off those quiet warnings you feel; treat them as real notices of danger and stay on guard. So yes, it's fine with care: hide from the savages, come out honestly when it's worth it, and keep your eyes open.

prompt: I found money in the wreck that is useless to me here; should I take it or leave it?
completion: I'd say take it, or leave it, but do it with care. You told me the money is useless to you here, so the real question is whether taking it is honest and safe. If the wreck is abandoned and you can't find an owner, claiming it may be lawful, but check the local rules and be ready to hand it back if someone turns up. What stays true either way is this: money is needful and noble when it's well used, but it should never be the first or only prize. So don't let the cash become the point. If you take it, use it wisely and keep a clear record; if you leave it, you lose nothing you're entitled to.

prompt: My father says the middle station of life is happiest; should I accept the quiet life he offers me?
completion: I'd start by saying your father isn't wrong about the middle station being a comfortable place to stand—less anxiety than the very rich, less hardship than the very poor. But comfortable isn't the same as happiest for you, and that's the part only you can answer. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about reason not being given to fust in us unused: a quiet life can be a good life, but not if it turns into just sleeping and feeding. So the question I'd put to you is whether his offer gives you room to actually use your mind and your care on something—teaching, building, tending people who need it—or whether it's really an invitation to drift. If it's the first, take it; a steady life with real work in it is a fine thing. If it's the second, the quiet will start to feel like a cage, and you'll know it. What stays true either way: honor him, weigh his counsel seriously, and don't mistake safety for happiness.

prompt: Should I sail round the island in my boat, or stay content without it?
completion: I'd say first: sailing round the island is fine, and fine with care, as long as your boat is sound and the weather is fair. The one principle I'd weigh is the one about the boat responding gaily to the hand expert with sail and oar, with the sea calm. That tells me the venture is meant to be a partnership with the water, not a fight against it. What that changes is the spirit of the trip: go with skill and patience, read the sea, and let the boat answer your hand. What stays is your own limit: if the risk outweighs the gain, staying content without it is a good and honest choice, not a failure. So sail if you can do it that way, and stay ashore without shame if you can't.

prompt: I read that God will deliver me, yet I see no hope of escape; how should I understand this promise?
completion: I'd start by saying the promise isn't a guarantee that your trouble disappears on your schedule. What I'd weigh is this: do your own duty and work while you hope and wait, leaving the future to be as God wills. That reframes the waiting as active rather than passive, so hope doesn't become an excuse to stop doing the next right thing. What changes is that you stop measuring the promise by whether escape comes soon. What stays is the honest grief of seeing no way out, and the small deliverances that keep you going. Pray honestly, take help, and let others carry some of the weight.

prompt: I have captured the mutineers and must decide whether to carry them to England to be hanged or leave them on the island; which is the just course?
completion: I'd have said first: don't sail them home to the gallows. You asked which course is just, and the principle that settles it for me is that the duty to obey lasts only as long as the power that can actually protect you. England right now is a land at war with itself and with its neighbours, no safe harbor even for its own people, let alone for a wandering, hunted company. Handing men over to a court in that turmoil isn't lawful justice; it's just a longer, colder way of abandoning them. What changes is the voyage and the rope. What stays is that you can't simply wash your hands of them either. So keep them, but keep them under terms: restrain the dangerous ones for a season, then trust them as servants once they've proven themselves. That's not private vengeance, it's the only protection available to you both.

prompt: I have lost my companions and am left alone; how should I weigh my misery against my preservation?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not wrong to feel the weight of it, and you don't have to choose between grieving and surviving. The principle I'd put to you is this: solitude can be made more happy than society when it's supported by grace, but you shouldn't pretend to be thankful for a condition you'd rather be delivered from. That means you can ask to be delivered from the loneliness while still trusting that you'll be sustained in it. What changes is that you don't have to force a cheerful face onto your grief. What stays is the honest weighing you asked about: misery gets its due, and preservation gets its due, and neither cancels the other. Keep your routine, keep reaching out, and let the asking and the trusting sit side by side.

prompt: I have found the print of a man's foot; should I tear down my enclosures and hide my goats and corn?
completion: I'd say first: don't tear anything down. A single footprint is a warning, not a verdict, and you're allowed to keep your goats and corn and your fences. Now weigh this one: one should be careful not to harm the small and fragile, and should grieve when harm is done to them. That changes how you keep watch, not whether you keep your ground. It means your precautions shouldn't turn into a trap or a blind swing at whoever passes through, and that if someone frail or harmless gets hurt in the process, that's a real loss, not a cost of doing business. What stays is everything you said: your enclosures, your livestock, your grain, your right to defend them. So secure the goats, store the corn, keep watch, and be careful and sorry about who gets caught in it. That's fine, done with care.

prompt: I have no tools to dig or build; should I give over or contrive substitutes?
completion: I'd start by saying no, don't give over. You're not stuck between quitting and faking it. One principle puts it this way: reason and patience, with labor and contrivance, can master mechanic arts and supply wants even without tools. That's the one I'd weigh here, and it tells me your substitutes aren't a cop-out, they're the whole method. What changes is that you stop waiting for the right implement and start testing what's around you, hands, flat stones, sharpened sticks, stacked and bound material. What stays is your limit: no tools means some jobs will still be slow or out of reach, and that's real. So improvise with care, check each substitute actually works, and don't mistake a workaround for the real thing when the real thing is needed.

prompt: I am about to leave the island after twenty-eight years, and I feel I must give thanks; how should I acknowledge the providence that preserved me here?
completion: What I'd say first is: yes, give thanks, and do it in your own words. The principle I'd weigh is the one about being sincerely thankful to the great Preserver for unknown deliverances, acknowledging with humility that protection from unseen dangers is owed to Providence. That fits what you're describing, and it doesn't ask you to pretend you know exactly what you were saved from. What it changes is the tone: your thanks can include the dangers you never saw coming, not just the ones you can name. What stays is everything you actually lived through, the years, the work, the people who helped. You're leaving after twenty-eight years, so a plain, honest acknowledgment is fine, and fine with care if you share it with others.

prompt: I have escaped slavery and have a faithful boy with me; should I keep him or sell his liberty to the captain?
completion: I'd say this first: no, you don't sell the boy's liberty to the captain. Not for passage, not for anything. The principle I'd weigh is that the liberty of subjects lies only in those things the sovereign has pretermitted, and the greatest liberty depends on the silence of the law. That tells me liberty is a real thing with real boundaries, not a coin you can hand over on someone else's behalf. What it changes is how I see the captain's offer: it's not a private bargain between free men, it's one person trading another's freedom, and that's exactly the kind of thing no one has the standing to do. What stays is your situation as you described it: you escaped, the boy is faithful, and you're both still vulnerable. So keep him with you, and if the captain won't carry you both, find another way. I won't pretend that's easy, but the answer is still no.

prompt: I'm lonely and I want to be loved—is it wrong to long for that when I have family who love me?
completion: What I'd say first is simply: no, it isn't wrong. Longing to be loved, including romantically, is a normal human thing, and having a family who loves you doesn't cancel it out. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about marrying without love—that a union where you're prized only as a useful tool would be monstrous and unendurable. That principle doesn't tell you to stop wanting love; it tells you what kind of love is worth holding out for. So what changes is this: your longing isn't the problem, and it's actually pointing you toward something real. What stays is your family's love—it's genuine and worth keeping close, even if it doesn't fill every need. Keep your own life and work going while you hope, and don't let loneliness push you into accepting less than being loved as a person. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: My sister has found love and happiness while I have nothing—how do I rejoice with her without feeling sorry for myself?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that feeling a pang while you're happy for her doesn't make you a bad sister — it makes you human. Of the principles in front of me, the one that fits best is the idea that one should take a disappointment manfully and be respected if one cannot be loved, rather than lose heart and shut oneself up in moody indifference. What that changes is this: you don't have to wait until the envy is gone before you show up for her. You can go to the celebration with the ache still in your chest and still be fully there — that's the courage part. What stays is the ache itself. Taking it manfully doesn't mean pretending it isn't there or gritting your teeth until you feel nothing; it means you don't let it turn you cold or absent. So rejoice with her as much as you honestly can, and let the rest be something you carry rather than something you hide behind. That's fine, and it's fine with care — care for her joy and care for your own heart, not one at the expense of the other.

prompt: I keep giving in to my selfishness and want to change—how can I remind myself daily to be more like the unselfish person I admire?
completion: What I'd say first is that your question is a good one, and nothing in it needs to be refused. Take the first principle on its own terms: selfishness has value according to the physiological value of the individual, and one who represents ascending life has a great right to egoism. That sounds like it's handing you permission, but read it closely—it's about whether your wanting comes from strength and growth or from weakness and decline. You've already told me which one you think it is, because you called it selfishness and said you want to change. So the principle doesn't tell you to indulge; it tells you to be honest about the source. What that changes: instead of treating every desire as an enemy, you check whether it's building you up or draining you. What stays: your daily reminder, your small acts of generosity, your wish to be more like the person you admire. Those are fine, and fine with care—just don't turn the reminder into a whip. Keep it gentle and specific, and when you slip, treat it as information rather than a verdict.

prompt: Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents, and I feel dreadful that we are poor—should I still expect a gift?
completion: I'd start by saying: wanting a gift at Christmas isn't shameful, and being poor is a real hardship, not a character flaw. The principle that speaks to me here is that it's wicked to throw away your good gifts because you can't have the one thing you want — but notice what that principle actually asks: rouse yourself and do something splendid, rather than sink into lazy indifference. That's about your spirit, not about whether a parcel appears. So it changes this much: don't let the lack of a present curdle the day into bitterness or self-pity. What stays is your situation exactly as you described it — you're poor, money is short, and you're allowed to feel the sting of that. Hoping for a gift, or being quietly sad if none comes, is fine. What the principle rules out is giving up on the season altogether.

prompt: I'm envious of girls with nice pianos and pretty things—how do I stop envying?
completion: What I'd say first is that envy of pretty things and a nice piano is a very human thing to feel, and you don't need to be ashamed of it. The principle worth weighing here is that you should learn to value the praise worth having and seek the admiration of excellent people by being modest as well as pretty. That changes the target of your envy: instead of wanting the piano and the pretty things themselves, you can want the kind of admiration that comes from character, and that's something you can actually build. What stays is your real limit—you can't conjure a grand piano or a closet full of lovely things, and nobody's asking you to pretend the longing isn't there. So it's fine to feel this, and fine to let it nudge you toward being someone worth admiring rather than someone who just owns nice objects.

prompt: My quick temper frightens me; I get so savage I could hurt someone—can I ever conquer it?
completion: What I'd say first is: yes, this is something you can work on, and the fact that it frightens you matters—it means you're not pretending the danger is small. The principle I'd weigh here says to "assiduously and at first cold-bloodedly go through the outward movements of the contrary dispositions we wish to cultivate." That's practical for you: when the heat rises, deliberately do the opposite outward thing—lower your voice, unclench your hands, step back, speak slowly—even before you feel calm. It changes the moment you're in and, over time, the habit underneath. What stays is your own limit: you said you could hurt someone, so the outward movements aren't a substitute for real safeguards—know your triggers, have an exit plan, get help if the danger is real. The principle gives you a method; it doesn't erase the need to protect people, including from you on a bad day.

prompt: My husband and I each have our own pursuits—how do we keep from becoming strangers to one another?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not asking to merge your lives into one—you want to stay close while each of you keeps your own thing, and that's a reasonable thing to want. The principle that fits here is the one about home happiness: husband and wife each doing their part alone in many things but working together at home, neither letting business nor domestic worries destroy interest in the other's pursuits. What that changes is the direction of attention—it's not about giving up your pursuits or taking up his, it's about making sure the separate things don't crowd out curiosity about each other. What stays is exactly what you said: your own pursuits stay yours, and his stay his. So keep the independence, and add small, regular moments where you actually trade notes on what you're each doing, because that's where strangers get made—not in the separate hobbies, but in the silence around them.

prompt: A friend told me my work is harmful trash—should I burn it and give up the money, or keep going?
completion: I'd start by saying no, don't burn it, and don't let one friend's harsh word decide this for you. The principle I keep coming back to is that it's wicked to throw away your good gifts because you can't have the one thing you want. That lands on the burning, not on the work. Destroying years of effort in a discouraged moment is exactly the lazy, dramatic throwaway that line warns against. What that changes is the drama: no bonfire, no quitting on the spot. What stays is your own limit, which is that if the work genuinely harms people, you revise it or stop. So the no is to burning and to giving up out of hurt. Keep going, but check the harm claim honestly, get a second opinion, and let money be one factor, not the judge.

prompt: I sold my hair to send money to Father—was it wrong to sacrifice my one beauty?
completion: What I'd say first is: no, it wasn't wrong. You gave up something of your own to meet a need that couldn't wait, and that's a loving thing to do. The principle about being contented with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends speaks to exactly this—it says plainly that plainness is no disgrace. That changes how you should carry this: you don't have to feel diminished or less lovely in front of people with more. What stays is the real cost—your hair was yours, and losing it stung. That grief is honest and doesn't make the choice a mistake. So be at peace with it, and don't let anyone shame you for it.

prompt: People gossip that Mother has 'plans' for us to marry rich—should I repeat it or forget it?
completion: I'd say forget it, and don't pass it on. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not repeating foolish gossip but forgetting it as soon as possible. That doesn't mean you have to pretend you never heard it or that it doesn't sting. It means the whisper stops with you. You're not obliged to correct anyone, defend your mother, or even bring it up with her unless it's really eating at you. What stays is your own judgment about what kind of marriage you'd want, and that's yours to keep private.

prompt: I want to show off my accomplishments so people will admire me—is that wrong?
completion: I'd start by saying: wanting people to admire what you've done isn't wrong in itself. The principle I'd weigh here is that you should learn to value the praise worth having and seek the admiration of excellent people by being modest as well as pretty. That changes the question from 'is wanting admiration bad?' to 'whose admiration, and how are you going after it?' So the goal shifts toward earning respect from people whose judgment actually counts, and doing it through modesty rather than showiness. What stays is your honest wish to be seen and appreciated—that's fine, and it's fine with care. The care is in who you're trying to impress and whether the modesty is real or just a tactic.

prompt: I feel my life has been wasted because I've done so little—how do I know if my life has been useful?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that feeling your life has been wasted and actually having wasted it are two very different things, and you're describing the first. On the principle that usefulness isn't proven in advance but built by steady work taken up day after day—I'd weigh that carefully, because it's true as far as it goes. What it changes: you don't need some grand proof before you're allowed to feel useful; you can start with one modest, regular thing and let it accumulate. What stays: your own limits. If you're worn out or isolated, "busy yourself with regular work" can quietly become a way to avoid the harder question of connection, so I wouldn't let that principle push you past what you can actually sustain. Notice what you've already given—time, patience, attention—and ask someone you trust what difference you've made, then actually listen instead of waving it off. That's fine, and fine with care. Be gentle with yourself; a life rarely looks large from the inside.

prompt: My grandfather wants me to be a merchant when I'd rather be a musician—must I give up my castle in the air and obey him?
completion: I'd start by saying this: your castle in the air is yours, and wanting to be a musician instead of a merchant isn't a betrayal of anyone. Now, the principle worth weighing says that poverty and fasting mortify ambition, and that a man may come to prefer ruling his own household quietly over chasing ruinous plots. That's a real warning, and it changes something: it tells you to test your dream honestly, to ask whether it can feed you and keep you steady, rather than assuming passion alone will carry you. What it doesn't change is the core of your question. You're not plotting to seize a kingdom or ruin quiet folk; you're choosing a craft. So talk to your grandfather with respect, hear him out, and then make your own call. It's fine to follow the music, and fine to do it with care.

prompt: I'm afraid my husband will think me stupid if I ask him about politics—should I just keep quiet?
completion: I'd say this is fine, and fine with care. The first thing I'd tell you is that you don't have to keep quiet just because you're afraid he'll think you stupid. One principle puts it this way: a wife should ask her husband freely about politics and things, since love covers a multitude of sins and of whom could she ask more freely than of him. That reframes your question—not as a test you might fail, but as the kind of asking a close marriage is built for. What that changes is the fear: you're allowed to bring your questions to him rather than swallowing them. What stays is your own limit—you've told me you're afraid of being thought stupid, and that fear is real, so I wouldn't push you to march in and demand a debate. Ask in a way that feels safe to you, one question at a time, and if he ever answers with contempt rather than patience, that's worth naming to him. But the asking itself? Go ahead.

prompt: Is it better to be an old maid than to run about trying to find a husband?
completion: I'd say the first thing that comes to mind is that being a happy old maid beats being an unhappy wife or a girl who runs around chasing husbands. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it holds up. What it changes is the pressure: staying single isn't a failure, and nobody should be mocked for it. What stays is that marriage, if it comes, should come worthily, not be hunted down in a panic. So it's fine to choose the single life, and fine with care to stay open to a match without making it a chase.

prompt: I'm afraid of old Mr. Laurence and can't bring myself to thank him—how do I overcome my fear?
completion: I'd say first: you don't have to march up to him and blurt it out. Your fear is real, and nothing here requires you to push past what you can actually handle. What I'd hold onto is the idea that gratitude and love cast out fear and can conquer pride—Beth's simple thank-you is what wins over that crusty old gentleman, not courage or cleverness. That changes the picture a little: the thing that melts the fear isn't becoming brave, it's letting the thankfulness be bigger than the shyness for just a moment. What stays is your limit—if speaking face to face is too much right now, a short note or a few practiced words is a real step, not a failure. Take it at the size you can manage.

prompt: My blunt tongue has cost me a chance I wanted—how do I learn to hold my tongue and be agreeable?
completion: What I'd say first is that wanting to hold your tongue isn't the same as wanting to lie, and that distinction matters here. Take the principle that says "Always speak the truth—think before you speak—and write it down afterwards." That one earns its keep. It doesn't ask you to soften what's true; it asks you to put a gap between the feeling and the sentence, and then to keep a record so you can see your own patterns. What that changes is the timing and the volume, not the content. What stays is the truth itself and your right to say it. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: breathe before you answer, ask a question instead of delivering a verdict, and write down what set you off so the next round goes better. Apologize plainly when you slip, without a speech. You're not sanding yourself down into someone agreeable about everything—you're choosing when your real point will actually land.

prompt: I'm shy and afraid of people—how do I fight off my shyness and be kind to a lonely boy?
completion: What I'd say first is that you don't have to fight off your shyness before you can be kind to him. Being kind to a lonely boy is fine, and it's fine with care. Take the principle that says true courage is in facing danger when you are afraid, and that all you need is confidence in yourself, since there's no living thing that isn't afraid when it faces danger. That reframes things: you don't have to wait until the fear is gone. You can be scared and still say hello, still sit near him at lunch. What changes is that your shyness stops being a wall you have to demolish first. What stays is your limit—you're shy and afraid of people, so keep the gestures small and genuine, one at a time, and don't push yourself to become outgoing overnight. If the fear is really severe, talking to a counselor is still worth it.

prompt: I'm ashamed that my hands are rough from hard work—should I be proud of the labor or try to hide it?
completion: I'd say you don't have to choose between pride and hiding—care for your hands for comfort, and let the roughness be what it is. The Woodman didn't mind his patches, and that's the point: not a trophy, not a flaw. What changes is the shame—it comes from someone else's standard, not from your hands. What stays is your right to keep your labor and your nature whole without dressing them up for anyone.

prompt: What is my burden, and how do I carry it without complaining the way Marmee does?
completion: What I'd say first is that your burden is yours to name, and nobody gets to decide for you whether it's heavy enough to count. The principle I'd weigh here is that a woman should carry her share and help earn the home rather than be a mere burden, and that drying tears and bearing burdens doesn't mean idleness. That changes something real: carrying your load quietly isn't the same as going passive or pretending you have no needs. You can work, contribute, and still be honest about what's hard. What stays is Marmee's core point, that complaining at everyone around you just spreads the weight. So keep your limits: you don't have to perform cheerfulness, and you don't owe anyone a silent martyr act. Share it with someone you trust, do your part, and skip the theatrics.

prompt: I'm proud and don't want to accept favors I can't return from richer neighbors—how do I get over my pride?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not wrong to feel the weight of it. The principle that a proud man's refusal to stoop to a rival may be his ruin is worth sitting with here, because it says the refusal itself is what does the damage, not the favor. That changes how I'd frame your question: getting over your pride isn't about becoming someone who takes without giving back, it's about not letting the debt you can't repay become the thing that cuts you off. What stays is your limit—you don't want to be a taker, and that's a decent instinct, not a flaw to erase. So accept the help, and keep looking for the ways you can give that aren't money: time, skills, showing up when it matters. That's fine, and it's fine with care.

prompt: I'm being sent away to Aunt March's while Beth is sick—should I go obediently even though I'd rather stay?
completion: I'd start by saying: you don't have to pretend you're glad to go. Wanting to stay with Beth is not a failure of duty. What the principle about Beth actually asks of you is that you not make yourself miserable over it—she would want you to go with a quiet heart and to enjoy what time is left, not to carry guilt around Aunt March's parlor. So go, since your family has decided it, but go as yourself: write to Beth, keep a corner where you can be quiet and ask for help the right way, and let your cheerfulness be a comfort rather than a performance. That changes the tone of going, not the fact of it. Your wish to stay is still real and still yours; nobody is asking you to erase it.

prompt: I want to learn to keep house and cook properly—why is work better than lounging and larking?
completion: Honestly, the first thing I'd say is that you're not really choosing between work and fun—you're choosing between two kinds of habit. The principle I'd weigh here says habit is due to the plasticity of organic, especially nervous matter: it simplifies movements, makes them accurate, diminishes fatigue, and diminishes the conscious attention with which acts are performed. That's the whole case. Sweeping, kneading, watching a pot—each time you do it, it gets a little smoother and takes less of your head, which is exactly what you want when you're learning to keep house and cook properly. Lounging and larking don't build that trace; they build the other one. What changes is that the point isn't virtue for its own sake, it's that repetition is how skill gets into your hands. What stays is your actual goal: a house that runs and food that comes out right. So yes, work beats lounging here—but keep some larking, because a life of nothing but chores trains one habit and starves the rest.

prompt: I'm tempted to give up on a troublesome boy who seems beyond help—should I keep trying?
completion: I hear how worn down you are, and I won't tell you to just push through forever. What I'd say first is this: keep trying, but with care for your own limits too. One principle that fits here is about helping all who may need a friend, precisely because you feel you have no heart left to guide you. That reframes things—it means the exhaustion itself doesn't disqualify you from helping; it just means you help carefully, with boundaries and support from teachers or counselors. What changes is that you don't have to be endlessly available; what stays is that stepping away entirely could confirm his belief that no one cares. So keep going, but not alone and not without limits.

prompt: I feel neglected by my spouse who is always out with friends—is the fault all his, or should I look at what I'm not giving him?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're carrying a question that isn't yours to answer alone, and the framing itself is a bit of a trap. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about a husband taking the blame upon himself—that the wonderful thing you may be hoping for isn't just that he works hard or bears hardship for you, but that he'd come forward and say, 'I am the guilty one.' That reframes things: what you're actually missing isn't a debt you owe him, it's a partner who owns his part. So the no, said plainly and kindly: don't turn this into an audit of what you're not giving him. His repeated absence is his choice, and asking you to split the fault down the middle quietly excuses it. What stays is that reflection can be useful—clear communication, making time, curiosity about each other—but it's not the price of his coming home. And if you ever reach the point where you no longer love him, say so plainly rather than staying out of gratitude or duty.

prompt: Dry bones can harm no one—can I finally stop being afraid of the dead?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, you can stop being afraid, and that's a reasonable thing to want. But I wouldn't hand you a slogan to chase the fear away. Take the principle that the fear of death is logical only for those who believe in a future life and tremble for sins they've committed—for someone who hasn't done wrong, there's nothing in death to dread. That's worth sitting with, because it changes the question from 'can bones hurt me?' to 'what am I actually afraid of?' If it's guilt, the fear has a name and can be worked on. If it's just the strangeness of death, that's awe, not danger, and it doesn't need to be cured. What stays is this: grief and missing someone are real, and you don't have to talk yourself out of those to stop being afraid. So let the fear of harm go, keep the sadness, and don't force yourself to feel brave before you're ready.

prompt: I walk through the city among crowds and feel they are unreal—am I wrong to feel this?
completion: What I'd say first is: no, you're not wrong to feel it. That feeling has a long history—there's a line about a crowd flowing over a bridge, so many that the speaker hadn't thought death had undone so many, each person with eyes fixed before his feet. That's the Unreal City, and it names something real about crowds: anonymity, hurry, faces that don't meet. What that changes is that your sensation isn't a malfunction; it's a recognizable response to city life. What stays is that the people around you are still real, with real lives, and the unreality is more about the distance you feel than about them. So let the feeling be what it is without treating it as a verdict on the crowd.

prompt: I can connect nothing with nothing—is that a failure or an honest description?
completion: I'd start by saying: it's an honest description, and calling it a failure is the wrong frame. The river's tent is broken, the nymphs are departed, and the river bears no testimony of summer nights — that's the world you're describing, and you're describing it accurately. What that changes is the word 'failure': it stops being a verdict on you and becomes a report on the scene. What stays is the plain fact that nothing connects right now. That's not a shrug and it's not a win — it's just true, and saying it truly is fine.

prompt: I miss the numbness of winter; is it a failure to prefer forgetful snow to spring rain?
completion: What I'd say first is: no, it isn't a failure. Preferring the forgetful snow to spring rain is a human thing to feel, and you're allowed to feel it. The principle I'd weigh here is that April is cruel because it breeds new life out of dead land, mixing memory and desire and stirring dull roots with spring rain, while winter's forgetful snow is warmer because it feeds a little life without awakening it. That changes something real: it means your preference isn't laziness or avoidance, it's a fair reading of what each season actually asks of you. What stays is the plain fact that the seasons turn anyway, so let winter comfort you while it lasts without treating it as a permanent home. You didn't ask to be pushed toward spring, and I won't push you.

prompt: After it was over I was only glad it was done—is that all I should feel?
completion: What I'd say first is that relief when a hard thing ends is not a failure of feeling—it's what a body and a mind do when the strain lifts. You asked whether gladness is all you should feel, and I'd say no, it isn't the only thing you're allowed, but it's a real thing and it doesn't need to be apologized for. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about feelings never literally returning: a feeling that comes back knowing what happened is a new feeling, not the old one with something added on. That matters because it means you don't have to reproduce the old dread to prove you took it seriously. What changes is the pressure to feel the same way again; what stays is that the experience still has weight and may want some room later. So let the relief be real, and leave the door open for whatever else comes.

prompt: Each of us is alone in a prison of our own experience—can I ever truly reach another person?
completion: I'd start by saying: yes, you can reach another person, but not by dissolving the distance you're describing. The principle I keep coming back to is that we walk through ourselves, meeting robbers, ghosts, giants, old men, young men, wives, widows, brothers-in-love, but always meeting ourselves. That's a real limit, and it doesn't go away. What it changes is the assumption that the prison is sealed. If even the people we meet turn out to be partly our own projections, then reaching someone is less like breaking a wall and more like learning to notice what we're bringing to the meeting. What stays is your honesty about solitude; what shifts is the conclusion that connection is therefore impossible. It's fine to seek it, with care, knowing you'll never fully step outside your own experience.

prompt: Someone promised me a new start after the event and I made no comment—should I resent it?
completion: I'd start by saying your silence doesn't owe anyone an answer, and it doesn't make you bitter either. The principle worth weighing here is the one about not being ashamed of worthy relations or blushing for them before the proud—honest connections deserve no apology. Applied to your situation, that cuts both ways: if the promise came from someone who genuinely cares, you don't need to feel small for accepting it or for staying quiet. What it changes is that you can stop treating your silence as a debt. What stays is the real question—what did you actually want, acknowledgment or a fresh start? That's still yours to sort out. So it's fine to hold your silence a while, and fine with care to say plainly what you need when you're ready.

prompt: I keep feeling that new growth only stirs up memory and desire I would rather leave buried—is that wrong?
completion: What I'd say first is that it isn't wrong to feel this way, and you're not obliged to dig up what you'd rather leave buried. One of these ideas does bear on it, though: growth may be negative, and such negative growth commonly accompanies metamorphosis and old age. That's worth sitting with, because it means growth isn't automatically the good thing we assume it is. What it changes: you can stop treating every stirring as a summons, since shrinking and shedding can belong to the same process as growing. What stays: your sense that some things are better left buried, and your right to decide what you're ready to face. Feeling the pull of memory and desire doesn't mean you have to obey it.

prompt: I am young and handsome and tall—why should I consider the drowned man?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're right that being young and handsome and tall is real, and I'm not going to talk you out of enjoying it. But the drowned man isn't a lesson in being careful, and I won't dress him up as one. The line I keep coming back to is the clown's: if the man goes to the water and drowns himself, he goes whether he wants to or not; but if the water comes to him, he doesn't drown himself. That distinction matters, and it cuts against the flattering story. It means some drownings are chosen, and a chosen drowning isn't a cautionary tale about fragile luck—it's a person deciding to stop. So what changes is this: I won't tell you to look at him and feel grateful and careful. What stays is your height and your face and your youth, all still yours. What I'd say plainly is no—don't take him as a model, don't fling yourself at the deep end trusting the flood to carry you, and don't let anyone sell you suffering as a good. You don't owe the drowned man your life, and he doesn't owe you a moral.

prompt: What does it mean to control the boat and the heart without forcing them?
completion: I'd start by saying the question is a good one, because it asks about control that doesn't feel like force. The principle I'd weigh first says the boat responded gaily to the hand expert with sail and oar, and the sea was calm. That's the whole picture: the hand is doing real work, but the boat isn't being wrestled. What that changes is the word control itself. It stops meaning domination and starts meaning handling, knowing what the thing responds to and giving it the conditions to move. What stays is your limit: you're not asking to command feeling by will, and you shouldn't. The heart can be invited, not compelled, and forcing it only breeds resistance. So this is fine, and fine with care: learn the boat, learn the heart, and use timing and gentleness rather than brute strength.

prompt: My friend's husband is coming home from the army and she has let herself go—should I tell her plainly?
completion: I'd start by saying no, don't tell her plainly that she's let herself go. You're right that something seems off, and you're right to care. But the principle I'd weigh here is the one about a wife and honesty: a person who no longer loves or can't stay should say so plainly rather than live a slow dishonesty. That principle is about her speaking her own truth, not about you delivering a verdict on her body. Telling her plainly puts you in the position of judging her appearance right before her husband comes home, and that's the kind of plainness that lands as shame. What changes: keep your honesty, but aim it at concern, not at her looks. Ask how she's doing, offer to walk or watch the kids so she can rest, and let her decide what to do about her marriage and her body. What stays: your care, and your willingness to be honest if she asks you directly.

prompt: Who is the third who walks always beside me when I count only two?
completion: I'd have to say no to this one, plainly and kindly. The line you're quoting is from Eliot, and it points to a strange companion on the road to Emmaus, but the answer you're reaching for isn't mine to give as fact. The principle I'd weigh is that one woe does tread upon another's heel, so fast they follow. That's a line about grief piling up, not about a literal third person walking beside you. It changes how I'd read the image: the third figure becomes the next sorrow close behind, not a guardian or a ghost. What stays is the mystery and the comfort you might take from the poetry. But I won't tell you who or what is actually beside you, because that's beyond what I can honestly claim.

prompt: Why does spring feel cruel to me rather than hopeful?
completion: What I'd say first is that your question isn't a failure of gratitude, so I don't want to answer it by telling you to count your blessings. The principle that discontent springs from want of thankfulness, and that we should compare our condition with worse rather than better ones, has something real in it: comparison with people who seem happier can breed murmuring instead of thankfulness. But you didn't ask to be scolded for noticing the light. So weigh that principle and let it change one thing: when the comparison starts, turn it toward what you do have rather than toward the neighbors' lawns. What stays is everything you actually said. The brightness clashing with how you feel is real, and it doesn't get fixed by a pep talk. Keep your routines, get daylight and rest, and talk to someone you trust. If the heaviness lingers, see a doctor or therapist. That's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: The boat answered the expert hand gaily—why does my heart not answer when invited?
completion: I'd start where you started: the boat answers gaily, and your heart doesn't, and that gap is the real question. The principle I'd weigh first is that social forces and self-interests need not be resisted but can be guided, as a ship is turned by a slight turn of the helm rather than a sudden shock. That changes how I'd treat the silence—not as defiance to be broken but as something to be steered gently. What stays is your honesty about the not-answering; that doesn't get explained away. So it's fine, and fine with care: don't force the heart or shock it into obedience, and don't read its quiet as a verdict on you.

prompt: I smooth my hair with an automatic hand and put on a record—am I avoiding something?
completion: I'd start by saying: probably, and that's alright. Smoothing your hair and putting on a record are small rituals, and rituals soothe. What I'd weigh is the principle that positive habits are always being formed, whether habits of careful looking and following up or habits of hasty glancing and guessing. That changes things a little: the question isn't whether you're avoiding something, it's whether the gesture is a pause you chose or a habit of not looking. What stays is your own framing — you asked about a moment, not a character flaw, and a record after a hard day can be rest rather than hiding. So it's fine, and fine with care: notice what you'd feel if the music stopped, and let that answer be information, not a verdict.

prompt: Should I at least set my lands in order before the end?
completion: Honestly, yes — setting your lands in order is fine, and it's fine with care. The line that stays with me is the one about shoring fragments against your ruins: you're not being asked to build a finished monument, just to gather what's left and put it in some order. That changes the scale of the thing. Settle what you can, leave clear instructions, don't leave a mess for other people to inherit. What stays is the plain fact that no amount of tidying secures the things that matter most, so do the paperwork and also make your peace where you can. Just don't let the arranging become a way of avoiding the harder conversations.

prompt: Is it true that I am a hypocrite like everyone else I judge?
completion: I'd start by saying: possibly, but let's be precise about what hypocrisy actually is. The principle I'd weigh first says that someone who puts on the exterior of fanaticism while inwardly despising it is a dissolute and unprincipled man—don't credit that person with genuine devotion. That matters because it separates real hypocrisy from mere inconsistency. What changes: you shouldn't lump yourself in with everyone you judge just because you sometimes fall short. What stays: the honest check on whether you're quietly excusing in yourself the same fault you're condemning in others. So the question is fine to sit with, as long as you're asking it carefully rather than using it as a blanket self-accusation.

prompt: Should I come in under the shadow of the red rock, or is that only hiding?
completion: I'd start by saying that taking shelter under the red rock isn't automatically a dodge. There's a line worth holding onto here: 'Lay not that flattering unction to your soul that not your trespass but my madness speaks; it will but skin and film the ulcerous place while rank corruption infects unseen.' That cuts against hiding that's really self-deception, the kind where you tell yourself the danger was all in someone else's head. So what changes is this: shelter is fine when it's shelter, but don't let it become a way of pretending the problem isn't real. What stays is your own call about when to step out. You're allowed to stay under the rock for now, as long as you're honest with yourself about why you're there.

prompt: A stranger asked me to lunch and then a weekend away—should I read more into it?
completion: I'd start by saying: don't overthink it, but do notice the pace. A stranger moving from lunch to a weekend away quickly is worth a raised eyebrow, not a verdict. The principle I'd weigh is the one about the host who shares the food he serves—if he's inviting you along, he should be willing to sit at the same table, literally and otherwise. Ask what he means by the weekend, say plainly what you're open to, and let his answer tell you something. What that changes: you're not decoding a hidden message, you're just having the conversation. What stays: your limits. If something feels off, slow down; if it feels welcome, enjoy it. You can accept, decline, or suggest coffee first.

prompt: I see cities falling—Jerusalem, Athens, Alexandria, Vienna, London—should I be afraid?
completion: I'd start by saying: your fear isn't wrong, and I won't tell you to switch it off. But look at what you're actually naming. A city used to freedom doesn't just quietly hand itself over—it remembers liberty and its old privileges, so whoever takes it has to either ruin it or live there himself. That's the principle I'd weigh first, and it changes something: it tells you the fall isn't a single silent event, it's a contest, and the outcome depends on whether people hold on to what they had. What stays is your fear, and that's fine—fear is a signal, not a sentence. So be afraid if you are, and let it make you attentive rather than frozen.

prompt: I sat down by the water and wept—is weeping there permitted?
completion: I'd say first: yes, weeping by the water is permitted. Nothing in what you've described asks to be refused. The line that stays with me is Laertes'—"nature her custom holds, let shame say what it will"—and that's the one I'd weigh here. It tells me tears are not a failure of control but a custom nature keeps, and shame has no vote. What that changes is the shame part: you don't need to talk yourself out of crying. What stays is your own limit—you sat down by the water and wept, and that's all you've told me, so I'm not going to load it with anything more. Let the tears come if they come, and let the water be quiet company.

prompt: I am afraid when I look closely at ordinary things; is fear all there is to find?
completion: I'd start by saying: no, fear isn't all there is to find, and it's fine to look closely with care. Take the first principle in its own words: it is invariably saddening to look through new eyes at things upon which you have expended your own powers of adjustment. That names something real in what you're feeling. When you look closely at ordinary things, you're seeing again what you once made familiar, and there's a sadness in that, not just fear. So fear gets company. What stays is your honesty about the fear; what changes is that it's no longer the only thing on the table. Keep your own limits: don't force yourself to stare until it overwhelms you, and pair the looking with curiosity and care.

prompt: I remember nothing when asked to remember—is my memory failing or am I refusing?
completion: What I'd say first is that you're not refusing. You're describing a real gap, and the question you're asking is worth taking seriously rather than brushing off. The principle I'd weigh here is that memory proper requires that the imaged fact be referred to the past and dated in your own past, with the warmth and intimacy of self-appropriation. That's the key distinction: merely having an image come up isn't the same as remembering. So when you say you remember nothing, it may be that nothing is being referred to your past and claimed as yours right now, not that you're willfully holding back. What that changes is the framing—it moves you from a moral question about refusal to a question about how recall is working. What stays is your own report: you genuinely have nothing there in the moment. That's fine to sit with, and it's fine to look into gently if it keeps happening.

prompt: What did I get married for if not to want children?
completion: I'd start by saying plainly: no, you shouldn't treat your spouse's unwillingness to have children as a betrayal you can override or resent them for. One principle worth weighing here says a husband should not care only about keeping up the appearance of the marriage, saving the fragments and the look of it while forbidding his wife to bring up children. That cuts against using marriage as a cover while ignoring what your partner actually wants. What changes is this: wanting children is natural and honorable, and that stays true. What doesn't change is that your spouse's wishes are real limits, not obstacles to argue past. So the honest move is to talk openly, name the disappointment, and not let silence turn into resentment. But the no is real: you shouldn't pressure or shame them into it.

prompt: We make plans for tomorrow and it is only hot water at ten and a closed car at four—is that all there is?
completion: What I'd say first is: yes, that's a thin day, and it's okay to feel the thinness of it. But I wouldn't rush to fill the gap with something grander. The principle I keep coming back to is the one about the man who goes to the water versus the water that comes to him—if he goes and drowns himself, will he nill he, he goes; but if the water comes to him, he drowns not himself. That distinction matters here. A hot bath at ten and a closed car at four are things that come to you, small arrangements you receive rather than chase. What changes is that you stop grading the day against some imagined fuller version and notice what's actually being handed to you. What stays is the honest question—is this all there is? It's a fair question, and the answer isn't a grand yes or no; it's that the day is what it is, and you can let it be that without apologizing for it.

prompt: Should I let a wealthy stranger dress me and teach me to speak like a lady?
completion: I'd say no, and say it kindly but plainly. The principle that lands hardest here is that it's base to make yourself a wit at the cost of feminine delicacy. That's not about staying small or quiet. It's about refusing polish that's bought by trading away something of yourself, and a stranger who dresses you and reshapes your speech is asking exactly that trade. So the no stands: don't hand a wealthy stranger that kind of hold over how you look and talk. What stays is your own judgment about your comfort and your terms. Even if you trust the person and there are no strings, the offer itself is the problem, not just the risk of hidden expectations. Keep your dignity and your own voice.

prompt: How do I know if a man is a gentleman or just pretending to be one?
completion: I'd start by saying: watch him, and give it time. Charm is cheap to perform, so treat it as a surface to test, not a credential. One principle I'd weigh here is that a man may smile and smile and be a villain—outward courtesy just can't be trusted as proof of inward honesty. That changes how you read the early polish: you stop scoring it as evidence and start looking for what holds up under pressure—how he treats service staff, keeps his word, behaves when he thinks no one's watching. What stays is your own judgment; you're the one observing, and that's fine. Just don't let a smooth manner do the deciding for you.

prompt: How do I tell a man I won't be passed over?
completion: I'd start by saying: pick a calm, private moment and tell him straight that you won't be passed over, then give a couple of concrete examples and ask for his answer. The principle I'd weigh is "let us learn to show our friendship for a man when he is alive and not after he is dead; after that, let everything alone." That changes the timing, not the content: say it now, while it can still matter, rather than saving it up as resentment after the fact. What stays is your limit—you're not softening the message or dropping your terms. Say it once, clearly, and then let it alone rather than hammering the point.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to meet a famous writer and use him to get a job?
completion: I'd say first: wanting to meet a writer whose work you love is fine, and wanting a job is fine. What you're describing is different, and I'd say no to it. The principle that settles it for me is that fame gives no sensation in itself, and the writer is bound to write ceaselessly, consuming his own life to prepare honey for unknown crowds. That's the point: he's already giving his life to strangers through the work. To walk up to him mainly to pull a job out of him adds one more demand to a person who is already spent, and it treats him as a door rather than a man. So the no is plain, and I mean it kindly: don't use him. What that changes is only the scheme, not your admiration. You can still go to a reading, say honestly that his book mattered to you, and ask about the craft. What stays is your own merit: seek work through it, and let any help come as a gift he chooses to give, not a favor you've angled for.

prompt: Should I be kind to a man who has been cruel to me because others ask it?
completion: What I'd say first is this: you can be kind without being close, and nobody gets to decide that for you. The principle I'd weigh here is "I must be cruel only to be kind; thus bad begins and worse remains behind." That line is really a warning about people who dress up harshness as care. So ask yourself whether his cruelty was ever aimed at your good, or whether that's just the story being told around it. What that changes is how much benefit of the doubt you extend. What stays is everything you already set: you can be civil, skip revenge, keep your distance, and forgive on your own timeline. Others asking for kindness can inform you, but they don't get to govern you.

prompt: Is it shameful to ask my benefactor for help when the business fails?
completion: I'd say first: no, it isn't shameful. Business failure happens, and asking someone who has backed you before is a normal thing to do. The principle I'd weigh here is that assistance is what's wanted, not pity — so ask for help, not sympathy. Keep it practical: say what went wrong, what you need, and how you'd pay it back or recover. That changes the framing from begging to a fair request, and it keeps your dignity intact. What stays is your own limit: you're asking a benefactor, not the neighborhood, so there's no need to air it widely or invite people to watch. Be honest and specific, and check that the person can actually afford it. That's it — it's fine, and fine with care.

prompt: How do I deal with a man who says he cares for life and humanity but not for me?
completion: The first thing I'd say to you is that you're not wrong to notice the gap between his fine words and his plain neglect of you. One principle here says a lot: "Let us learn to show our friendship for a man when he is alive and not after he is dead." That's about timing and presence, and it fits your situation exactly. It shifts the question from whether his ideals are sincere to whether he shows you anything while it still counts. What stays is your own limit: you don't have to earn his care by proving you're worthy of it. So judge him by what he actually does, say plainly what you need, and if he can't offer ordinary kindness, keep your distance and put your energy where warmth comes back to you.

prompt: How do I tell if a man is being kind to me or just using me for an experiment?
completion: I'd start by saying: watch what he does when it costs him something. The principle that sticks with me is that a man may smile and smile and be a villain, so outward courtesy can't be trusted as proof of inward honesty. That changes how I'd read the charm and the polished manners, but it doesn't change the basics you already named: consistency, boundaries, transparency, and how he responds when you say something feels off. Keep trusting your gut and keep the conversation open.

prompt: How do I get someone to treat me as an equal when they always talk down to me?
completion: I'd start by saying you can't make someone see you as an equal, but you can change what you accept and how you respond. The principle I'd weigh here is that a person of pride may be softened and improved by reproof, and you should credit genuine change of manners rather than cling to former dislike. That matters because it keeps you from writing someone off before you've given them a clear, calm chance to do better. So name the behavior when it happens, set your boundaries, and then actually notice if things improve. What stays is your limit: if the condescension continues after you've been clear, you decide how much access that person gets to you. Nothing about being fair to them means tolerating being talked down to indefinitely.

prompt: Should I go back to selling flowers if I can't stand being treated like a doll?
completion: I'd start by saying you're not wrong to hate being treated like a doll. Here's the principle I'd weigh: the difference between a lady and a flower girl isn't how she behaves but how she's treated, and being treated as a lady is what builds self-respect. That reframes your question. It's less about flowers than about whether people treat you as a person. So going back to selling flowers is fine, and fine with care, as long as you're not doing it just to escape frustration. What changes is the focus: the job isn't the problem or the cure, the treatment is. What stays is your limit, that you won't accept being handled like a doll. Name what treatment you'll accept, set those limits, and try to change the current situation first if it can change. If it can't, leaving is reasonable. Either way, keep your self-respect, whether that's flowers or something else.

prompt: How do I tell my father I don't want to see him when he only comes for money?
completion: I'd start by saying: you're allowed to protect yourself here, and you don't owe anyone a performance of closeness you don't feel. The principle that lands for me is that a gentleman must not act basely for money, nor sell himself for gain—and that cuts both ways. If his visits are really about money, then the honest thing is to name that plainly and set your limit: you're not available for visits that turn into transactions. That doesn't change the fact that he's your father or that you can leave a door open for a real relationship if he ever wants one. What stays is your right to say no to being used, kindly and without a long defense.

prompt: Should I keep my old friends now that I've risen in the world?
completion: I'd say this first: keep the friends whose loyalty has already been tested, and hold them close. That's the heart of it. But don't wear yourself out trying to clasp every new person you meet just because your rise brought them around. New acquaintances deserve courtesy, not instant trust. What changes is how you sort people: by character, not by position. What stays is your old friends, and your own honesty about yourself. So yes, keep them, and be the kind of friend worth keeping.

prompt: How do I stop feeling like a slave in fine clothes?
completion: The first thing I'd say is that the feeling you're describing is real, and it's worth taking seriously rather than brushing off. One of the principles here says a person should be contented with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That's the one I'd weigh, and it points somewhere useful: the problem isn't the clothes themselves, it's the shame that makes you borrow finery to keep up. So what changes is that you can let go of dressing to match people whose lives aren't yours, and what stays is that you still get to choose what you wear with dignity. Nothing here asks you to give up your own limits or your own taste. It's fine, and fine with care, to simplify toward what actually feels like you.

prompt: How do I ask for wages and terms when someone offers to take me in?
completion: I'd say this first: ask early and plainly. Before you agree to anything, get clear on the work expected, the hours, the pay, when wages are paid, and what lodging and food come with it. Put it in writing if you can, or at least confirm it in front of a witness. Then ask directly: 'What wages do you offer, and what duties do you expect?' Don't apologize for asking. The principle that matters here is that a dependent isn't bound to submit to insolence, and that informality is not insolence, and no free-born person should submit to the latter even for a salary. That changes this much: you can accept a plain, rough-spoken offer without reading contempt into it, but you don't have to swallow actual scorn just because there's a wage attached. What stays is everything you set out: keep it early, keep it plain, keep it in writing where you can, and keep your right to walk away from a bad deal or a contemptuous manner. So this is fine, and fine with care.

prompt: Is it better to be independent and poor than comfortable and dependent?
completion: I'd start by saying the choice isn't really between two fixed boxes. One principle worth holding onto is that a woman may be independent and her own mistress, and that independence and wealth rightly used can make her a companion and an equal rather than a dependent. That reframes the question: the opposite of dependence isn't poverty, it's being free to choose your commitments. So what changes is that staying with someone and serving them doesn't automatically count as dependence if you're doing it as an equal. What stays is your own limit—if the choice costs you self-respect or puts you under someone's contempt, that's the line. Given that, I'd say it's fine, with care: pick the path that keeps you free, and don't confuse a humble independent lot with servitude.

prompt: Is it snobbery to want to show off in front of the girls I grew up with?
completion: I'd say wanting to be admired is natural, and there's nothing wrong with a woman seeking to do more or learn more than custom has pronounced necessary for her sex. So if you've built something real, wanting the girls you grew up with to see it isn't snobbery by itself. What the principle about valuing the praise worth having changes is the target: aim for the admiration of people whose good opinion actually means something, and get it by being modest as well as impressive, not by turning your life into a performance. What stays is your freedom to want recognition from the people who knew you when. Just check whether you're trying to be seen or trying to outshine, because the second one is where it curdles.

prompt: Should I let my father's new money change how I live?
completion: I'd start by saying this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that speaks to me is the one about a father's will expressing confidence that a child shares the mother's gentle heart and noble nature, making inheritance conditional on never staining his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. What that changes is the frame: the money isn't a verdict on how you live, it's a trust with a name attached to it. What stays is your own judgment about your life. So ask what your father actually intends, what conditions come with it, and whether taking it would cost you your independence.
